**Request trailers.** `x-geo-country` and its underscore spellings (`x_geo_country`, `x_geo-country`, `x-geo_country`) are removed from client request trailers on every protocol path, with the same folded match the initial header block uses, so a trailing block cannot restate a country a CGI-style backend would fold onto the gateway's assertion.

**Loading.** The `.mmdb` file is read into an owned immutable byte buffer at plugin startup, with metadata and bounded-read checks rejecting files larger than 512 MiB before parsing. Non-regular paths (including FIFOs and devices) are rejected by path metadata before open; Unix also opens non-blocking so a regular path raced to a special file cannot wedge startup or reload, then verifies the opened handle's type and identity.

**Memory budget.** One validation generation and its cache-build load session share a fixed 512 MiB aggregate budget across the declared sizes of all distinct MMDB paths. Ferrum first streams a SHA-256 digest through a fixed-size buffer, allowing identical content to reuse a live snapshot without allocating a duplicate. Changed content must reserve the candidate size against all live and concurrently in-flight snapshots before allocating its owned buffer; a reload that would exceed the 512 MiB peak fails closed before that allocation. Because a changed candidate overlaps the live snapshot until atomic publication, any replacement whose live plus candidate sizes exceed 512 MiB cannot be hot-replaced: install the replacement and restart the gateway so it loads without the outgoing snapshot. This restart-required constraint commonly applies to same-sized databases larger than 256 MiB; unchanged content reuses the live digest snapshot and does not incur the overlap. The resulting plugin-cache generation independently enforces the same limit across all distinct snapshots it retains, including geo instances preserved from the preceding generation during an incremental update.

**Verification.** Ferrum fully verifies the search tree and data section, checks for a supported country-capable product (`GeoIP2`/`GeoLite2` Country or City, or GeoIP2 Enterprise), and scans every country record against the same supported-code set used by policy admission before publishing the plugin.

**Reload handoff.** Generic plugin validation checks policy structure without opening node-local files; the mode-aware dependency stage deduplicates identical content by its verified digest and owns every successful snapshot or classified load failure as part of that configuration generation. Async file, database, MongoDB, and DP full or incremental reload paths perform the synchronous digest, verification, and record scan on Tokio's blocking pool rather than a runtime worker. A successful generation hands its snapshots, failures, and aggregate accounting to a build-scoped load session, which shares one verified snapshot or prior failure among every geo instance using the path; rejected generations release their handoffs, and a newly accepted generation supersedes any older unclaimed generation. Claiming an accepted handoff refreshes the relevant geo plugin instances and atomically republishes the request epoch even when only file contents changed and the serialized config has no delta; unrelated stateful plugin instances remain shared with the prior cache.

**Content identity on reload.** Every reload candidate is bounded-read and SHA-256 digested because portable filesystem metadata cannot prove content identity. After both the identity pass and owned-buffer read, Ferrum re-stats the configured path and rejects a target change; Unix compares device/inode plus size and timestamps, while other platforms additionally re-open and stream the path digest without retaining another snapshot buffer. Identical bytes reuse a live content-addressed snapshot without another verification or record scan, while the accepted validation handoff avoids a second construction-time read entirely. Consequently, an atomic rename during a reload or a same-length, timestamp-preserving replacement cannot leave the new generation serving stale bytes. Existing live plugin generations keep their immutable snapshot while a restart or eligible config reload validates and publishes the replacement.

**Failure handling.** A readable oversized, aggregate-over-budget, corrupt, incompatible, wrong-product, or unsupported-code database is rejected; only an initially absent or unreadable node-local file degrades to `on_lookup_failure` in modes that permit that fallback.

Aggregate admission identifies snapshots by the SHA-256 digest computed from the already-opened, identity-checked file. It does not canonicalize path strings, so symlink resolution cannot introduce a new path-based TOCTOU window; different spellings of identical content consume one snapshot charge.

Database full loads carry an explicit purpose. Runtime loads validate node-local plugin files and hand snapshots to the immediately following plugin-cache build; CP distribution and backup-export loads skip node-local files entirely because neither consumer constructs proxy plugins. Every accepted DP full snapshot explicitly refreshes each configured node-local MMDB under the same aggregate budget even though CP file validation was skipped, including snapshots with no serialized config delta.

**CP/DP deployment note:** In control plane / data plane deployments, the `.mmdb` file only needs to exist on the **data plane** nodes where proxy traffic is handled. The control plane accepts `geo_restriction` plugin configs via the admin API without requiring the file locally. If the `.mmdb` file is missing on a data plane node at startup, the plugin degrades gracefully — all GeoIP lookups fall back to the `on_lookup_failure` policy (default: `allow`) until the file is deployed and the config is reloaded. Other proxies and plugins are unaffected.

A node that has **already loaded a valid snapshot** is treated differently from that first-load case. Because the control plane deliberately skips node-local file validation, a DP full snapshot forces a node-local refresh, and a file that is only *temporarily* unreadable at that moment (an in-progress database swap, a transient mount or permission fault) would otherwise downgrade an actively enforcing geo gate to its `on_lookup_failure` fallback. Instead the refresh retains the last known good snapshot for that `db_path` and logs a warning naming the path, the load error, and the retained snapshot size. Retention is keyed on `db_path`, and the plugin instance is always rebuilt from the **incoming** configuration: a concurrent change to `allow_countries`, `deny_countries`, `inject_headers`, or `on_lookup_failure` takes effect immediately over the retained data, and a configuration that repoints `db_path` never inherits the previous file's snapshot — it follows the ordinary first-load fallback for the new path. A readable but corrupt, wrong-product, or over-budget file still rejects the new plugin generation and is never retained around.

**Behavior by mode:**

| Mode | MMDB dependency behavior at startup/reload |
|------|--------------------------------------------|
| **File** | An absent, unreadable, or invalid file is fatal — the gateway refuses to publish the config. |
| **Database** | Warning logged for an absent/unreadable file; plugin degrades to `on_lookup_failure`. Readable invalid files are rejected during plugin construction. |
| **Control Plane** | Strict plugin structure is validated, but the CP does not open the node-local path because it does not proxy traffic. |
| **Data Plane** | Warning logged for an absent/unreadable node-local file and the plugin degrades to `on_lookup_failure`; a readable invalid file rejects the new plugin generation. On a forced node-local refresh, an instance that already holds a valid snapshot for the same `db_path` retains it instead of degrading, while still applying the incoming geo policy. |

> **Note:** Ferrum Edge does not ship or bundle any GeoIP database. Operators are responsible for obtaining a MaxMind GeoIP2 or GeoLite2 `.mmdb` file, accepting MaxMind's license terms, and managing updates. GeoLite2 (free) requires a [MaxMind account](https://www.maxmind.com/en/geolite2/signup) and is subject to the [GeoLite2 EULA](https://www.maxmind.com/en/geolite2/eula). MaxMind publishes weekly database updates.

```yaml
plugin_name: geo_restriction
config:
  db_path: /etc/ferrum/GeoLite2-Country.mmdb
  allow_countries: [US, CA, GB, DE, FR]
  inject_headers: true
```

### `rate_limiting`

**Priority:** 2900 · **Phases:** on_request_received (IP mode), authorize (consumer mode), `before_proxy`, `after_proxy`, `apply_websocket_handshake_response_headers`, `on_stream_connect` · **Protocols:** HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, TCP, UDP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Enforces request rate limits per time window. Supports limiting by client IP, authenticated consumer identity, peer SPIFFE identity, or one aggregate budget per policy shared by every caller (`limit_by: service`).

Configure one or more rules in `limits`. Exactly one rule must use `scope: default`; it applies to every IP/SPIFFE key, every consumer without a specific rule, and the IP fallback when `limit_by: consumer` has no identity. Additional `scope: consumers` rules are only valid with `limit_by: consumer`; each rule can name one or many consumer identities in `consumers`, and each listed identity gets its own independent counter using that rule's windows.

Each `limits[]` rule configures rate windows in one of two ways:
1. `window_seconds` + `max_requests` — custom window
2. One or more of `requests_per_second` / `requests_per_minute` / `requests_per_hour`

**Schema parity.** `RateLimitingConfig` and `RateLimitingRuleConfig` in
`openapi.yaml` encode the constructor's admission rules, so a schema-driven
editor agrees with file and admin admission: exactly one `scope: default` rule,
`scope: consumers` only with `limit_by: consumer`, `sync_mode: redis` requiring
`redis_url`, positive `redis_connect_timeout_seconds` /
`redis_health_check_interval_seconds`, a non-empty `redis_key_prefix`, unique
identities within one `consumers` list, and the case-insensitive spellings of
`limit_by` / `sync_mode` / `scope` (`limit_by: null` means `ip`, exactly as
omitting it does). Three residual rules JSON Schema cannot express are enforced
by the constructor alone and are documented on the fields themselves: one
consumer identity named in two *different* `scope: consumers` rules, an
out-of-range TCP port in `redis_url`, and a `redis_url` database index above the
server's own `databases` setting.

**Configuration bounds.** Every explicit `window_seconds` accepted by the
rate-limit plugins is capped at `2678400` seconds (31 days). Ordinary HTTP,
GraphQL, and gRPC method request caps are capped at `1000000`; zero and values
above those bounds are rejected. The window bound keeps the value representable
as a monotonic duration, as a signed Redis `EXPIRE` TTL (`2 × window + 1`), and
as the stale-state retention horizon (an unbounded value would wrap into a
zero/negative TTL that deletes the counter on every increment). Local HTTP/GraphQL/gRPC sliding-window state uses a fixed
ring of aggregate count buckets (`SLIDING_WINDOW_BUCKET_COUNT = 64`) per key, so
per-key memory stays O(1) in the request cap; the request-cap bound is an
operational ceiling on budgets and Redis/header arithmetic, not a timestamp-log
size limit. The `rate_limiting`, `graphql`, `grpc_method_router`,
`udp_rate_limiting`, `ws_rate_limiting`, and `ai_rate_limiter` roots reject
unknown keys, consistently in runtime admission and OpenAPI.

At least one rate window must be configured in every rule. Do not combine the custom-window pair with preset `requests_per_*` fields in the same rule. When multiple preset windows are configured in a rule, each request must satisfy ALL windows. Consumer identities are matched against the effective identity used by the plugin: mapped Consumer username first, then external authenticated identity.

For IP-based keys, this plugin defaults to an IPv6 `/64` prefix; `ipv6_prefix`
can override that grouping for this plugin only. The sibling `graphql`,
`grpc_method_router`, `udp_rate_limiting`, and `ai_rate_limiter` plugins use a
fixed `/64`; gateway-wide `FERRUM_*_PER_IP` caps also group IPv6 by `/64`.

**Local-mode algorithm selection** (automatic):
- Windows ≤ 5 seconds → token bucket (O(1) memory, ideal for TPS limiting)
- Windows > 5 seconds → bounded aggregate sliding window (fixed 64 count buckets
  per key: one current bucket plus 63 sub-intervals per configured window).
  A slot is reused only after its entire interval expires; the oldest bucket is
  counted in full, so enforcement stays fail-closed relative to an exact
  timestamp log and deliberate over-count is bounded by one sub-interval
  (`ceil(window / 63)`), without the boundary burst of a pure fixed window.

The two local algorithms make **different promises**, and neither is the
centralized one:

- The **sliding aggregate** (windows > 5 seconds) is a trailing-window cap: no
  more than `max_requests` admissions inside any window-length interval, plus
  the bounded `ceil(window / 63)` over-count described above.
- The **token bucket** (windows ≤ 5 seconds) is a **burst-plus-refill**
  contract, *not* a trailing-window cap. It starts full and refills
  continuously at `max_requests / window_seconds`, so a `10`-per-second bucket
  admits ten requests immediately and another every 100ms after that — more
  than ten can land inside one trailing second. It bounds the *sustained* rate
  and the instantaneous burst, and it deliberately smooths rather than
  enforcing an exact interval count.

Centralized (`sync_mode: "redis"`) mode replicates neither; it counts a
sub-bucketed trailing window with its own documented bound (see **Centralized
mode** below). Do not read a single guarantee across all three.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `limit_by` | String | `ip` | Rate limit key: `ip`, `consumer`, `spiffe_identity` (`spiffe` alias accepted), or `service` (one aggregate budget for every caller of this policy) |
| `ipv6_prefix` | Integer | `64` | For IP keys, group IPv6 source addresses by this prefix length (1–128); IPv4 stays host-specific |
| `expose_headers` | bool | `false` | Inject `x-ratelimit-*` headers |
| `max_state_entries` | Integer | `100000` | Hard cap on distinct keys held in local (and Redis-fallback) state (1–10000000). At the cap existing keys keep their budgets and a previously unseen key is refused with `429`; see **Memory protection** below |
| `limits` | Array | required | One default rule plus optional consumer-scoped rules |
| `limits[].scope` | String | required | `default` or `consumers`; exactly one `default` rule is required |
| `limits[].consumers` | String array | — | Required for `scope: consumers`; one or many effective consumer identities, each with an independent counter using this rule's windows |
| `limits[].window_seconds` | u64 (optional) | — | Custom window duration in seconds. Must be paired with `max_requests`. Range 1–2678400 (31 days) |
| `limits[].max_requests` | u64 (optional) | — | Maximum requests allowed within `window_seconds`. Must be paired with `window_seconds`. Range 1–1000000 |
| `limits[].requests_per_second` | u64 (optional) | — | Max requests per second. Range 1–1000000 |
| `limits[].requests_per_minute` | u64 (optional) | — | Max requests per minute. Range 1–1000000 |
| `limits[].requests_per_hour` | u64 (optional) | — | Max requests per hour. Range 1–1000000 |
| `mcp_tool_calls` | Object (optional) | — | Count MCP JSON-RPC `tools/call` requests instead of HTTP requests — see **Counting MCP tool calls** below. `{}` counts every `tools/call` |
| `mcp_tool_calls.endpoint_path` | String (optional) | — | Narrows MCP recognition to exactly this path (set it to `mcp_gateway`'s `endpoint.path`); unset means all paths. Must start with `/`; no query, fragment, or control character |
| `mcp_tool_calls.tools` | String array (optional) | — | Only calls naming one of these public tool names (for example `pets.createPet`) are counted. 1–256 unique names, each 1–255 bytes |
| `mcp_tool_calls.per_tool` | bool | `false` | Keep a separate budget per listed tool instead of one shared by every counted call. Requires `tools` |
| `sync_mode` | String | `local` | `local` (in-memory per instance) or `redis` (centralized) |
| `redis_url`, `redis_tls`, `redis_pool_size`, `redis_connect_timeout_seconds`, `redis_health_check_interval_seconds`, `redis_username`, `redis_password` | — | — | Shared [Redis connection options](#redis-connection-options); `redis_url` database selector `0`–`2147483647`. |
| `redis_key_prefix` | String | `{FERRUM_NAMESPACE}:rate_limiting:{plugin-config-id}` | Redis key namespace prefix. Defaults to the gateway namespace, the plugin name, and this plugin config's stable resource id (for example `ferrum:rate_limiting:rl-public-api`), so two independent policies of this type in one namespace never share counters. Must be non-empty when set; setting it explicitly is the documented opt-in for a deliberately shared budget. |
| `redis_failure_policy` | String | `local_fallback` | Behavior when the centralized store cannot be consulted (outage, egress/DNS screen failure, or an endpoint rejected as Redis Cluster). `local_fallback` keeps enforcing the configured quota in each pod's memory during an outage; explicit `fail_closed` refuses with `503`. Only meaningful when `sync_mode: "redis"`, but validated in either mode |

> **Note:** When `redis_tls` is enabled, CA certificate verification and skip-verify behavior are controlled by the gateway-level `FERRUM_TLS_CA_BUNDLE_PATH` and `FERRUM_TLS_NO_VERIFY` environment variables, not per-plugin settings. A `redis_url` fragment (`#insecure` or any other) is rejected at plugin construction; it is not a per-URL skip-verify switch. A configured CA bundle is exclusive: if the path is set and verification is on, a load failure refuses plugin construction instead of falling back to system/public roots. `FERRUM_TLS_NO_VERIFY=true` remains the sanctioned skip-verify path and does not treat an unloadable CA as a construction error.

#### Redis connection options

Every Redis-backed plugin (`rate_limiting`, `graphql`, `grpc_method_router`, `ai_rate_limiter`, `ws_rate_limiting`, `udp_rate_limiting`, `request_deduplication`, `ai_semantic_cache`, and the `jwks_auth` / `hmac_auth` / `soap_ws_security` replay stores) parses these connection fields with one shared parser. Each plugin's own table lists its `sync_mode`, `redis_key_prefix` default, failure policy, and any delta.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `redis_url` | String (optional) | — | Redis connection URL (required when `sync_mode: "redis"`). Must not carry a URL fragment (`#insecure` or otherwise); TLS skip-verify is only `FERRUM_TLS_NO_VERIFY`. The path, when present, is the database selector and is validated at plugin admission: a canonical decimal integer from `0` through `2147483647`, without a sign, zero-padding, or extra slashes (`redis://host:6379/0`). An absent path or bare slash selects database 0. A non-numeric, multi-segment, negative, or out-of-range selector is refused at construction rather than failing at first use. |
| `redis_tls` | bool | `false` | Enable TLS for Redis connection: upgrades a `redis://` URL to `rediss://`. The URL scheme is matched case-insensitively and stored lowercase at admission, so `REDIS://` with `redis_tls: true` is upgraded and `REDISS://` gets the same SNI and `FERRUM_TLS_*` handling as `rediss://` |
| `redis_pool_size` | u64 | `4` | Number of multiplexed Redis connections (must be between 1 and 128), selected round-robin. A broken connection is re-established through Ferrum's DNS/egress/`INFO CLUSTER` screening path |
| `redis_connect_timeout_seconds` | u64 | `5` | Connection-attempt timeout in seconds (must be ≥ 1) for TCP connect, the TLS handshake when enabled, and the Redis protocol handshake, and the deadline for the proactive `INFO CLUSTER` topology screen (plus the no-eviction memory screen where a plugin runs it). Ordinary commands keep their own shorter response bound. Gateway DNS screening/resolution of the Redis hostname runs before this timeout starts |
| `redis_health_check_interval_seconds` | u64 | `5` | Interval for background health check pings when Redis is unavailable (must be ≥ 1) |
| `redis_username` | String (optional) | — | Redis ACL username (Redis 6+) |
| `redis_password` | String (optional) | — | Redis password |

**Behavior by mode:**
- `limit_by: "ip"` — Enforces in `on_request_received` phase (before auth), keyed by client IP. IPv6 sources in one configured `ipv6_prefix` network share a budget; the default `/64` prevents address rotation within a typical allocation from creating fresh budgets.
- `limit_by: "consumer"` — Enforces in `authorize` phase (after auth), keyed by the authenticated identity: mapped consumer username when present, otherwise external `authenticated_identity`. Falls back to client IP if neither exists.
- `limit_by: "spiffe_identity"` — Enforces in `authorize` phase (after [`spiffe_identity`](#spiffe_identity)), keyed by `ctx.peer_spiffe_id`. Falls back to client IP if no peer SPIFFE identity exists.
- `limit_by: "service"` — Enforces in `authorize` phase (after authentication), keyed by one constant per policy, so every caller of the route, proxy group, or global policy draws from **one aggregate budget** — the total rate a shared backend can take, whoever sends it. Requests an authentication plugin refuses never reach it and spend nothing. With `sync_mode: "redis"` the default key prefix already isolates the policy by namespace and plugin-config id, so every gateway serving the policy shares the one budget while independent policies never do. `scope: consumers` rules are not valid with it (use a second, `limit_by: consumer` instance). To enforce both a per-caller and a total limit, attach two `rate_limiting` instances — for example `limit_by: consumer` at `100/s` and `limit_by: service` at `1000/s`: each request must pass both, and the header contract below still publishes one verdict. TCP/UDP stream connections and sessions likewise share the one budget.
- Stream (`on_stream_connect`) — `consumer` mode uses the stream Consumer identity when available. `spiffe_identity` mode uses `peer_spiffe_id` metadata written by the stream [`spiffe_identity`](#spiffe_identity) hook. Both modes fall back to client IP when their identity is absent.

The resolved request client identity canonicalizes IPv4-mapped IPv6 to native IPv4 once before plugin execution. Every local or Redis fallback key therefore uses the same canonical text without reparsing it in each limiter.

**Rate limit headers** (when `expose_headers: true`): `x-ratelimit-limit`, `x-ratelimit-remaining`, `x-ratelimit-window`. Every admitted (counted) request's client-visible response carries them — including the successful WebSocket handshake response (H1 `101`, H2/H3 Extended CONNECT `200`), which bypasses `after_proxy` and is decorated through the handshake hook instead, and gateway-generated responses such as cache hits, response mocks, serverless short-circuits, and rejections raised by plugins that run after `rate_limiting`; requests that never reached the rate-limit check carry no metadata and get no synthesized headers. The limiter key/identity is never exposed: for `limit_by: "consumer"`/`"spiffe_identity"` it would echo the gateway's internal caller identity (consumer username) or the peer workload SVID back to the client.

**Composed limiters publish one verdict.** The three header names are a single public contract, so when a route carries more than one `rate_limiting` instance exactly one instance's values are published, and the choice does not depend on plugin order. A limiter that *refuses* the request owns the header set: its `limit` / `remaining: 0` / `window` survive the shared rejection finalizer, and a sibling that admitted the same request earlier never re-publishes its positive budget over the `429`. When every limiter admitted, the tightest remaining budget wins — the same rule one instance already applies across its own windows — so the client backs off against the limit that will refuse it next. Two responses carry no `x-ratelimit-*` headers at all: a refusal from a limiter configured with `expose_headers: false` (that policy's verdict is that the client is told no budget; its quota `429` still carries `Retry-After`, below), and any fail-closed `503`, where the gateway has no authoritative counter to report.

Returns HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` when exceeded. Every quota `429` carries a standard **`Retry-After`** header (whole seconds, at least `1`), independently of `expose_headers`, because HTTP clients and SDKs honour it on their own: it names when the refusing window has budget again, absent further traffic — and when several windows refuse at once, the longest of their waits, so a client that honours it is not refused again by a longer window (`x-ratelimit-window` still names the first refusing window). It is exact for the local token bucket (time until the next token refills) and the local sliding aggregate (time until the oldest counted sub-interval leaves the window — up to `ceil(window × 64 / 63)`), and a conservative upper bound in centralized mode, where the gateway only learns window sums: the time until the newest charge has left the sub-bucket ladder of every reader settlement admits — including a retrying gateway whose learned offset makes it select one sub-bucket behind the bucket Redis executes it in — which is at most three sub-buckets (`3/16` of the window) longer than the window itself. The state-capacity `429` (an unseen key at `max_state_entries`) and the fail-closed `503` carry no `Retry-After`, since neither is a budget verdict. The MCP tool-call JSON-RPC refusal on HTTP `200` carries none either.

**Counting MCP tool calls** (`mcp_tool_calls`). An agent-facing MCP endpoint is one HTTP route that carries every JSON-RPC method, so a plain request limit also spends the budget on `initialize`, `tools/list`, and notifications and cannot tell tools apart. With an `mcp_tool_calls` object the same limiter — the same `limits`, `limit_by`, consumer overrides, local state, and `sync_mode: redis` shared store — counts MCP `tools/call` requests instead:

```yaml
plugin_name: rate_limiting
config:
  limit_by: consumer
  expose_headers: true
  limits:
    - { scope: default, requests_per_minute: 60 }
    - { scope: consumers, consumers: [batch-agent], requests_per_minute: 600 }
  mcp_tool_calls:
    endpoint_path: /mcp        # the mcp_gateway endpoint.path
    # tools: [pets.createPet, pets.deletePet]   # optional: count only these
    # per_tool: true                            # optional: one budget per listed tool
```

- **Only `tools/call` is charged.** `initialize`, `tools/list`, `prompts/*`, `resources/*`, `ping`, `notifications/*` methods, and JSON-RPC responses pass uncounted and receive no rate-limit headers. A `tools/call` notification (a call without an `id`) is still charged. A JSON-RPC batch is one charge per `tools/call` member (notification-form members included), taken in order; the first refused charge refuses the whole request, since one HTTP exchange cannot be forwarded in part, and charges admitted before it stay charged (a batch that crosses the boundary spends what was left of the budget). With `tools`, only calls naming a listed tool are charged; with `per_tool`, each listed tool has its own budget under the same `limits` (the tool name is length-prefixed in the key, so it can never collide with another caller's key, and `per_tool` requires `tools` so a caller cannot mint limiter state with invented names). For different limits per tool, compose several `rate_limiting` instances with different `tools` lists: the header contract below still publishes one verdict.
- **Recognition matches `mcp_gateway`.** The body is read after it is buffered, in `before_proxy` (the plugin's `on_request_received` / `authorize` charges do not run in this mode). Member names are decoded before comparison (an escaped `"m\u0065thod"` is `method`), the media types are the ones the gateway admits (`application/json`, `application/json-rpc`, any `+json`, or no `Content-Type`), and a batch is read within fixed recognizer bounds of 32 members, 1 MiB, and 256 KiB per member. Raising `mcp_gateway.validation.max_batch_items`, `max_batch_bytes`, or `max_batch_item_bytes` above these bounds means the limiter refuses larger batches with JSON-RPC `-32600`. A body with duplicate member names, or a batch past those bounds, is refused with JSON-RPC `-32600` instead of being counted one way here and parsed another way downstream. So is any in-scope request whose `Content-Type` declares a `charset` other than UTF-8 (including RFC 2231 `charset*` forms), exactly as `mcp_gateway` refuses it, and a body that strict UTF-8 JSON cannot read but that could still carry a `tools/call` for a lenient upstream parser — UTF-16 / UTF-32 JSON, a byte-order mark, `NaN` / `Infinity`, comments, trailing commas, or invalid UTF-8 (Python's `json.loads` on bytes accepts the first three): the strict recognizer's "no `tools/call`" is not proof the upstream executes none. The limiter requests the raw body bytes for this, so an in-scope POST with no body snapshot to inspect is refused too rather than passed uncounted. The refusal reason is recorded as `ratelimit_mcp_uninspectable` metadata (`true` for an ambiguous or over-bound body, `unsupported_charset`, `unparseable_body`, `missing_body`, or `unsupported_content_encoding`). A strictly valid JSON body that merely contains a JSON escape or the literal text `tools/call` outside a method still passes uncounted. Any in-scope POST with non-identity `Content-Encoding` is refused with `-32017`, even when its body has no `tools/call`, because its body cannot be inspected; earlier request decompression removes the encoding and keeps normal recognition. `endpoint_path`, when set, narrows which POSTs are in scope. Ordinary JSON traffic that cannot spell `tools/call` is answered by a byte scan without parsing, and with `endpoint_path` set no other path is buffered at all.
- **Placement.** The charge runs at priority 2900, before `mcp_gateway` (2992): every `tools/call` attempt counts, including one the gateway then refuses (unknown or ungranted tool, invalid arguments, an aggregate batch member answered `-32009`). To count only calls the gateway admitted, give the instance a `priority_override` above 2992.
- **Refusal is a JSON-RPC error on HTTP `200`.** An exceeded budget answers `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":<the call's id>,"error":{"code":-32015,"message":"MCP tool-call rate limit exceeded"}}` with `Content-Type: application/json` and, with `expose_headers`, the usual `x-ratelimit-limit` / `x-ratelimit-remaining: 0` / `x-ratelimit-window`. A batch gets one error per request-form member (by its own id; an id longer than 4096 bytes is answered with `id: null`), and a refused request with no request-form member gets one error with `id: null`. HTTP `200` is deliberate and matches `mcp_gateway`, which answers every JSON-RPC error on `200`: MCP streamable HTTP clients resolve the pending request from a JSON-RPC error on a 2xx response and surface its code and message to the agent, while a `429` POST response is raised as a transport failure that loses both. A state-capacity refusal also answers `-32015`; a fail-closed Redis outage (`redis_failure_policy: fail_closed`) answers `-32016` (`MCP tool-call rate limit unavailable`) with no rate-limit headers. Because the refusal rides HTTP `200`, status-code metrics do not see it; `ferrum_rate_limit_exceeded_total` and the `ratelimit_mcp_tool_calls` metadata (the number of charges the request carried) do.
- **Scope.** The mode is HTTP-only (a stream, WebSocket, or gRPC request has no `tools/call` to count) and changes the limiter's local-state identity, so switching an instance between request counting and tool-call counting never reuses a live budget. A native-gRPC or WebSocket request on a route with a tool-call limiter is refused with `403` / `PERMISSION_DENIED` (see [Protocol Support](plugin_execution_order.md#protocol-support)).

**Counter storage** (`sync_mode`): only `local` and `redis` are supported. There is intentionally no database-backed counter policy; database writes on the hot path are non-performant and can cause operational issues.

**Memory protection:** Local (and Redis-fallback) state is capped at `max_state_entries` keys (default 100,000, configurable from 1 through 10,000,000). Size it to the number of distinct callers one gateway process must track inside the longest window's retention horizon: per-key state is fixed (token-bucket scalars, or one 64-bucket ring of about half a KiB per sliding window), so memory scales linearly with the cap. The cap is read on every admission and is deliberately not part of the local-state compatibility fingerprint, so raising or lowering it on a live policy keeps every consumed budget. Sampled piggyback sweeps (every 1,024 requests, cooldown-gated to at most once per second) prune idle keys even below that hard cap. Hard cardinality is enforced by atomic reservation on admission: existing keys continue at capacity, and previously unseen local/fallback keys are denied fail-closed. Cleanup never force-evicts still-active budgets.

For grouped consumer rules, the list is not a shared budget. For example, `consumers: [premium-app, partner-app]` with `requests_per_minute: 1000` gives `premium-app` 1000/minute and `partner-app` 1000/minute independently.

**Centralized mode** (`sync_mode: "redis"`): Rate limit counters are stored in Redis so multiple gateway instances (e.g., multiple data planes) share a single global rate limit. Admission is **charge-then-compensate**, using only native RESP commands on the ordinary pooled connections — no Lua, no `EVAL`/`EVALSHA`, no `WATCH`. One atomic `MULTI`/`EXEC` charges **every** configured window and ends with one `TIME`, and the decision is read off that increment against the Redis server clock. If any window refuses, a compensating `MULTI`/`EXEC` hands the charge back on **every** window the request incremented, so **a refused request leaves no lasting charge on any window** and a tighter window's refusal never consumes a looser window's budget. Every decision costs exactly one round trip on the request path; the hand-back is issued off it. Under contention a concurrent request for the same identity can be refused slightly early against a charge that is about to be handed back; the limiter never over-admits. Cancelling a request while its charge is in flight cannot strand an over-limit increment. A refusal leaves a lasting charge (until the window's TTL elapses) only when Redis goes away before the hand-back — the failure is recorded and `redis_failure_policy` governs the next decision — or the process exits between the charge and its hand-back. **Algorithm — sub-bucketed trailing window.** Every configured window is split into **16** equal sub-buckets keyed `{prefix:key}:{window_seconds}:{sub_index}`, and a window's count is the full sum of nineteen counters (the sub-bucket the request lands in, the 17 before it, and the one after it) at face value, so a burst clustered anywhere inside the exact trailing window is always counted whole. See the [design notes](plugins/rate_limiting_redis.md#charge-then-compensate) for the transaction and ladder mechanics.

**What the over-count costs, per limit.** Counting the oldest sub-buckets at face value means the ladder covers *more* than the exact trailing window, so a client sending at **exactly** its configured rate is throttled. Measured from the instant Redis *executes* a decision the ladder reaches back up to three sub-buckets further than the window itself — settlement deliberately admits a reader whose ladder was built one sub-bucket before the bucket it executes in, and the charges it counts may have been keyed at the bucket they executed in. The extra history counted is therefore at most three sub-buckets — up to `ceil(3 * limit / 16)` requests — so the steady-state admitted fraction at exactly the configured rate is **at least** `limit / (limit + ceil(3 * limit / 16))`:

| Configured limit per window | Steady-state admitted fraction at exactly that rate (bound) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 50% (1/2) |
| 2 | ~67% (2/3) |
| 8 | 80% (8/10) |
| 100 | ~84% |

A stream whose requests all carry the *same* placement lag does better — `limit / (limit + ceil(2 * limit / 16))`, so ~89% (8/9) at a limit of 8 — because the widest coverage needs the reader to straddle a sub-bucket boundary that the charges it counts did not. The table is the bound, not the typical case.

There is **no unconditional 8/9**: the quantisation falls hardest on small quotas, and it is inherent to any bucketed counter that counts its oldest bucket in full. It is deliberately **not** fixed by decaying the oldest sub-bucket on a timestamp, which would reopen the boundary-burst over-admission above. A client spaced three sub-buckets slower than its nominal rate (`window + 3 * window/16` between arrivals) is admitted in full at every limit. If a small quota must admit its full nominal rate, configure it over a longer window: `10` per `10s` rather than `1` per `1s`.

**Concurrency, clocks, and latency.** Sub-buckets are selected and settled on the **Redis server's clock** (`TIME` inside each charge transaction), not on each gateway's, and settlement is two-sided, so no charge executed inside a reader's trailing window is ever missing from that reader's count, whatever the gateways' reply latencies. Residual over-admission is bounded by the concurrent in-flight requests of a single gateway during the two-pass settlement rebuild. Run NTP on every gateway host as ordinary hygiene, but the request-quota count does not depend on it. A Redis whose *execution* stalls for more than one sub-bucket — roughly 62.5–125ms for a one-second window and 3.75–7.5s for a one-minute one, scaling with the window — makes requests mis-settle; after one rebuild such a request is routed as an *unavailable centralized store* through `redis_failure_policy` (`local_fallback` for `rate_limiting`, `fail_closed` elsewhere), not as a quota refusal. There is no local-clock mode: a connection that cannot answer `TIME` (see **Redis ACL requirement** below) is discarded and `redis_failure_policy` governs exactly as during a Redis outage. Clock-offset learning, stale-reply handling, and rebuild mechanics are described in the [design notes](plugins/rate_limiting_redis.md#concurrency-and-clocks).

Local mode's token bucket and 64-bucket sliding aggregate are deliberately **not** replicated in Redis, and their contracts are **not** the Redis one — see **Local-mode algorithm selection** above for what each guarantees. `ai_rate_limiter` and `ws_rate_limiting` are **token**-accounting rather than request quotas and keep the two-window weighted approximation described in their own sections. Background Redis health observers and recovery checkers are owned by the limiter/client instance and stop when that generation is dropped (config reload or shutdown), so retired instances do not retain connections or keep pinging obsolete endpoints. If Redis becomes unreachable, `redis_failure_policy` decides what happens: the default `local_fallback` uses pod-memory counters, which enforce the configured limit once *per gateway process* for the duration of the outage. Explicit `fail_closed` returns `503` with no rate-limit headers when centralized enforcement is unavailable. Fallback emits one warning per outage, counts every decision it serves in `ferrum_rate_limit_local_fallback_decisions_total`, and marks request metadata with `ratelimit_local_fallback: true`, independently of `expose_headers`. The marker covers every decision this instance took on the fallback budget: admissions, quota refusals, and the `429` a previously unseen key receives when the local map is at its `max_state_entries` cap — that capacity refusal is a degraded-enforcement symptom, not client behaviour, so it is attributed the same way. Attribution follows the decision, not the client's current reachability: a *per-decision* fallback — a sub-bucket rollover that refused twice, or a reply the gateway could not pair with its windows — routes that one request onto the per-process budget while the endpoint itself stays reachable, and its capacity `429` still carries the marker and the counter. Explicit `fail_closed` counts each `503` it returns in `ferrum_rate_limit_enforcement_unavailable_total`. Either way the client switches back automatically when connectivity is restored: admission reads the shared client's own availability signal on every request, so the first request after the client recovers is centrally enforced again — the background health observer only logs the transition and never adds a second recovery interval in front of admission. Compatible with any RESP-protocol server running in single-endpoint topology: Redis, Valkey, DragonflyDB, KeyDB, or Garnet.

> **Redis ACL requirement.** Admission needs ordinary keyspace commands on the configured `redis_key_prefix` — `GETRANGE`, `INCR`, `DECR`, `EXPIRE`, `MULTI`, and `EXEC` — in addition to the connection/health commands, plus the server command **`TIME`**. No scripting category is required. **`TIME` is mandatory for these three request-quota plugins**: every connection a request-quota policy opens probes `TIME` once, standalone, before it may carry a policy command, and **every** unsuccessful answer — a `NOPERM`, an `ERR unknown command` from a server that does not implement `TIME`, a reply that is not a clock, a timeout, a transport failure — discards that connection exactly like a failed `INFO CLUSTER` screen and marks the client unavailable. `redis_failure_policy` then governs every decision (`local_fallback` for `rate_limiting`, `fail_closed` elsewhere), which is the same degraded behaviour a Redis outage produces and never a quieter, weaker centralized contract. A `NOPERM` and an unknown command still pick the *diagnostic* — the warning tells you to grant `+time`, or that this server has no `TIME` at all — but not the outcome. Grant `TIME` (`+time`, or the `@slow`/`@fast` category that already contains it). The background recovery checker proves the same thing: for a request-quota client a successful `PING` and topology screen are **not** a recovery until a bounded, well-formed `TIME` also answers, so an endpoint that is reachable but still withholds the clock is never republished as available and never logs a restored-access message. None of those refusals is terminal — an ACL granted under a live gateway is picked up on the next interval — and the recovery probe's own sample is discarded rather than adopted as an offset, because it is bounded only by `redis_connect_timeout_seconds`. Clients that read no clock send no `TIME` in recovery either. **The requirement stops at request quotas.** It follows what a consumer computes, not what a connection is: `rate_limiting`, `graphql` and `grpc_method_router` charge a sub-bucket ladder that every gateway must agree on, while `ai_rate_limiter`, `ws_rate_limiting` and `udp_rate_limiting` index their windows locally, `request_deduplication`, `soap_ws_security`'s shared replay authority and the `jwks_auth` / `hmac_auth` replay clients claim markers with `SET NX EX`, and `ai_semantic_cache` stores a blob. None of those reads the server clock, so their connections never send `TIME` and a Redis whose ACL withholds `+time` leaves them fully enforcing. A deployment that uses only those plugins needs no ACL change at all. Command volume per configured window is eighteen `GETRANGE`s (each bounded to 21 bytes, the widest `i64` plus one so a truncated or non-integer counter fails the charge closed instead of being materialized whole) plus one `INCR` and one `EXPIRE` over nineteen keys, plus one `TIME` per transaction, still inside one `MULTI`/`EXEC` and one round trip. Request-quota keys use the `{prefix:key}:{window_seconds}:{sub_index}` layout; counters written under the older `{prefix:key}:{window_index}` layout are not read and expire on their own TTL, so upgrading from that layout starts fresh counters (see [CHANGELOG.md](../CHANGELOG.md)). A denied or failed command is not a quota refusal: it is an unavailable centralized store, so `redis_failure_policy` governs (`local_fallback` for `rate_limiting`, `fail_closed` elsewhere) and the endpoint is logged as failing.

> **Topology: Redis Cluster is not supported.** The shared Redis client is a single-endpoint client; it is not Cluster-aware and cannot follow `MOVED`/`ASK` redirections. Rather than degrading silently, it screens the endpoint: each new connection issues `INFO CLUSTER` and is refused when the server reports `cluster_enabled:1`, and any command answered with a Cluster-only error code (`MOVED`, `ASK`, `CROSSSLOT`, `CLUSTERDOWN`, `TRYAGAIN`) permanently marks the endpoint unusable. Servers that do not implement `INFO`, or that answer it with an ordinary command error (unknown command, restricted ACL), are not rejected by the proactive screen. The screen is bounded by the configured `redis_connect_timeout_seconds` — there is no separate knob — so an endpoint that accepts and authenticates a connection but never answers `INFO` cannot stall the first enforcement operation; a probe that does not complete is treated as an ordinary retryable outage (never as proof of Cluster topology), the unscreened connection is discarded rather than used, and `redis_failure_policy` governs that request. Rejection is terminal for that plugin generation — a Cluster node answers `PING` while still redirecting every key, so recovery pings never clear it and `redis_failure_policy` governs until the configuration changes. Terminal also means terminal under concurrency: once any task proves Cluster topology, a connection, command, or recovery probe that succeeds afterwards is neither published nor reported as a success (a command that already mutated Redis is failed conservatively, which can only over-count), and health observers cannot advertise a recovery for that endpoint. Independently, every key touched by one atomic operation carries a shared hash tag (`{escaped-prefix:escaped-rate-key}` followed by the suffix components — `:{window_seconds}:{sub_index}` for a request quota, `:{window_index}` elsewhere), so a multi-window charge or a multi-key datagram/byte transaction is slot-stable; `%`, braces, and `:` are percent-escaped inside the tag so caller-controlled identities cannot truncate it.

> **Local counters survive a compatible reload.** Local (and Redis-fallback) enforcement state is owned by the policy — `namespace` + plugin type + plugin-config id — not by the plugin instance a config generation happened to construct. A full reload (file-mode `SIGHUP`, a data plane receiving a full control-plane snapshot, the database-mode fallback after a rejected delta), a change or deletion of *any* global plugin config in the namespace, an edit to the owning proxy's plugin associations, or a rebuilt shared HTTP client all reconstruct the plugin instance; none of them resets a consumed budget. Compatibility is decided on the **effective enforcement semantics after parsing**, never on raw configuration syntax: an omitted optional field and its explicit effective default, a spelling the parser normalizes (case, surrounding whitespace, a gRPC method path with or without its leading `/`, `spiffe` vs `spiffe_identity`, `requests_per_minute: 60` vs `window_seconds: 60` + `max_requests: 60`), and an omitted rate map vs an explicit empty one all describe one budget and keep one set of counters. A **semantic** change does start fresh state, so a retired generation can never charge against the replacement: for `rate_limiting` the parsed limit dimension, the default window list, and the per-consumer window lists; for `graphql` the limit dimension and the parsed type/operation rate maps; for `grpc_method_router` the limit dimension and the normalized per-method rate map; for `ai_rate_limiter` the effective `token_limit`, `window_seconds`, `count_mode`, `limit_by`, `provider`, and `on_unmetered_response`; for `ws_rate_limiting` the effective sustained frame rate, burst capacity, and `limit_by` dimension; for `udp_rate_limiting` the effective per-window datagram and byte budgets, the window length, the IPv6 grouping prefix, and the counted direction, where an unbounded axis is distinct from any bounded one. Whether a centralized store is enabled (`sync_mode`) is part of that set for every one of them, and when it *is* enabled so are the effective `redis_failure_policy` and the effective `redis_key_prefix`, because they decide whether the local map may admit at all during an outage and which counter domain it belongs to. With `sync_mode: local` there is no centralized store to lose, so changing `redis_failure_policy` alone changes nothing that is enforced and does **not** reset the local budget. Presentation-only fields (`expose_headers`, `close_reason`) and stateless checks (GraphQL depth/complexity/alias limits, gRPC `allow_methods`/`deny_methods`) are deliberately *not* part of the set — changing them must not hand every caller a fresh budget. Retention is bounded: state is held weakly and released as soon as the last plugin instance using it is dropped, so a removed policy is reclaimed and a policy re-added later starts fresh. Credentials, URLs, usernames, passwords, and TLS material are never part of this decision and never logged. This applies to `rate_limiting`, `graphql`, `grpc_method_router`, `ai_rate_limiter`, `ws_rate_limiting`, and `udp_rate_limiting`.

The default Redis prefix is already determined by the stable policy identity, so it is not hashed again as a compatibility input; this keeps validation and runtime construction equivalent even when their shared HTTP clients carry different namespaces. An explicitly configured `redis_key_prefix` remains a compatibility input and isolates local fallback state. When a semantic change creates a fresh local generation alongside a live one, Ferrum emits one structured info log carrying only `namespace`, `plugin`, and `config_id`; the fingerprint is never logged.

> **Namespace and policy isolation:** The default `redis_key_prefix` (see each plugin's `redis_key_prefix` row) combines the gateway namespace, the plugin name, and the plugin-config id. The namespace component prevents collisions when gateway instances with different namespaces share one Redis cluster; the plugin-config id component prevents collisions between two independent policies of the same plugin type *inside* one namespace. The id is the configured plugin-config resource id, so replicas of the same policy across data planes still share one distributed budget. This applies to `rate_limiting`, `graphql`, `grpc_method_router`, `ai_rate_limiter`, `ws_rate_limiting`, and `udp_rate_limiting`. An explicit `redis_key_prefix` overrides this behavior entirely and is the supported way to opt two policies into a deliberately shared budget. Redis ACLs must allow `GETRANGE`, `INCR`/`INCRBY`, `DECR`, `EXPIRE`, `MULTI`, and `EXEC` on those keys, in addition to the connection/health commands; no scripting category is needed by any rate-limit plugin.

```yaml
plugin_name: rate_limiting
config:
  limit_by: consumer
  expose_headers: true
  sync_mode: redis
  redis_url: "redis://redis-host:6379/0"
  redis_failure_policy: local_fallback # Default; use fail_closed to require Redis.
  redis_tls: true
  redis_key_prefix: "myapp:rate_limiting"
  limits:
    - scope: default
      requests_per_minute: 100
    - scope: consumers
      consumers: [premium-app, partner-app]
      requests_per_minute: 1000
    - scope: consumers
      consumers: [batch-worker]
      window_seconds: 60
      max_requests: 250
```

### `request_deduplication`

**Priority:** 3010 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `on_final_response_body`, `on_response_stream_terminated`, `on_response_committed` · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Prevents duplicate API calls by tracking idempotency keys. When a request arrives with an idempotency key header and the same logical request was completed within the configured TTL, the plugin returns the cached response instead of forwarding to the backend.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `header_name` | String | `"Idempotency-Key"` | Header name to read the idempotency key from (case-insensitive). Must be a valid RFC 9110 HTTP field-name token. A name in the gateway-owned `x-consumer-*` namespace (either spelling, see [Consumer Identity Headers](#consumer-identity-headers)) is rejected at config load: the gateway strips it from every client request, so no request could carry the key |
| `ttl_seconds` | u64 | `300` | Time-to-live for cached responses (must be > 0) |
| `inflight_ttl_seconds` | u64 | `ttl_seconds` | How long an in-flight marker remains valid before being treated as stale and replaced by a fresh request (must be > 0). Set at or above the longest backend request that should be protected from concurrent duplicate execution — if set too low, a slow legitimate request still running past this TTL can have a duplicate retry bypass the in-flight lock and re-execute side-effecting operations. Defaults to `ttl_seconds` |
| `max_entries` | u64 | `10000` | Maximum number of tracked local entries and the hard maximum number of persistent per-key execution barriers. Active in-flight work is never evicted while live and may temporarily exceed the entry target, up to the separate hard `max_inflight_entries` ceiling. If completed external operations fill the per-key barrier budget, additional barriers collapse into one fixed process-global deadline and applicable idempotency-key requests receive 503 until it expires |
| `max_inflight_entries` | u64 | `max_entries` | Hard ceiling on live local in-flight markers per policy identity: requests currently executing plus interrupted or ambiguous requests (for example a client that reset a streamed response) whose markers are retained until `inflight_ttl_seconds` (must be > 0). A request with a **new** idempotency key that cannot reserve a slot is refused with `503` (`Idempotency in-flight capacity is saturated`) and any Redis ownership it acquired is released; requests for keys already tracked still replay or conflict, and live ownership is never evicted to admit new work. Execution barriers are bounded separately by `max_entries` |
| `max_entry_size_bytes` | u64 | `1048576` | Maximum retained size of one completed response entry. Oversized responses return the original response to the client without retaining a replayable entry. In local mode, ordinary oversized responses clear in-flight state without retaining it, so a later retry can re-execute. A completed external operation instead replaces its exact owner with a fixed-size local execution barrier for `max(ttl_seconds, inflight_ttl_seconds)`. In Redis mode, when a replayable response does not fit, a small non-replayable completion tombstone is atomically published so peers refuse identical retries for the same barrier window. Neither barrier lifetime is shorter than the state it replaces |
| `max_total_size_bytes` | u64 | `104857600` | Exact maximum retained size across local completed response entries. Responses that would exceed this cap are returned normally and are not retained. In local mode, ordinary skipped responses clear the in-flight marker immediately; completed external operations use the fixed-size execution barrier without charging response bytes. In Redis mode, an ordinary local-total-cap skip keeps local and distributed in-flight locks only if Redis publication fails |
| `applicable_methods` | String[] | `["POST", "PUT", "PATCH"]` | HTTP methods to apply deduplication to. Must contain at least one entry, and every entry must be a valid HTTP method token |
| `scope_by_consumer` | bool | `true` | Additionally include the authenticated consumer's display identity in the key. Caller isolation does not depend on this flag — every key binds a mandatory caller-authorization partition (see below) |
| `anonymous_caller_scope` | String | `"caller_address"` | How **anonymous** callers are partitioned. `caller_address` binds the gateway-resolved canonical peer address; a request whose canonical address cannot be parsed is not deduplicated (and is refused with `503` when `enforce_required` is set) rather than keyed incompletely. `shared` is an explicit operator attestation that the origin does not vary by caller address on this route. It does not apply to authenticated callers, which always bind their canonical address |
| `caller_partition` | String | `"credential"` | How the caller dimension of the logical key is bound; matched exactly. `credential` binds the full caller-authorization partition described below (credential digests and canonical peer address), so a refreshed token, a per-request signature (`hmac_auth`, SigV4), or a new client address is a different caller. `authenticated_identity` is an operator opt-in for clients whose credentials or addresses change between retries: when the gateway verified a principal — a resolved Consumer, a peer SPIFFE identity, or an external identity committed with its verified realm through the authentication boundary — the key binds that principal only (no credential digests, no peer address), and the fingerprint binds the presence but not the values of credential headers, of credential query parameters an authentication plugin captured from its configured query location (`jwt_auth` `token_lookup: query:<name>`, `key_auth` query keys), and of exactly these signature-context headers that an `hmac_auth` or SigV4 re-signature or an AWS SDK retry attempt regenerates: `date`, `x-amz-date`, `x-amz-content-sha256`, `amz-sdk-invocation-id`, `amz-sdk-request`, `digest`, and `content-digest` (the body itself stays bound through its own digest). A credential header or query parameter that an earlier `request_transformer` renamed keeps that classification under its new name (renames are followed in order, chained renames included; a name the credential was moved away from, or that an ordinary field was renamed onto, is value-bound again, including original built-in/configured credential header names reused for business data). Query names are matched after the same percent-decoding the gateway uses for `query_params` (a literal `+` is not a space). A credential query name is presence-bound only when it occurs once in the final query: query rename preserves pre-existing destination pairs, so repeated names (including percent-encoded aliases and chained rename collisions) stay fully value-bound. An unchanged colliding query can replay, but changing any of its values, including a refreshed token, returns a fingerprint-mismatch `409`. Every other header and query pair stays value-bound. Two credentials of one principal with different scopes then share an operation, so scope-level distinction rests on the authorization plugins that ran before deduplication. Requests without a verified principal fall back to `credential`. The mode is framed into the key, so changing it never reuses retained state |
| `enforce_required` | bool | `false` | Reject requests missing the idempotency header with 400 |
| `sync_mode` | String | `"local"` | `local` (in-memory) or `redis` (centralized) |
| `redis_url`, `redis_tls`, `redis_pool_size`, `redis_connect_timeout_seconds`, `redis_health_check_interval_seconds`, `redis_username`, `redis_password` | — | — | Shared [Redis connection options](#redis-connection-options); `redis_url` database selector `0`–`2147483647`; `redis_url` must use the `redis://` or `rediss://` scheme with a hostname. |
| `redis_key_prefix` | String | `"{FERRUM_NAMESPACE}:dedup"` | Redis key namespace prefix. Defaults to `ferrum:dedup` when namespace is `"ferrum"`. Must be non-empty when supplied. Sibling instances stay isolated under a shared default/explicit prefix via stable `plugin_config_id` in logical keys, and matched proxy namespaces remain isolated even when an explicit prefix is shared across namespaces |
| `on_redis_unavailable` | String | `"fail_closed"` | Behavior when `sync_mode: "redis"` is configured but Redis cannot be consulted. `fail_closed` refuses the request with 503; `local_only` explicitly opts into process-local deduplication for availability. Only valid when `sync_mode: "redis"` |

Unknown top-level keys are rejected with a path-qualified error and a spelling
suggestion, so a typo such as `enforce_requred` or `sync_mod` fails admission
instead of silently reverting to a permissive default. Redis-only keys (every
`redis_*` field and `on_redis_unavailable`) are rejected outside
`sync_mode: "redis"` for the same reason: supplying them in local mode is
almost always a misspelled `sync_mode`. File-mode validation makes this fatal at
startup, database/CP admin returns HTTP 400, and a DP rejects the update and
keeps its last-known-good runtime config.

**Client-visible outcomes:**

| Situation | Response |
|---|---|
| Same key and fingerprint, completed within `ttl_seconds` | Stored response with `X-Idempotent-Replayed: true` |
| Same key, different fingerprint | `409 Conflict` |
| Same key and fingerprint while the first request is in flight, or while its marker is retained until `inflight_ttl_seconds` (interrupted stream, non-2xx plugin reject, possibly executed dispatch failure) | `409 Conflict` |
| Stored response under a superseded or unestablished presentation policy, or a Redis record with missing, malformed, oversized, or invalid contents | `409 Conflict` |
| Completed external operation with no replayable representation (completion tombstone) | `409 Conflict` for `max(ttl_seconds, inflight_ttl_seconds)` |
| Idempotency header missing with `enforce_required: true` | `400` |
| Declared body unavailable for fingerprinting, malformed or over-limit Brotli body, or case-variant duplicates of a header the key or fingerprint reads | `400` |
| New key while `max_inflight_entries` is saturated, or while the process-global execution-barrier deadline is active | `503` |
| Shared decode budget exhausted, anonymous caller address unparseable with `enforce_required: true`, or Redis unavailable with `on_redis_unavailable: fail_closed` | `503` |
| Replayed bytes that `ai_response_guard` or `ai_tool_governor` must redact under current policy and cannot | `502` |
| Size-skipped response, streamed response, or proven pre-wire dispatch failure | Original response; nothing replayable is retained |

**Composition restrictions:**

- **`request_deduplication` and `mcp_gateway` cannot be enabled on the same proxy.** The composition is rejected at config admission (admin API `400`, fatal in file mode, rejected update in DP) and again at plugin-cache construction, with an error naming both plugin config IDs. `mcp_gateway` rewrites upstream resource, tool, and prompt identifiers into public ones using a per-session catalog it re-lists from upstream on its own discovery TTL — entries are added, removed, remapped, hidden, or made ambiguous with no configuration change at all. Even though MCP request validation/routing runs before deduplication, a finalized replay skips MCP's later response-body rewrite. No static digest can witness the live catalog that rewrite consumes, so the pair is refused rather than replaying bytes whose producing policy cannot be established. Disable one of them on the proxy; to keep both behaviors, put them on separate proxies
- **`request_deduplication` and `a2a_gateway` cannot be enabled on the same proxy while `a2a_gateway` derives its public base from the request** — that is, with `discovery.public_base_url` unset and `discovery.trust_forwarded_headers: true`. The refusal is per instance, not by name: with a configured `discovery.public_base_url` the Agent Card rewrite is a pure function of configuration, enrolls in the static digest above, and composes normally. In the request-derived mode the rewritten origin comes from `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `X-Forwarded-Host` / `Host` and, absent a forwarded scheme, from whether the connection itself is secure (TLS on HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, always on HTTP/3); the fingerprint below binds neither the complete forwarded header set nor the transport's security, so two requests sharing a replay key can legitimately deserve cards advertising different origins. Set `discovery.public_base_url`, or disable one of them on the proxy
- Same-protocol plugins that may still mutate request headers, query, or destination at or after deduplication, and deferred body transformers that cannot prove byte-identical output, are rejected (see **Lookup observes routing and request shaping** below).

**Behavior:**
- `br` request bodies are fingerprinted only after the shared charged strict
  decoder accepts them. Malformed or over-limit Brotli is rejected with `400`;
  if the shared decode budget is exhausted, the gateway returns `503`. Malformed
  gzip retains the existing behavior of fingerprinting its original bytes.
- Logical idempotency keys are scoped by the stable plugin-config identity, the effective destination partition (matched proxy namespace and ID, listen path, upstream id or direct host/port/scheme, route authority, rewritten path, route-override backend TLS and DNS policy), a mandatory caller-authorization partition (or, with `caller_partition: authenticated_identity`, the verified principal), the authenticated display identity when `scope_by_consumer: true`, and the idempotency header value. The matched route's response-header policy (a `mesh_route_dispatch` `response_transform`) is deliberately **not** in the logical key: it changes how a result is presented, not which operation an identical retry would execute. It is bound into the request fingerprint instead, so after a response-header-only route reload a same-key retry receives `409 Conflict` rather than addressing a fresh key and executing the operation a second time, and an unchanged policy still replays. Namespace is part of the logical digest even under a custom Redis prefix, so equal resource IDs in separate namespaces never share ownership or replay state. The stored key is a canonically length-framed SHA-256 digest, not a delimiter-joined raw string
- **Caller authorization, not a display subject.** The key binds the authentication mechanism, resolved identity and consumer, peer SPIFFE identity, and SHA-256 digests of every credential header presented, so two tokens resolving to one `sub` with different scopes or tenancy claims cannot claim or replay one another's operation. Both credential views are bound under separate provenance labels — the pristine inbound wire headers and the live backend-visible headers — so an earlier plugin that rewrites credentials cannot erase the original caller distinction. **Every** caller also binds its canonical peer address, which the origin observes through Ferrum's regenerated `X-Forwarded-For`; only an anonymous caller's address binding can be relaxed, via `anonymous_caller_scope: shared`. `caller_partition: authenticated_identity` replaces this whole dimension with the verified principal when one exists (see the parameter table)
- The idempotency header, and the authority/`Host`/`Content-Encoding`/`Content-Length`/`Transfer-Encoding` fields the fingerprint reads by name, must resolve to one value. If an earlier plugin left case-variant spellings with different values in the header map (for example `idempotency-key: A` and `Idempotency-Key: B`), the request is refused with `400` rather than keyed by whichever entry the map yields first
- **Credential headers participate in the request fingerprint as digests** rather than being excluded for scoped callers. The raw secret never enters a key or a log line, and a same-subject/different-scope credential produces a different fingerprint and is refused as a conflict instead of replaying
- **Lookup observes routing and request shaping.** Priority `3010` places deduplication after the built-in route dispatchers and `request_transformer`, but before terminate-mode `serverless_function`. The logical key therefore binds the effective post-routing destination, while the fingerprint binds the transformed header map and the published outbound query. Every same-protocol plugin that may still mutate request headers, query, or destination at or after deduplication is rejected, including through a priority override. Because ordinary request-body transforms run only after all `before_proxy` hooks, a same-protocol deferred body transformer is also rejected unless it proves its final bytes are exactly the body already produced by the pre-`before_proxy` normalization phase. A plugin with both an observable early body normalization and a later header mutation is still rejected on the header boundary
- Request fingerprints bind the logical key to the HTTP method, authority/host, exact path, the request-transformer-published outbound query when present (otherwise the raw query string), deterministic request headers that can affect routing/transforms, and a SHA-256 request-body digest. Per-request W3C trace-context, B3, AWS X-Ray, generic trace, request, and correlation identifiers are excluded so a retry can carry a fresh trace without producing a false conflict; other routing, security, and representation headers remain semantic. Raw request bodies, credentials, cookies, identities, and idempotency values are not stored in keys or fingerprints
- Multiple scoped instances of `request_deduplication` on one proxy each own request-private completion state (logical key, fingerprint, local owner token, and optional Redis lock token) keyed by process-local instance identity outside public transaction metadata. Composing two instances with distinct headers therefore marks, publishes, and token-releases independently — an earlier instance cannot lose its completion slot to a later sibling, and a successful response cannot leave a stale in-flight conflict under the earlier policy. Local mode and uniquely-prefixed Redis mode share that contract; Redis logical keys remain further partitioned by stable `plugin_config_id` so neighboring dedup/cache metadata under a shared default prefix cannot collide
- **Local-mode state survives plugin-cache reload generations.** Active idempotency leases, retained completed responses, execution barriers, and their accounting are owned by a stable policy identity (`namespace` + plugin-config id), not by the plugin instance. A routine configuration reload that rebuilds the affected proxy/global plugin list hands the replacement instance the *same* local state, so an in-flight request cannot have its duplicate admitted against an empty map, and a completed entry is not forgotten (GHSA-wmqm-6mxj-gm9p). A scope move (`global` ↔ `proxy` ↔ `proxy_group`) that keeps the resource id keeps the state; two tenants that reuse a bare plugin-config id never share it. Changing `header_name`, switching between `local` and `redis`, or changing `on_redis_unavailable` is a semantic change: the replacement isolates onto fresh state, and the retired generation's late completion lands on the state it took its lease from rather than corrupting the new policy. `ttl_seconds`, `inflight_ttl_seconds`, `max_entries`, `max_entry_size_bytes`, and `max_total_size_bytes` are compatible changes that do not reset the protection domain. Each admitted operation, completion, and execution barrier retains the protection window under which it was created, so shortening `inflight_ttl_seconds` cannot make a replacement generation re-execute an older live operation; new operations use the replacement settings. The registry retains every still-live semantic generation, so an A → B → A policy sequence recovers A's active protection domain instead of admitting against a new empty state. Retention is bounded: an identity's state lives only while a configured instance or an in-flight request still holds it, and removing the policy releases it
- On cache hit with the same fingerprint: returns the cached response with `X-Idempotent-Replayed: true` header. Cached bytes are the already-finalized client representation and do not run through ordinary presentation transforms again on replay (same private finalized-replay contract as `response_caching` HIT/REVALIDATED); response inspectors and final-body validators still evaluate the replayed bytes. If current inspection records a redaction decision, that policy's transform alone must rewrite the replay under the current policy or the replay fails closed with 502
- **Presentation-policy provenance.** Every retained response is stamped with digests of the response presentation policy it was produced under: the published `response_transformer` RTDS gate map and the static `response_transformer`, `sse`, and configured-public-base `a2a_gateway` rules on the proxy, in execution order. A replay is served only while both still match. Otherwise — including a Redis record with missing or malformed provenance, or a request that straddled a gate publication — the lookup returns `409 Conflict` rather than re-executing a possibly completed side effect. `compression`, `grpc_web`, `ai_response_guard`, and `ai_tool_governor` are outside the digest; the two guards re-inspect replayed bytes under the current policy and can fail closed with `502`. Only digests are stored. See the [design notes](plugins/request_deduplication.md#presentation-policy-provenance)
- Reusing the same logical idempotency key for a different fingerprint returns `409 Conflict`
- Concurrent duplicates with the same fingerprint return `409 Conflict` while the first request is still in-flight
- Applicable methods with a declared body are buffered before `before_proxy`, even if the idempotency header is not present yet, so earlier header-transform plugins can add the key without making the body unavailable for fingerprinting
- If a request declares a body but the body bytes are unavailable for fingerprinting, the request is rejected with 400 instead of being deduplicated unsafely
- Streamed non-buffered responses, including `text/event-stream`, keep the in-flight marker while the stream is active. On a clean completion the marker is released without retaining a replayable response, so the next matching request re-executes normally. If the stream is interrupted — a client disconnect or mid-stream error — the marker is instead retained until `inflight_ttl_seconds`, so an immediate retry of the same idempotency key cannot re-run a side-effecting backend operation that has no replay/tombstone protection. If the stream sits behind a declared completed external operation, the terminal hook publishes the durable non-replayable tombstone instead of a bare marker, on both clean and interrupted terminations. Each instance applies that stream retention/release decision only to its own ownership tokens
- Gateway-authored backend dispatch failures are never stored as completed responses. A proven pre-wire failure releases only the matching local/Redis owner token when the response is finalized, so a retry can execute. If any attempt may have executed (including an earlier retry attempt), the existing in-flight lease remains until `inflight_ttl_seconds`; a timeout is not an authoritative failure of the operation. Real backend responses, including 500, 502 and 504, remain replayable. This decision uses trusted dispatch provenance, not the HTTP status or a response header
- Stale in-flight markers (request died after `before_proxy` but before buffered/committed response completion or a clean streamed completion — e.g., backend timeout, non-2xx downstream plugin reject, process crash — plus interrupted streams that deliberately retain their marker) are treated as fresh after `inflight_ttl_seconds` so duplicates aren't blocked indefinitely. Tune `inflight_ttl_seconds` to cover your longest legitimate backend request; setting it too low risks duplicate side-effecting executions for slow-but-alive requests. Non-2xx plugin rejects and downstream rejection replacements are intentionally TTL-backed: they do not publish a replayable completion and do not clear the in-flight marker on the commit path, so an identical retry stays conflicted until `inflight_ttl_seconds` expires
- Successful synthetic short-circuits from a later `before_proxy` plugin (for example `response_mock`, `fault_injection`, or `request_termination`) release token-matched local and Redis in-flight ownership once the shared H1/H2/H3 reject finalizer commits a final HTTP 2xx. That release is body-independent: empty 200 and 204/205 responses skip the synthetic response-body hook pipeline, but the finalizer still records a finalized-synthetic lifecycle signal that `on_response_committed` consumes. Non-2xx responses such as 304 remain TTL-backed. Ownership release always matches the exact local owner token and Redis lock token, so a late finalizer cannot clear a successor request's marker. Synthetic bodies are never stored under the idempotency key
- Completed response storage is bounded by `max_entry_size_bytes` and `max_total_size_bytes`. Size-skipped responses still return to the original client, but no replayable response is retained. In local mode, ordinary skipped responses clear the in-flight marker so a later retry can execute normally. A terminate-mode `serverless_function` response, or a buffered backend fallback after that function may have executed, instead atomically replaces the exact owning marker with a fixed-size execution barrier carrying `max(ttl_seconds, inflight_ttl_seconds)` whenever the settled response cannot be retained; it stores no response bytes and a stale hook cannot clear it or a successor. The protection is scoped to outcomes where a side effect may have occurred: a serverless invocation that fails **proven pre-wire** (payload serialization, provider request signing, or a transport class that never reached the function — connect refused/timeout, DNS, TLS, pool/port exhaustion, or an egress-policy denial) releases the in-flight marker like any other pre-invocation rejection, because no function ran; only an ambiguous or post-wire failure (a timeout after send, a mid-response reset, an oversized/unreadable response) publishes the barrier. In Redis mode, the distributed publication remains ownership-fenced, while an ordinary local-total-cap skip keeps local and distributed locks only if Redis publication fails
- **Synthetic and external-operation responses.** A short-circuit that only fabricated a representation (`response_mock`, `fault_injection`, `request_termination`, an `ai_semantic_cache` or `response_caching` hit) releases ownership once committed, and its body is never stored. A short-circuit that performed the protected operation — `serverless_function` terminate mode, or an `ai_federation` provider call once response headers arrived or after an ambiguous post-wire failure — never releases ownership: a retainable terminate-mode `serverless_function` response is published as an ordinary replay, and every other outcome publishes a durable non-replayable `409` completion tombstone for `max(ttl_seconds, inflight_ttl_seconds)`. A `serverless_function` failure proven pre-wire releases ownership. A custom plugin that spends money or mutates remote state behind a short-circuit must declare this provenance or define its own completion contract.
