| `allow_plaintext` | Boolean | `false` | Admit an `http://` `gateway_addresses` entry whose host is not a loopback IP literal (`localhost` included). The trigger key and the triggering request's credentials then cross the network in clear; prefer `https://` peers |

**Ramp behavior:** When `ramp: true`, all client tasks are spawned immediately but each sleeps a stagger delay before sending requests. The delay for client _i_ is `duration * i / concurrent_clients`. All clients share the same deadline, so later clients get less sending time.

Example with `concurrent_clients: 10, duration_seconds: 30, ramp: true`:

| Client | Delay | Starts at | Sends until | Active time |
|--------|-------|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| 0 | 0s | 0s | 30s | 30s |
| 1 | 3s | 3s | 30s | 27s |
| 2 | 6s | 6s | 30s | 24s |
| 3 | 9s | 9s | 30s | 21s |
| 4 | 12s | 12s | 30s | 18s |
| 5 | 15s | 15s | 30s | 15s |
| 6 | 18s | 18s | 30s | 12s |
| 7 | 21s | 21s | 30s | 9s |
| 8 | 24s | 24s | 30s | 6s |
| 9 | 27s | 27s | 30s | 3s |

With `ramp: false` (default), all clients start sending at t=0 simultaneously.

**Caveats:**
- **HTTP/1.1 replays**: Synthetic and fan-out requests are sent over HTTP/1.1 so the preserved `Host` is the request authority. Cohorts therefore measure the backend and the plugin pipeline, not the gateway's HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 frontend framing.
- **HTTP and GraphQL only**: Synthetic requests are plain HTTP via reqwest. gRPC proxies require HTTP/2 with protobuf length-prefixed framing, and WebSocket proxies require an upgrade handshake — neither is supported. GraphQL works because it is standard HTTP POST. TCP/UDP stream proxies are excluded.
- **Auth forwarding**: Synthetic requests forward the triggering request's headers. For auth schemes with short-lived tokens (HMAC timestamps), tokens may expire during long tests.
- **Rate limiting**: Synthetic requests pass through rate limiting plugins, which is realistic but may throttle throughput if limits are tight.

```yaml
plugin_name: load_testing
config:
  key: replace-with-random-32-byte-secret
  concurrent_clients: 50
  duration_seconds: 30
  ramp: true
  request_timeout_ms: 30000
  max_response_body_bytes: 1048576
  gateway_tls: true
  gateway_port: 8443
  gateway_addresses:
    - https://node2:8443
    - https://node3:8443
```

## AI / LLM Plugins

Ferrum includes purpose-built AI/LLM API gateway plugins. Response-parsing AI plugins auto-detect common provider JSON structures, supporting **OpenAI** (and compatible), **Anthropic**, **Google Gemini**, **Cohere**, **Mistral**, and **AWS Bedrock** where applicable.

### AI plugin config validation

AI plugins reject configurations that would otherwise silently degrade to a no-op or fail open; each plugin's section lists its own rules. What a rejected AI plugin config does to the surrounding generation follows the plugin's failure policy (see [Config admission and failure policy](#config-admission-and-failure-policy)). Most AI plugins are generation-rejecting (`FailClosed` or `KeepLastKnownGood`). For an invalid enabled config of such a plugin:

- **Admin API** create/update returns `400` before storing it.
- **File mode** startup refuses to start.
- **Database mode** cold start without a usable `FERRUM_DB_CONFIG_BACKUP_PATH` backup refuses to start; with one, it serves the backup generation with `config_rejected` raised.
- **File, database, and DP reloads** reject the candidate and keep serving the previous valid generation.

`ai_token_metrics` is the exception: it is registered `OptionalFailOpen`. The Admin API still rejects its invalid config directly with `400`, but a serving load logs the constructor error and omits that plugin instance from the published cache instead of rejecting the whole generation. Do not generalize that omission to the generation-rejecting AI plugins above.

### `ai_tool_governor`

**Priority:** 2978 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `on_final_request_body`, `on_response_body`, `transform_response_body`, `on_final_response_body`, `response_stream_inspector`, `on_response_stream_terminated` · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Deterministic allow, deny, argument-redaction, and approval policy for AI tool
definitions and calls across buffered JSON, streaming SSE, MCP, and A2A
surfaces. When composed with `mcp_gateway` `aggregate_router`, policy keys remain
public namespaced tool names across the gateway's trusted upstream-name rewrite.
See the dedicated
[`ai_tool_governor` configuration guide](plugins/ai_tool_governor.md) for the
complete schema, fail-closed behavior, examples, observability contract, and
documented lifecycle limitations.

**Provider coverage.** The buffered and streaming paths cover **different**
provider sets, so read them separately.

| Path | Provider shapes read |
| --- | --- |
| Buffered request tool definitions | OpenAI `tools[].function.name` and legacy `functions[].name`, Anthropic `tools[].name`, Google `tools[].functionDeclarations[].name`, Bedrock `toolConfig.tools[].toolSpec.name` |
| Buffered response tool calls | OpenAI Chat Completions `choices[].message.tool_calls[]` and legacy `function_call`, OpenAI Responses `output[]` `type: "function_call"` items, Anthropic `content[]` `tool_use` blocks, Google `candidates[].content.parts[].functionCall`, Cohere v2 `message.tool_calls[]`, Bedrock Converse `output.message.content[].toolUse` |
| Streaming SSE tool-call deltas | OpenAI Chat Completions `choices[].delta.tool_calls` and legacy `delta.function_call`, OpenAI Responses `response.output_item.added` / `response.function_call_arguments.delta` (every `.done` / `response.completed` restatement must match the accumulated call exactly), Anthropic `content_block_start` / `input_json_delta`, Cohere v2 `tool-call-start` / `tool-call-delta`, Google `candidates[].content.parts[].functionCall` — **these five only** |

**Amazon Bedrock streaming is not accumulated.** There is no
`application/vnd.amazon.eventstream` parser in this plugin: Bedrock's binary
event stream is never parsed as SSE at all, while Bedrock Converse delivered as
a buffered JSON body is governed normally. See the guide's
[limitations](plugins/ai_tool_governor.md#limitations-mvp).

**Policy keys and callers.** `tools` keys are exact tool names or `*` globs
(`github.*`, `*delete*`); an exact key always wins, and among matching globs the
one with the most literal bytes wins (then fewer wildcards, then byte order). A
policy can be scoped with `allowed_consumers` / `denied_consumers` /
`allowed_groups` / `denied_groups` against the mapped Consumer; a deny entry
wins, and with any scope configured a request without a mapped Consumer is
denied. `blocked_arg_patterns` also match the JSON-decoded view of string
arguments, so an escaped spelling cannot hide a match (`redact_args` denies a
match it cannot redact in place). The approval webhook receives an
authority-qualified `principal` (mapped Consumer namespace + id, or external
subject + realm mechanism + opaque authority digest) that also keys the approval
cache, resolves a batch with at most 8 calls in flight, accepts
`approval.headers` (literals or `${FERRUM_PLUGIN_SECRET_<NAME>}` references
resolved at the first call), and admits `http://` only to a loopback IP literal
unless `approval.allow_plaintext: true`. See the guide's
[actions](plugins/ai_tool_governor.md#actions) and
[approval](plugins/ai_tool_governor.md#approval-required-production-writes)
sections.

**Mode semantics.** `mode: enforce` is the only mode that rejects or cuts; it
fails closed on governed, uninspectable cases where the configured posture
requires it, within the configured inspection surfaces and supported
extraction scope. That is not unconditional: a JSON-labelled plaintext
response that is malformed JSON is forwarded (see the guide's
[limitations](plugins/ai_tool_governor.md#limitations-mvp)) — well-formed JSON
beyond the inspection parser's nesting/numeric limits, and an SSE event that is
not valid UTF-8, fail closed instead —
[`approval.fail_on_error`](plugins/ai_tool_governor.md#approval)`=warn`/`allow`
deliberately fails open on an approval endpoint error (the default `reject`
fails closed), and
`unknown_shape_action=allow` is the documented opt-out for a marker-bearing
payload the extractors cannot fully read — a backstop that applies when no
supported call was extracted and, when calls were extracted, to a marker in
any location the extractors did not read. It keys on the documented marker
names, so a dialect with no recognizable marker is still out of scope. `mode: dry_run` never rejects
and never calls the approval webhook — it evaluates policy, records what
enforce *would* have done, and forwards — so it is the safe rollout/observe
posture. Global dry-run **preserves the would-be policy label** rather than
relabelling it: an ordinary denied call is recorded as
`ai_tool_governor.mode=dry_run` with `ai_tool_governor.decision=deny`, and an
approval-gated call with `decision=require_approval`. `decision=dry_run` is
reserved for the distinct per-tool `action: dry_run` policy and for the
dry-run duplicate-key (`uninspectable_reason=ambiguous_json`) observation. Find
global dry-run findings by querying `mode`, not `decision`.

**Unreadable shapes.** A payload carrying a tool-call marker the
plugin cannot read is an **extraction failure, not an allow**:
`unknown_shape_action` (default `deny`) makes enforce fail closed on it, while
the documented `allow` opt-out forwards it. Both settings record the fixed
`ai_tool_governor.uninspectable_reason=unrecognized_tool_call_shape`
observation, so the case is never silent in either mode. The observation
writer itself never invents a policy decision; on the forwarding paths
(`allow`, or `dry_run`) it does not set `decision` (a stronger decision from
another surface can still stand), while the default enforce rejection path
records `ai_tool_governor.decision=deny` as the rejection outcome alongside
the fixed reason — when metadata emission is enabled.

**Bounded observation metadata.** The cumulative comma-delimited fields
(`tool_names`, `policy_ids`, `approval_id`, `arguments_hashes`,
`redacted_tools`) aggregate by winning decision rank across the governed
surfaces of a request and the completed batches of a response stream: a
lower-rank batch is ignored, an equal-rank batch merges into the retained
ledger, and a stronger batch replaces the weaker decision's ledger basis.
Each field is capped at 64 distinct values and 8192 bytes (the byte cap
includes comma and marker bytes), with individual values retained to at most
256 bytes plus a trailing `…` marker when shortened (259 bytes in total). A
stream that keeps emitting distinct tool names cannot grow that state without
limit — unlimited streaming is a documented response-byte setting, so no
wire-byte ceiling bounds it. Distinct truncated values dropped by an entry or
byte cap during a merge are counted in
`ai_tool_governor.observations_omitted` (it is not a count of rank-displaced
observations); enforcement, the sticky highest `decision`, and `risk` — the
maximum within the winning decision rank, so a stronger decision can replace
a previous rank's higher risk — are unaffected. See the guide's
[observability metadata](plugins/ai_tool_governor.md#observability-metadata).

### `ai_transcript_audit`

**Priority:** 2740 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `on_final_request_body`, `after_proxy`, `on_final_response_body`, `on_response_committed`, `response_stream_inspector`, `on_response_stream_terminated`, `log` · **Protocols:** HTTP, gRPC · **Failure policy:** `KeepLastKnownGood`

Controlled AI payload capture for compliance review, incident response, support debugging, and evaluation datasets. It captures redacted AI requests and responses, keyed body hashes, model/provider, token, guardrail, tool, and cache metadata, and exports them asynchronously in batches to an HTTP collector. It observes and redacts; it does not enforce policy.

```yaml
plugin_name: ai_transcript_audit
config:
  sink:
    type: http
    endpoint_url: https://audit.example.com/v1/transcripts
```

Full configuration reference, behavior, and examples: [plugins/ai_transcript_audit.md](plugins/ai_transcript_audit.md).

### `ai_federation`

**Priority:** 4060 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `transform_request_body_with_context`, finalized request egress, `enforce_final_backend_header_policy`, `on_final_request_body_with_context`, origin response-header boundary, `after_proxy`, `response_stream_inspector`, on_response_stream_terminated (HTTP only) · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `KeepLastKnownGood`

HTTP-family AI gateway that routes OpenAI Chat Completions JSON to supported providers, translates native request/response shapes, and returns an OpenAI-shaped synthetic response. Provider dispatch runs from the finalized-request-egress phase, after request decompression, body transforms, and every final request-policy hook. Streaming is an explicit opt-in; native gRPC is unsupported.

```yaml
plugin_name: ai_federation
config:
  providers:
    - name: openai
      provider_type: openai
      api_key: "sk-..."
      model_patterns: ["gpt-*"]
```

Full configuration reference, behavior, and examples: [plugins/ai_federation.md](plugins/ai_federation.md).

### `ai_stream_router`

**Priority:** 2984 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `transform_request_body`, `enforce_final_backend_header_policy`, `on_final_request_body`, `normalize_response_body`, `after_proxy`, `response_stream_inspector` · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Streaming counterpart to `ai_federation`. It claims only OpenAI Chat Completions requests with a real `"stream": true` boolean, rewrites the routing decision to the matching provider, and lets the normal proxy dispatch path stream the provider response back to the client. Non-streaming requests are left for `ai_federation`.

```yaml
plugin_name: ai_stream_router
config:
  providers:
    - name: openai
      provider_type: openai
      endpoint: https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions
      api_key: ${FERRUM_PLUGIN_SECRET_OPENAI_API_KEY}
      model_patterns: ["gpt-*"]
```

Full configuration reference, behavior, and examples: [plugins/ai_stream_router.md](plugins/ai_stream_router.md).

### `ai_semantic_firewall`

**Priority:** 2968 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `on_final_request_body`, `on_response_body`, `on_final_response_body`, `response_stream_inspector`, `on_response_stream_terminated` · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Semantically inspects LLM request and response bodies for prompt injection, jailbreaks, system-prompt and sensitive-data exfiltration, indirect injection in RAG/tool/document content, tool-call abuse, business-topic allow/deny lists, and response leakage, using a configured embedding provider. It does not implement size limits, timeouts, token budgets, or regex PII scanning; use the native gateway controls and the other AI guard plugins for those.

```yaml
plugin_name: ai_semantic_firewall
config:
  mode: dry_run
  on_error: warn
  provider:
    type: openai_compatible_embeddings
    endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/embeddings
    model: text-embedding-3-small
    api_key_env: FERRUM_PLUGIN_SECRET_EMBEDDING_API_KEY
```

Full configuration reference, behavior, and examples: [plugins/ai_semantic_firewall.md](plugins/ai_semantic_firewall.md).

### `ai_semantic_cache`

**Priority:** 4057 · **Phases:** `on_final_request_body_with_context`, `after_proxy`, `on_final_response_body`, `on_response_committed` · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `KeepLastKnownGood`

Caches LLM responses keyed by family-correct prompts across Ferrum's recognized AI request families. The default exact-match key preserves LLM-significant prompt case and whitespace; optional semantic similarity looks up prompt embeddings, computed by a configured embedding provider, in a local vector index. Exact responses are stored in local memory or centralized Redis.

```yaml
plugin_name: ai_semantic_cache
config:
  ttl_seconds: 600
  max_entries: 5000
  max_entry_size_bytes: 2097152
  include_model_in_key: true
  scope_by_consumer: true
```

Full configuration reference, behavior, and examples: [plugins/ai_semantic_cache.md](plugins/ai_semantic_cache.md).

### `ai_token_metrics`

**Priority:** 4070 · **Phases:** `on_response_body`, `response_stream_inspector`, `on_response_stream_terminated` · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `OptionalFailOpen`

Extracts token usage from LLM HTTP JSON response bodies and from streamed SSE / AWS event-stream responses, and writes it to request metadata for downstream logging and observability plugins. This plugin is observability-only: it never rejects requests and does not enforce a token budget. Use `ai_rate_limiter` for enforced budget controls. Streamed responses are metered incrementally by default, without buffering (see **Streaming token accounting** below). Native gRPC protobuf responses are not supported: the plugin advertises only HTTP attachment rather than pretending arbitrary protobuf messages have a verifiable usage schema.

Runs after `ai_federation` (4060) and before `ai_response_guard` (4075). A guard rejection stops the `on_response_body` loop and replaces a 2xx body the provider already generated, and a streaming guard cut stops later stream inspectors from seeing the terminal usage event. Running first keeps that consumed generation's tokens and estimated cost in metadata and Prometheus while the client still receives the guard's error.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `provider` | String | `"auto"` | LLM provider format |
| `include_model` | Boolean | `true` | Extract model name into metadata |
| `include_token_details` | Boolean | `true` | Extract prompt/completion tokens separately |
| `metadata_prefix` | String | `"ai"` | Prefix for metadata keys (1–64 ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `_`, or `-`) |
| `buffer_streaming_responses` | Boolean | `false` | Buffer `text/event-stream` responses and meter them after the full response is collected; this disables streaming delivery for those responses. Not required for SSE token accounting, which observes streams incrementally by default |
| `cost_per_prompt_token` | Number or null | *(none)* | Prompt-token cost rate, from `0` through `18446744073709.55`; omission or `null` disables this rate |
| `cost_per_completion_token` | Number or null | *(none)* | Completion-token cost rate, from `0` through `18446744073709.55`; omission or `null` disables this rate |
| `model_pricing` | Object[] | `[]` | Ordered per-model rate overrides (at most 128). Each entry has a `model` glob plus `cost_per_prompt_token` and/or `cost_per_completion_token` (same range as the flat rates; at least one must be a number). The first entry whose glob matches the response's model supplies the rates; when none matches, or the response reports no publishable model, the flat rates apply |

**Note**: Requires response body buffering for JSON responses. `text/event-stream` responses are not buffered by default so LLM streaming remains live, including on retry-enabled routes without an `Accept` header: origin SSE and AWS event-stream headers release this plugin's buffering requirement. Non-2xx responses are never collected for this plugin, since their bodies are not inspected. Other active body plugins or an explicitly buffered route may still require collection; a collected SSE body is then metered from the buffered body whether or not `buffer_streaming_responses` is set. Set `buffer_streaming_responses: true` only when an encoded (`gzip`/`br`) SSE origin must be metered — the incremental observer cannot read content-coded streams — and streaming delivery may be sacrificed for it.

**Streaming token accounting:** A streamed 2xx `text/event-stream` or `application/vnd.amazon.eventstream` response is metered by a pass-through stream inspector on H1/H2 and native H3. Every chunk is forwarded unchanged and immediately while the shared bounded usage extractor (the same parser `ai_rate_limiter` uses, with 64 KiB line/event and AWS message caps and verified AWS prelude/message CRCs) reads it, so first-token latency and backpressure are unaffected. When the stream ends — normally, on a backend error, on a later inspector's cut, or by client disconnect — the terminal stream hook publishes the usage the provider reported (metadata, cost, and the typed Prometheus snapshot) exactly once before the transaction is logged; a stream cut short publishes what it reported so far. The provider label follows the stream's shape under `provider: auto` and the configured provider otherwise. At most 4,096 streams are observed concurrently per process; beyond that, and for content-coded origin streams or transports that cannot attach an inspector, the stream is delivered untouched and labelled `stream_not_inspected`. OpenAI-compatible providers report streamed usage only when the request sets `stream_options.include_usage: true`.

**Model pricing:** `model_pricing` globs use the same anchored, `*`-only grammar as `ai_federation` / `ai_stream_router` `model_patterns`: 1–256 ASCII bytes of letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-`, `:`, `/`, `+`, or `*`, without `..`; `*` never crosses `/ ? # & \` or whitespace. List more specific patterns first (for example `gpt-4o-mini*` before `gpt-4o*`). An entry's omitted rate leaves that side unpriced for matching models rather than falling back to the flat rate. Federation usage carries no trusted model, so it is priced at the flat rates.

**Unmetered responses:** When a 2xx JSON or streamed response yields no usage, `{prefix}_unmetered_reason` names why, so dashboards and alerts can tell "unmetered" apart from "zero usage": `body_too_large` (a collected body, as received and before any decoding, above the 4 MiB inspection limit — this applies to plain JSON too), `decode_failed` (unsupported, malformed, or over-limit `Content-Encoding`), `malformed_body` (unparseable JSON), `provider_undetected` (`provider: auto` could not identify the shape), `no_usage` (empty body or no usage fields), `stream_not_inspected`, or `stream_without_usage` (the stream ended without a usable usage report, including one whose malformed counters invalidated it). A later malformed usage update that invalidates all previously observed counters leaves the response labelled: live streams use `stream_without_usage`, and collected SSE bodies use `no_usage`. This also applies when a live stream ends by client disconnect. Synthetic short-circuit bodies, non-2xx responses, and non-JSON/non-stream content types are not labelled. Only extraction of at least one usable counter, including an explicit zero, clears the key.

**Model name bound:** The backend-reported model is published as `{prefix}_model` (and used to select `model_pricing`) only when it is 1–256 bytes without control characters; a longer or control-bearing value is omitted while token counts and the flat-rate cost are still recorded.

`provider` must use one exact lowercase enum value: `auto`, `openai`, `anthropic`, `google`, `cohere`, `mistral`, `bedrock`, or `tgi` (Hugging Face TGI native `/generate` shapes, whose counter is `details.generated_tokens`). Surrounding whitespace and alternate casing are rejected. Every unknown root configuration key is rejected at startup with the allowed-key list, so misspellings cannot silently change accounting or cost behavior.

**Token categories.** Every metering surface counts the same categories: `ai_token_metrics`, `ai_rate_limiter`, the `ai_stream_router` normalizers and the `ai_federation` normalizers.
- Anthropic `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` are added to `input_tokens`, since Anthropic reports them beside it rather than inside it.
- Bedrock Converse `cacheReadInputTokens` and `cacheWriteInputTokens` are added to `inputTokens`.
- Gemini/Vertex `toolUsePromptTokenCount` is added to the prompt, and `thoughtsTokenCount` (billed output that is not part of `candidatesTokenCount`) to the completion.
- For Gemini and Bedrock (Converse and invocation metrics), a provider total stays authoritative but is never published below the sum of the counters it reports. When it is lower and a component is unknown, the report is inconsistent and no complete total is published. OpenAI-compatible totals are passed through as reported.
- A cache category reported without the base count its provider always sends (Anthropic `input_tokens`, Bedrock `inputTokens`) leaves the whole usage unmetered; the federation normalizers refuse it.
- On the native Anthropic stream, the `message_start` `output_tokens` placeholder is not taken as the completion count; the cumulative output on `message_delta` is.

OpenAI already includes cached and reasoning tokens in `prompt_tokens` / `completion_tokens`. The cost rates are flat per category, so for a prompt-cached request the estimate is approximate. Cache reads, which providers bill below the base input rate, are overestimated. Cache writes, which Anthropic bills at 1.25× or 2× the base input rate, are underestimated. Prompt-token budgets charge the whole billed input.

Categories merge field by field across a stream, so an event that restates only some of them (for example an Anthropic `message_delta` carrying `input_tokens` without the cache counters) never erases what an earlier event reported. A malformed counter, an overflowing sum, or a cache category without its required base makes the WHOLE usage unmetered (prompt, completion and total), so the configured unmetered-response policy decides rather than a partial count, a `null` counter is absence, and a Gemini base omitted by proto3 zero-omission counts as zero when a sibling category on that side is reported. A category sum that overflows is treated like any other overflowing usage: the whole usage is unmetered rather than saturated or wrapped. An explicit provider total is never below the components the same usage reports, even when only one side is present. On the `ai_stream_router` and `ai_federation` normalizers, a malformed or overflowing counter fails the response instead (stream terminated / normalization error).

**Status filtering**: Only 2xx responses are inspected for token usage. Error responses (4xx, 5xx) are typically not LLM-shaped JSON and would otherwise pollute token metrics and chargeback accounting.

**Provider and streaming support:** OpenAI Chat Completions and the Responses API (`input_tokens`/`output_tokens`, including the terminal `response.completed` and `response.incomplete` events) are supported. Anthropic `message_start` and `message_delta` usage is merged without losing an earlier input count. Gemini/Vertex `usageMetadata`, Cohere token counts, Bedrock Converse usage, and Amazon Titan InvokeModel `inputTextTokenCount` plus a single `results[].tokenCount` are supported. TGI native JSON and terminal SSE use `details.generated_tokens`; prompt counts are available only with a non-empty `details.prefill` array, and missing prompt counts are not invented. AWS binary event-stream frames are parsed by the same bounded extractor whether the response streams or was collected (for example by a sibling plugin). Buffered SSE events join multiple `data:` fields with newlines and accept LF, CRLF, or CR line endings; a blank line dispatches each event, leading BOMs are ignored, and a final event whose terminating blank line (or newline) is missing is still dispatched at end of body, as on the streaming path. Cumulative and partial snapshots are merged field-by-field; repeated cumulative terminal events replace their fields instead of being summed, and `response.failed` and the progress `response.*` events are not treated as authoritative usage (`response.incomplete` is terminal — a finished response that stopped early, for example at `max_output_tokens` — and its reported usage is read like `response.completed`). Malformed, non-integer, ambiguous, or overflowing usage is ignored rather than saturated or invented. Model name is extracted from the first parseable event that carries a publishable one. Sets `{prefix}_streaming: true` metadata when processing a streamed or buffered SSE / event-stream response.

**Cohere accounting:** Counts come from `usage.tokens` (v2 JSON), `delta.usage.tokens` (v2 terminal SSE), or `meta.tokens` (v1), in that precedence order. Separate `billed_units` objects are not used; a billed-units-only response contributes no usage. Estimated cost multiplies the extracted token counts by the configured rates and does not represent provider billable-unit accounting.

**Origin content encodings:** Buffered JSON and SSE inspection supports case-insensitive `gzip` and `br`, including correctly ordered coding chains. Inspection is bounded to four codings, 4 MiB for every decoded layer, and 8 MiB cumulative decoded work across the chain. Parameterized, unsupported, malformed, truncated, trailing/concatenated, or oversized encodings are skipped safely. Decoding is inspection-only: the original encoded response bytes and headers remain exactly client-visible.

**Prometheus export:** A globally scoped `prometheus_metrics` plugin exports prompt, completion, and total token counters plus estimated cost from typed usage snapshots produced only by direct `ai_token_metrics` inspection or `ai_federation`. Public transaction metadata is never provenance for export. Labels are limited to `proxy_id`, the bounded provider family, and the configured metrics namespace—raw model names, metadata prefixes, federation provider aliases, and arbitrary request metadata are never labels. Multiple `ai_token_metrics` instances contribute one most-complete token snapshot and at most one independently selected trusted cost per request, so a detailed unpriced instance cannot discard configured pricing and overlapping prefixes cannot double count. Configured rates also price trusted federation usage when the instance provider matches the serving provider family. Estimated cost retains a sub-micro fixed-point remainder while accumulating, publishes rounded totals atomically, and is emitted in currency units with exactly six decimal places.

```yaml
plugin_name: ai_token_metrics
config:
  provider: auto
  buffer_streaming_responses: false
  cost_per_prompt_token: 0.000003
  cost_per_completion_token: 0.000012
  model_pricing:
    - model: "gpt-4o-mini*"
      cost_per_prompt_token: 0.00000015
      cost_per_completion_token: 0.0000006
    - model: "gpt-4o*"
      cost_per_prompt_token: 0.0000025
      cost_per_completion_token: 0.00001
```

### `ai_request_guard`

**Priority:** 2975 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `transform_request_body`, `on_final_request_body` · **Protocols:** HTTP, gRPC · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Validates and constrains AI/LLM API requests before they reach the backend.

Request buffering is enabled for `POST` requests when at least one guard or transform rule is configured. The scope is **not** selected from the client's `Content-Type` alone, because many backends parse the body as JSON whatever its declared media type: a declared JSON `POST` is inspected as JSON, and a `POST` whose `Content-Type` is missing, non-JSON (`text/plain`, a form type, ...), or a duplicated/joined value (`text/plain, application/json`) is buffered and *sniffed* — when its UTF-8 body opens a JSON object (`{`, after an optional BOM and whitespace) it is evaluated exactly like a declared JSON body (malformed JSON then fails closed as below); anything else (prose, forms, non-UTF-8 bytes) passes through. Only framed gRPC / gRPC-Web and opaque upload media types (`multipart/*`, `application/octet-stream`, `audio/*`, `image/*`, `video/*`, unless the value also mentions `json`) stay unbuffered and streaming. By default, configured guard policies fail closed when an in-scope body cannot be inspected: malformed JSON, ambiguous JSON (see **Duplicate object members** below), empty JSON bodies, non-UTF-8 declared-JSON bodies, or missing buffered-body metadata are rejected before backend dispatch. Oversized bodies are rejected earlier by the proxy request-body buffer limit. Production AI proxies should keep this default so malformed or unbuffered requests cannot bypass model, token, prompt, or metadata policy; set `fail_on_uninspectable_body: false` only for compatibility when the upstream service must own malformed JSON handling.

Every configured key is validated at startup. Unknown top-level keys are rejected instead of being ignored, so a misspelled policy cannot silently leave the guard only partially configured.

**Compressed request bodies fail closed.** A co-located `compression` plugin with `decompress_request: true` normalizes supported gzip/Brotli uploads before the guard's `before_proxy` phase, so the guard applies reject-style policy directly to bounded plaintext. The guard also revalidates in `on_final_request_body` after all later request-body transforms so a transform cannot reintroduce a prohibited value:

- If a matching compression plugin recognizes the coding, malformed or over-limit compressed data is rejected before the guard runs; a successful decode removes `Content-Encoding` and the guard inspects plaintext normally.
- If nothing decompressed the body (no compression plugin or an unsupported coding), the body remains compressed and uninspectable, so the guard rejects it by default (reason `compressed_body`). Set `fail_on_uninspectable_body: false` only when the upstream intentionally owns that representation.

Every in-scope request is revalidated in `on_final_request_body` after all request-body transforms, so a later `request_transformer` cannot replace a validated model, token cap, prompt, system role, schema marker, or required field. The final hook cannot rewrite body bytes: if a later transform reintroduces a value above a clamp limit or removes or corrupts a required default output cap, the request is rejected rather than forwarded outside policy. The same rule applies after decompression; clamp/default mutation is not re-applied in the final hook, so the final body must already carry numeric, compliant caps.

**Framed gRPC and gRPC-Web bodies are skipped, not rejected.** `application/grpc*` and `application/grpc-web*` content types (including the `+json` variants such as `application/grpc-web-text+json`) carry length-prefixed — and, for `-text`, base64 — gRPC wire frames, not bare JSON documents, so the JSON policies do not apply and the request passes through. In a normal deployment the `grpc_web` plugin rewrites gRPC-Web to native `application/grpc` before this plugin runs; the gRPC-Web skip ensures a proxy that has `ai_request_guard` but no `grpc_web` plugin does not 400 real gRPC-Web traffic.

The residual **content-type confusion** gap is now limited to requests the guard deliberately leaves unbuffered or cannot sniff: non-`POST` methods, opaque upload media types (`multipart/*`, `application/octet-stream`, `audio/*`, `image/*`, `video/*`), and a body that is both compressed (`Content-Encoding` other than `identity`, with no `compression` plugin normalizing it first) **and** labelled non-JSON. A client that sends a JSON payload under one of those presentations to a backend that parses it as JSON regardless of `Content-Type` (and, for the compressed case, also decompresses it) can still bypass policy. Closing that remainder requires the backend itself refusing any request that is not a well-formed JSON `POST`, or a co-located `compression` plugin with `decompress_request: true` so compressed bodies are normalized before the guard runs. JSON-labelled `POST` bodies that are absent, empty, malformed, non-UTF-8, ambiguous, or still compressed are not part of this gap: they fail closed by default (see above).

**Duplicate object members are rejected.** `serde_json` keeps the LAST of two same-named members while many backends and SDKs keep the FIRST, so a body such as `{"model": "o3", "model": "gpt-4o-mini", ...}` would be evaluated as one document and executed as another. Both `before_proxy` and the final-body pass screen the exact bytes with the shared bounded `json_dup_keys` scanner before parsing — escaped spellings of the same name (`"mod\u0065l"`) and duplicates under any nested object count — and reject a hit as an uninspectable body (reason `ambiguous_json`, HTTP 400; a document beyond the scanner's budgets is refused the same way). `fail_on_uninspectable_body: false` passes such a body through unevaluated, like every other uninspectable body.

**Anthropic Message Batches.** A body with a top-level `requests` array whose entries carry `params` objects (`{"requests": [{"custom_id": ..., "params": {...}}]}`) is evaluated **per entry**: every configured policy (strict schema, model, tokens, completions, messages, prompt characters, temperature, system prompts, required fields) applies to each `params` object as one complete request, clamp and `default_max_tokens` rewrite each entry, and the final-body pass re-checks each entry. Limits are per entry, not summed across the batch. An entry without a `params` object is rejected (`Invalid batch request entry`). An envelope that carries any other top-level member beside `requests` is additionally evaluated (and rewritten) as a request itself, so a request field cannot sit beside the batch unevaluated.

**Request-supplied integer controls.** Output-token caps and completion counts are read the way the governed providers read them, so a value a backend honors is never treated as "no value": JSON integers, integral floats and exponents (`8192.0`, `5e5`), and quoted spellings of those (Gemini ProtoJSON accepts quoted integers; lax Python servers coerce them) are evaluated by value — reject compares it, clamp replaces an over-limit value with the numeric limit, and a value above `uint64` saturates. A present cap that is negative, fractional, non-finite, boolean, an array/object, or an unparseable string is rejected with HTTP 400 (`Invalid max_tokens field`) whenever `max_tokens_limit` or `default_max_tokens` is configured, in both reject and clamp modes. JSON `null` means "unset": it is treated as absent, so `default_max_tokens` replaces it. Gemini fields are read in both ProtoJSON spellings (`generationConfig` / `generation_config`, `maxOutputTokens` / `max_output_tokens`, `candidateCount` / `candidate_count`); a body that carries both spellings of one field — even when one of them is `null`, which a ProtoJSON parser applies as "clear this field" — is ambiguous and rejected (`Conflicting field spellings`); a single `null` spelling is just "unset" and `default_max_tokens` replaces it under that same spelling whenever a token, completion-count, or temperature policy is configured.

**Decision metadata.** Every rejection records `ai_request_guard.action = "reject"` and a fixed-cardinality `ai_request_guard.reason`: `unsupported_schema`, `conflicting_fields`, `model_blocked`, `model_not_allowed`, `invalid_model`, `missing_model`, `invalid_max_tokens`, `max_tokens_exceeded`, `invalid_choice_count`, `max_choices_exceeded`, `too_many_messages`, `prompt_too_long`, `invalid_temperature`, `conflicting_temperature`, `temperature_out_of_range`, `system_prompt`, `missing_user`, `missing_metadata_field`, `invalid_batch_entry`, `missing_max_tokens` (a later transform removed a required default cap), or `uninspectable_body` (detailed by the existing `ai_request_guard.uninspectable_body_reason`). A clamp or default-cap rewrite records `ai_request_guard.action = "modify"` with reason `max_tokens_clamped`, `default_max_tokens_injected`, or `max_tokens_clamped_and_default_injected`. A request that passes unmodified carries neither key. The values never echo request content.

At least one policy field (`max_tokens_limit`, `default_max_tokens`, `max_choices`, `allowed_models`, `blocked_models`, `require_user_field`, `max_messages`, `max_prompt_characters`, `temperature_range`, `block_system_prompts`, `strict_schema`, or `required_metadata_fields`) must be configured. The plugin rejects empty configs at construction time so a misconfigured instance never silently passes everything through. Model allow- and block-lists are matched case-insensitively. When `allowed_models` or `blocked_models` is configured, requests must include a non-empty string `model` field by default; missing or non-string model values fail closed with HTTP 400. Set `require_model_for_model_policy: false` only for compatibility with backends that intentionally derive the model outside the request body — the opt-out relaxes **only** the genuinely-absent case. A `model` that is present but invalid (a non-string value, or an empty/whitespace string) is still rejected with HTTP 400 even with the opt-out, so a malformed value can never skip the allow-/block-list.

**Models in the request path.** Gemini/Vertex, Bedrock, and Azure OpenAI select the model in the URL rather than the body, so model policy also reads the canonical request path (matched per segment, ASCII case-insensitively, anywhere in the path so a route prefix does not hide it): Gemini/Vertex `.../models/{model}:{method}` and `.../tunedModels/{model}:{method}`, Bedrock runtime `.../model/{modelId}/converse|converse-stream|invoke|invoke-with-response-stream|count-tokens` (an unencoded ARN containing `/` is rejoined), and Azure OpenAI `.../openai/deployments/{deployment}/...` (list deployment names in `allowed_models` / `blocked_models`). Every model found — in the path and in the body — must pass the allow-/block-list, so a body `model` cannot override a blocked path model or vice versa. A path model also satisfies the "model must be present" rule, so a Gemini `generateContent` body without `model` is admitted when its path model is allowed. Other path shapes (for example a route rewritten to hide the model) are not recognized; pair the guard with routing that pins the backend path when that matters.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max_tokens_limit` | Unsigned integer (`uint64`) | *(none)* | Maximum allowed output-token request value across OpenAI and provider-native token fields. `0` is accepted (refuses any request asking for a positive number of tokens); must be `>= default_max_tokens` when both are set |
| `enforce_max_tokens` | String | `"reject"` | `reject` (400 error) or `clamp` (silently cap) |
| `default_max_tokens` | Unsigned integer (`uint64`) | *(none)* | Must be `<= max_tokens_limit` when that limit is also configured. Inject a default output-token limit if no supported token field is present (a `null` cap counts as absent); an OpenAI-shaped body keeps a top-level `max_tokens` fallback (so a spoofed provider marker cannot uncap it), while an unambiguously provider-native body receives only its native cap (including TGI `parameters.max_new_tokens`). Under `supported_schema: bedrock_converse` every body receives `inferenceConfig.maxTokens` (created when absent) and no top-level cap |
| `max_choices` | Unsigned integer (`uint64`) | *(none)* | Maximum completions one request may ask for, across OpenAI `n` / `best_of`, Cohere `num_generations`, Gemini `generationConfig.candidateCount` (both ProtoJSON spellings), and TGI `parameters.best_of`. `max_tokens_limit` bounds tokens **per completion**, so the per-request worst case is `max_choices` × `max_tokens_limit`. A larger or non-integer value is rejected. A request that omits the count (or sends `0`) is counted as the provider default of one completion, so `0` refuses every request |
| `supported_schema` | String | `"auto"` | Schema family used when `strict_schema` is true: `chat_completions`, `responses`, `provider_native`, `bedrock_converse`, or `auto`. `bedrock_converse` admits `messages`-array bodies and also binds `default_max_tokens` injection to Bedrock Converse |
| `strict_schema` | Boolean | `false` | Reject request bodies that do not match `supported_schema` coverage |
| `allowed_models` | String[] | `[]` | Allowlist of exact model names, matched case-insensitively (empty = allow all; no glob patterns) against the body `model` and every request-path model (see **Models in the request path**) |
| `blocked_models` | String[] | `[]` | Blocklist of exact model names, matched case-insensitively (takes precedence), against the body `model` and every request-path model |
| `require_model_for_model_policy` | Boolean | `true` | Require a non-empty string `model` when `allowed_models` or `blocked_models` is configured, unless the request path selects a model. Set `false` to allow a genuinely-absent `model`; a present-but-invalid `model` (non-string or empty/whitespace) is rejected regardless |
| `require_user_field` | Boolean | `false` | Require a non-empty string `user` field in the request body (`null` and blank values are rejected) |
| `max_messages` | Unsigned integer (`uint64`) | *(none)* | Maximum message entries across `messages`, Responses `input`, Gemini `contents`, and Cohere `chat_history` arrays, plus a non-empty Cohere top-level `message` (the current turn) counted as one entry. `0` is accepted (refuses any request carrying a counted message entry) |
| `max_prompt_characters` | Unsigned integer (`uint64`) | *(none)* | Maximum total prompt characters across prompt/input/system fields, message text, text multimodal parts, Bedrock Converse `messages[].content[]` `toolResult` content and `guardContent` text, tools (including Bedrock Converse `toolConfig.tools[]`), tool arguments (including Bedrock Converse `messages[].content[].toolUse.input`) and Gemini `contents[].parts[].functionResponse.response` tool results, document/RAG fields (including Anthropic text-document `source.data` and every eligible member of a Cohere `documents[]` map), Google Vertex legacy `predict` `instances[].prompt`, and Azure "On Your Data" `data_sources[].parameters.role_information`. `0` is accepted (refuses any request carrying counted text) |
| `temperature_range` | Float[2] | *(none)* | Allowed [min, max] range for top-level `temperature`, Gemini `generationConfig.temperature` / `generation_config.temperature`, and Bedrock `inferenceConfig.temperature`; wrong-typed or conflicting aliases are rejected. Both bounds must be finite and `temperature_range[0] <= temperature_range[1]` |
| `block_system_prompts` | Boolean | `false` | Reject system/developer prompt fields and roles, including Responses `instructions`, provider-native top-level system fields, and Azure "On Your Data" `data_sources[].parameters.role_information` (a de-facto system instruction the backend applies) |
| `system_prompt_aliases` | String[] | `[]` | Additional message roles or top-level fields treated as system prompts when `block_system_prompts` is true |
| `required_metadata_fields` | String[] | `[]` | Required top-level fields in the request body; each must be present, not `null`, and not a blank string (other value types are accepted) |
| `fail_on_uninspectable_body` | Boolean | `true` | Reject in-scope `POST` requests whose body is missing, empty, non-UTF-8, malformed JSON, ambiguous JSON (duplicate object members or over the duplicate-scan budgets), or still compressed after request transforms (no `compression`/`decompress_request` decoded it) |

**Numeric configuration contract.** `max_tokens_limit`, `default_max_tokens`, `max_choices`, `max_messages`, and `max_prompt_characters` are unsigned 64-bit integers. A negative, fractional, or above-`uint64` value is rejected at plugin construction (`ferrum-edge validate` and startup both fail), and `0` is a valid, maximally strict setting rather than "unset" — omit the field to leave that policy unconfigured. Two relationships between sibling values are also enforced at construction and cannot be expressed in JSON Schema 2020-12, so the published `AiRequestGuardConfig` component admits configurations the gateway then refuses; operator tooling that generates or validates configs must apply both as supplemental checks:

- `default_max_tokens <= max_tokens_limit` whenever both are configured (the injected default is never clamped, so a larger default would make the gateway emit a value that violates the operator's own limit).
- `temperature_range[0] <= temperature_range[1]`, with both bounds finite.

**Schema coverage**

| Schema family | Message count | Prompt character coverage | System prompt blocking | Output-token fields |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OpenAI Chat Completions | `messages[]` | `messages[].content`, text multimodal parts, `tools[]`, function-call `arguments`, document/RAG fields | `messages[].role: "system"|"developer"` and aliases | `max_tokens`, `max_completion_tokens` |
| OpenAI Responses API | `input[]` message entries | `instructions`, `input` string/array/message content, `tools[]`, function-call `arguments`, `function_call_output.output` tool results | `instructions`, `input[].role: "system"|"developer"` | `max_output_tokens`, `max_tokens` |
| Anthropic Messages | `messages[]` | top-level `system`, `messages[].content`, text-document `content[].source.data`, `content[]` `tool_use` block `input` tool arguments, `documents`, `context`, `retrieved_context`, `tool_results` | top-level `system`, system/developer roles if present | `max_tokens` |
| Gemini/Vertex native-ish | `contents[]` | `systemInstruction`, `system_instruction`, `contents[].parts[].text`, `contents[].parts[].functionCall.args` tool arguments and `functionResponse.response` tool results (both ProtoJSON spellings), tools, document/RAG fields | `systemInstruction`, `system_instruction`, aliased roles/fields | `generationConfig.maxOutputTokens` (and the `generation_config` / `max_output_tokens` ProtoJSON spellings), top-level `maxOutputTokens` |
| Bedrock Converse/native-ish | `messages[]` | `system`, `toolConfig.tools[]` tool definitions, `messages[].content`, `content[].toolUse.input` tool arguments (the canonical Converse spelling) and `content[]` `tool_use` block `input` (the typed Anthropic spelling), `content[].toolResult` content, `content[].guardContent` text, tool results, document/RAG fields | top-level `system`, system/developer roles if present | `inferenceConfig.maxTokens`, top-level `maxTokens` (see token-injection note) |
| Cohere native-ish | `chat_history[]` plus `message` | `preamble`, `message`, `chat_history[].message`, every eligible member value of each `documents[]` map (excluding `id` and `_excludes`-named members), tool arguments/results | `preamble`, aliased roles/fields | `max_tokens`, `max_new_tokens` |
| Amazon Titan text-generation | *(not a message array)* | top-level `inputText` | system/developer roles if present | `textGenerationConfig.maxTokenCount` |
| Azure OpenAI "On Your Data" | `messages[]` (chat completions shape) | `messages[].content` and other chat-completions fields, plus `data_sources[]`/`dataSources[]` `parameters.role_information`/`roleInformation` | `messages[].role: "system"|"developer"`, aliases, and any non-empty `role_information`/`roleInformation` | `max_tokens`, `max_completion_tokens` |
| Legacy completions / text-generation | *(not a message array)* | top-level `prompt`, `input`, TGI/HuggingFace `inputs` | system/developer roles if present | `max_tokens`, `max_new_tokens`, `max_tokens_to_sample`, TGI `parameters.max_new_tokens` |
| Google Vertex legacy `predict` | *(not a message array)* | `instances[].prompt` | system/developer roles if present | top-level `maxOutputTokens` only — the Vertex-native `parameters.maxOutputTokens` is **not** read, so token policy does not apply to a canonical `predict` body |

`max_prompt_characters` counts Unicode scalar values, not UTF-8 bytes. It counts only string *values*, including those inside tool/function definitions; JSON-Schema boilerplate keys (`type`, `properties`, `description`, ...) are not counted. Multimodal image, audio, and file parts are ignored unless they expose a recognized text field or text content-part type (`text`, `input_text`, `output_text`). Tool-call argument payloads are counted, but only from the legitimate tool-call locations of the supported schemas — OpenAI Chat Completions `messages[].tool_calls[].function.arguments`, OpenAI Responses `input[].arguments`, Anthropic `messages[].content[]` `tool_use` block `input`, the canonical Bedrock Converse spelling of the same call (`messages[].content[].toolUse.input`, an untyped union member rather than a `type: "tool_use"` block), and Gemini `contents[].parts[].functionCall.args` — not arbitrary `arguments`/`input` keys elsewhere in the body (e.g. `metadata.arguments`). Only the arguments are counted from a tool-call block; the sibling `toolUseId`/`name`/`id` call plumbing is not model-visible prose. `system_prompt_aliases` is case-insensitive for role names and top-level field names. System-prompt blocking inspects message/content arrays only at the array-item level (`role`/`author` on each entry), so a nested `role`/`author` key buried in arbitrary user data (e.g. an embedded transcript under `metadata`) does not trip `block_system_prompts`. The one nested field treated as a system prompt is the Azure OpenAI "On Your Data" data-source instruction — both the GA snake_case `data_sources[].parameters.role_information` and the original extensions-API camelCase `dataSources[].parameters.roleInformation` are recognized: it is a free-text instruction the backend applies as a de-facto system prompt, so a non-blank value trips `block_system_prompts` (even when `messages` carry only ordinary user turns) and its text counts toward `max_prompt_characters`. A blank `role_information` (empty or whitespace-only) is intentionally allowed (it carries no directive, so blocking it would falsely reject Azure requests that merely attach data sources). Both casings of both the array key and the inner field are inspected (an empty/`null` `data_sources` next to a populated `dataSources`, or a blank `role_information` next to a populated `roleInformation`, does not bypass the check). Only `role_information`/`roleInformation` is inspected/counted under `parameters` — the surrounding connection config (endpoint, key, index name, embedding settings) is neither blocked nor counted.

**Document/RAG fields.** Top-level `documents` entries are read **member-wise**, because a Cohere v1 document is an arbitrary string-to-string map and the provider serializes its eligible members into the prompt the model reads: `{"title": ..., "snippet": ..., "url": ...}` counts every one of those values, not just a recognized `text`/`content` member. Two members are excluded because Cohere itself keeps them out of the model-visible rendering — `id` (the citation identifier) and `_excludes` (the control list, plus every member it names, which stay available for citation retrieval only). Member *names* are not counted, matching the tool-definition rule above. An entry that carries a `type` discriminator is treated as a content *part* rather than a document map, so multimodal image/audio/file parts and base64 document sources stay excluded from prose accounting while Anthropic text-document `source.data` is still counted. `retrieved_context`, `tool_results`, and `toolResults` keep the recognized-content-member reading.

`supported_schema: auto` accepts any covered family — including legacy OpenAI completions (`{"model", "prompt"}`), canonical TGI/HuggingFace text-generation (`{"inputs", "parameters": {"max_new_tokens": ...}}`), Amazon Titan text-generation (`{"inputText", "textGenerationConfig"}`), and Google Vertex legacy `predict` (`{"instances": [{"prompt": ...}]}`) bodies — and `strict_schema: true` admits all of these while rejecting unknown JSON shapes. Vertex `predict` is recognized (and admitted under `supported_schema: provider_native`) by the **shape**, not by a bare `instances` key: at least one entry must carry a `prompt`, since `instances` is an ordinary word in unrelated JSON and this predicate decides what strict mode admits. TGI and Titan bodies are also admitted under `supported_schema: provider_native` so their native output-cap reject/clamp logic runs. Plain `messages[]` payloads without provider-specific fields can be indistinguishable across OpenAI Chat, Anthropic Messages, and Cohere v2, so strict provider matching is intentionally schema-family based rather than vendor-authentication based. Note that `supported_schema: chat_completions` is stricter than a bare `messages` array check: a body that also carries a provider-native top-level marker (`system`, `preamble`, `message`, `chat_history`, `inputs`, `documents`, `retrieved_context`, `tool_results`) is treated as that provider's schema and rejected under strict `chat_completions`.

**`default_max_tokens` injection note:** `default_max_tokens` keeps a top-level fallback when the body carries a top-level prompt field that a top-level-capped upstream reads — `messages` (OpenAI Chat, Anthropic Messages, Cohere v2, Bedrock Converse), `prompt` (legacy completions), `input`/`instructions`/`previous_response_id` (Responses), or `message`/`chat_history` (Cohere v1) — or carries no provider-native container at all. The injected field is **family-correct**: `max_output_tokens` for a Responses-shaped body — a top-level `input`/`instructions`/`previous_response_id` and **no** chat `messages` array (a body carrying `messages` is Chat/Anthropic/Cohere even if it also includes a Responses marker, so a spoofed `input` cannot divert the cap into a field the chat upstream ignores) — and `max_tokens` otherwise. This defeats the spoof where a client appends a provider-native marker to a top-level-shaped body to route the default into a field the real upstream ignores. The fallback is suppressed only when the body's **own family cap field** is already set (`max_output_tokens` for Responses; `max_tokens` or `max_completion_tokens` otherwise) — a stray cross-provider alias an OpenAI-family upstream does not read (e.g. a top-level `max_new_tokens`, `maxOutputTokens`, or `maxTokens` on a Chat/legacy body) is **not** accepted as the cap, so it cannot be spoofed to suppress the fallback; the default lands in the family field and the stray alias is left intact. A body that is **unambiguously provider-native** — a native container (`generationConfig`/`contents` for Gemini, `inferenceConfig` for Bedrock Converse, `inputs` for TGI) with *no* top-level prompt field — is left to its native cap only, so a strict provider backend is not handed an unsupported top-level cap field: `generationConfig.maxOutputTokens` for Gemini/Vertex, `inferenceConfig.maxTokens` for Bedrock Converse, and `parameters.max_new_tokens` for TGI/HuggingFace. Bedrock Converse is the one provider-native shape that carries a top-level prompt marker (`messages`), and it caps via `inferenceConfig.maxTokens` (the AWS Converse API rejects an unexpected top-level `max_tokens`). But a model-less `{messages, inferenceConfig}` body is indistinguishable from an OpenAI-compatible backend that derives the model outside the JSON body (Azure OpenAI / deployment-in-URL routes), so the top-level fallback is suppressed for such a body **only under `supported_schema: provider_native`** (an explicit operator opt-in); in `auto` or OpenAI-family modes it fail-closes and keeps the top-level cap so an Azure/OpenAI upstream is not left uncapped (a genuine Bedrock deployment should set `provider_native`). A Bedrock body that omits `inferenceConfig` — or an Amazon Titan body (`textGenerationConfig.maxTokenCount`) — routes to the top-level target, **unless** the operator declares the backend with `supported_schema: bedrock_converse`: that dialect is configuration rather than a request marker, so every body (with or without `inferenceConfig`) receives `inferenceConfig.maxTokens` — the container is created when absent — and never an unsupported top-level cap, and the final-body pass requires that native cap. Titan has no operator-bound dialect yet; a Titan body still routes to the top-level target. `enforce_max_tokens` (reject/clamp) still reads `inferenceConfig.maxTokens`, `textGenerationConfig.maxTokenCount`, and TGI `parameters.max_new_tokens` when present.

For Gemini/Vertex, a lone `generationConfig: null` or `generation_config: null` is unset. When `default_max_tokens` is configured, the guard replaces that container in place with an object containing `maxOutputTokens`, preserving the container spelling so injection does not create conflicting aliases.

```yaml
plugin_name: ai_request_guard
config:
  supported_schema: auto
  strict_schema: true
  allowed_models: [gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o, claude-sonnet-4-20250514]
  blocked_models: [o3]
  max_tokens_limit: 4096
  enforce_max_tokens: clamp
  default_max_tokens: 1024
  max_prompt_characters: 24000
  block_system_prompts: true
  system_prompt_aliases: [policy]
```

### `ai_rate_limiter`

**Priority:** 4200 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `on_final_request_body_with_context`, `after_proxy`, `on_response_body`, `response_stream_inspector`, `on_response_stream_terminated` · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Rate-limits consumers by LLM token consumption instead of request count. It reserves an estimated token cost before proxying AI `POST` requests and reconciles the reservation against reported usage after the response, or per `on_unmetered_response` when the provider reports none. Streaming responses are metered incrementally without buffering. HTTP-only.

```yaml
plugin_name: ai_rate_limiter
config:
  token_limit: 500000
  window_seconds: 3600
  limit_by: consumer
```

Full configuration reference, behavior, and examples: [plugins/ai_rate_limiter.md](plugins/ai_rate_limiter.md).

### `ai_prompt_shield`

**Priority:** 2925 · **Phases:** `before_proxy`, `transform_request_body`, `on_final_request_body` · **Protocols:** HTTP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Scans AI/LLM request bodies for PII and either rejects, redacts, or warns.

This plugin is HTTP-only. Native gRPC has no supported prompt-schema or frame-decoding contract, so the plugin is not registered for the gRPC protocol view and must not be treated as a fail-closed PII control for unary or streaming native gRPC traffic. A native-gRPC or WebSocket request on a route that carries the shield is refused with `403` / `PERMISSION_DENIED` rather than served uninspected (see [Protocol Support](plugin_execution_order.md#protocol-support)). Request buffering is enabled for every in-scope `POST` when the plugin has at least one valid pattern to scan (see **Request scope** below). Ordinary scan modes skip framed native gRPC / gRPC-Web bodies, recognized by the proxy's own delimiter-aware classifiers: a lookalike such as `application/grpc-webhook+json` is ordinary `+json` and is inspected. In `scan_fields: mcp_arguments`, `+json` gRPC-Web media types are accepted only when the body is bare JSON. Framed payloads, including `application/grpc-web-text+json`, fail JSON parsing and pass uninspected; `mcp_gateway` refuses them. A body that fails the whole-document parse but looks like a JSON document that may still carry a `tools/call` is refused instead (see **Unparseable bodies** under `mcp_arguments` below).

**Request scope (`content` / `all`).** Every `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` that is not framed gRPC is in scope, whatever its `Content-Type` says — a client can omit or relabel that header while an upstream decodes the body as JSON anyway. The header decides only how the body is treated:

- **Declared JSON** (`application/json`, any `+json`): inspected as before, and a body the shield cannot read as UTF-8 JSON is uninspectable. `reject` and `redact` refuse it with `400` and `warn` records it and forwards: a non-UTF-8 body (`ai_shield_rejected=non_utf8_body`, including UTF-16 / UTF-32 with or without a BOM, which Python's `json.loads(bytes)` auto-detects), a body the strict parser refuses (`malformed_json` — `NaN`, comments, trailing commas, truncation; in `all` mode `reject`/`warn` first scan the raw text and report a PII hit by name), and a `Content-Type` declaring any `charset` other than UTF-8 (`unsupported_charset`, decided before the parse, with the same `charset` rules as `mcp_arguments` below). An empty or whitespace-only body carries nothing to read and passes.
- **Sniffed** (no `Content-Type`, or any other media type): the body is buffered and, when it **may be a JSON document**, held to exactly the declared-JSON rules — inspected, redacted, and re-checked, and refused when non-UTF-8, unparseable, above the scan ceiling, or labelled with a non-UTF-8 `charset`. "May be a JSON document" is deliberately broader than strict JSON: a byte-order mark, UTF-16 / UTF-32 (NUL bytes ahead of a JSON-shaped first character), a leading comment (`/`, `#`) or Unicode whitespace, an object or array opener, a root string (opens and closes with `"`), a root number, or one of the `true` / `false` / `null` / `NaN` / `Infinity` literals. Anything else — a binary upload, ordinary text — is left alone at any size. A sniffed body that still carries a content coding is claimed by enforcing actions like declared JSON, so the representation gate decodes it before the sniff (and refuses a coding it cannot decode); `warn` never claims and leaves it alone.

Because every `POST` / `PUT` / `PATCH` on the route is now buffered — and, for `reject` / `redact`, a compressed one is decoded by the representation gate — the global request-body limit and the gate's decode limits apply to non-AI uploads on the same route too; keep the shield off routes that also carry large or compressed non-AI uploads.

**Method scope is one decision.** Buffering, `before_proxy`, the representation claim, the request-body transform, and final validation all apply the same method scope: `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` in `content` / `all` mode, and `POST` in `mcp_arguments` mode (the MCP transport's method). Another body plugin can force a request onto the buffered path, and the shared transform loop then visits every body-modifying plugin regardless of which one asked for the buffer — so without a method check on the transform itself, adding an unrelated body rule to a route would silently extend the shield's redaction to methods the same shield configuration otherwise leaves untouched. The context-free `transform_request_body` compatibility API proves that scope from an explicit `:method` pseudo-header and declines when it cannot.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `action` | String | `"reject"` | `reject`, `redact`, or `warn` |
| `patterns` | String[] | `["ssn", "credit_card", "api_key", "aws_key"]` | Built-in patterns to enable; each name at most once |
| `custom_patterns` | Object[] | `[]` | Custom `{name, regex}` patterns, at most 256 entries. Closed member set: an unknown member is fatal. `regex` must not match the empty string; `name` is at most 128 characters. Match enumeration is work-bounded (see **Bounded match iteration**) |
| `scan_fields` | String | `"content"` | `content` (LLM prompt fields only), `all` (entire body), or `mcp_arguments` (only `params.arguments` of MCP `tools/call` requests — see **MCP tool arguments** below) |
| `exclude_roles` | String[] | `[]` | Message roles to skip scanning. **`scan_fields: "content"` only** — see below |
| `redaction_placeholder` | String | `"[REDACTED:{type}]"` | Template for redacted text; the rendered result is at most 512 UTF-8 bytes |
| `max_scan_bytes` | Integer | `1048576` | Maximum scanned body size, `1`–`67108864` (64 MiB hard ceiling); `reject`/`redact` fail closed above it, while `warn` records an oversize warning and continues |

**Built-in patterns**: `ssn`, `credit_card`, `email`, `phone_us`, `api_key`, `aws_key`, `ip_address`, `iban` — the shared catalog described under [`ai_response_guard`](#ai_response_guard) (Mastercard 2-series and 4-6-5 American Express cards, multi-segment `sk-proj-…` / `sk-ant-api03-…` keys, IPv6, spaced IBANs). This plugin applies the `credit_card` regex as a shape match; the Luhn confirmation `ai_response_guard` and `ai_transcript_audit` perform is not applied here.

Unknown configuration fields, unknown built-in pattern names, and built-in patterns that fail to compile are fatal at construction time rather than silently weakening policy. The closed-field contract extends into `custom_patterns`: each entry accepts exactly `name` and `regex`, and any other member is rejected with its field path (`custom_patterns[1].note`), so an unsupported nested option is diagnosed at admission instead of being read and dropped. At least one built-in or custom pattern must be effective; custom-only configurations use `patterns: []` with a non-empty `custom_patterns` list. All configured patterns are merged into a single `RegexSet` for O(text_len) detection per scan, regardless of pattern count. Configured redaction placeholders are always literal: `$0`, `$1`, `${name}`, and `$$` are not expanded as regex capture references.

`max_scan_bytes` accepts `1`–`67108864` (a 64 MiB hard ceiling on the body this plugin regex-scans and may rewrite synchronously); the published component and the constructor reach the same verdict for every input. A mathematically integral value is the same published integer however it is spelled, so `1024` and `1024.0` are both accepted; a fractional, negative, zero, or out-of-range value is rejected at construction rather than truncated by a lossy cast.

**Bounded redaction output.** Redaction replaces each match with a placeholder that can be longer than the value it removes, so an admitted expanding policy would otherwise turn a `max_scan_bytes`-bounded body into an unbounded rewrite. Three controls bound it. A `custom_patterns` regex that matches the empty string is refused at construction (a zero-width rule inserts the placeholder at every position), and a zero-width span produced at run time by a contextual assertion is refused too. `name` is capped at 128 characters (the published `maxLength`) and the *rendered* placeholder — the template with `{type}` substituted, which is what every match re-emits — at 512, so a template that repeats `{type}` is bounded by what it produces rather than by its own length. Finally, one aggregate allowance per request caps how much redaction may grow the body: four times the body's own size, with a 64 KiB floor and a 64 MiB ceiling. Growth is measured on the JSON-escaped form (a control-character placeholder escapes six-fold), and the live intermediate buffers of sequential patterns are bounded by the same allowance. Only net growth is charged, so a redaction that shrinks or preserves the body spends nothing. Exhausting the allowance returns `413` with `ai_shield_rejected=redaction_budget_exceeded`; no partially redacted body is ever forwarded.

**Bounded match iteration.** Each regex search is linear, but enumerating every match is not: a custom pattern such as `.*[^A-Z]|[A-Z]` scans to the end of the string before reporting each one-byte match, so a 500 KB prompt would cost quadratic work in one synchronous rewrite. Every walk over the matches of a custom pattern — redaction, the cross-part boundary pass, the `all`-mode raw pass, and the contextual-removability check — is therefore charged, per match, the most bytes the search could have scanned: up to the match start plus the pattern's longest possible match (computed once at construction), or to the end of the string when that length is unbounded (`+`, `*`, `{n,}`). One walk may spend 256 times the length of the string it scans (4 MiB floor). A pattern whose longest match is under 256 bytes can never exhaust it; an open-ended pattern exhausts it only with hundreds of matches in one large string. Exhaustion fails closed: redaction returns the same `413` (`redaction_budget_exceeded`), and a detection walk counts the pattern as matched. Built-in patterns are fixed expressions and are not charged.

`scan_fields: "content"` (default) scans LLM prompt text across the common request shapes: chat `messages[].content` (string or multimodal text parts), plus the top-level `prompt` (OpenAI legacy completions), `input` (Responses API and embeddings), `instructions` (Responses API), `system` (Anthropic), `inputText` (Amazon Bedrock Titan text generation), `message` and `preamble` (Cohere v1 `/chat`), and `inputs` (Hugging Face TGI text generation) fields — each accepted as a string, an array of strings, or an array of content parts. Google Gemini / Vertex bodies carry no `messages` array at all, so `contents[].parts[].text` and the system instruction under **both** the JSON `systemInstruction` and proto `system_instruction` spellings are scanned as well; `contents[].role` is filtered by `exclude_roles` exactly like `messages[].role`, and `exclude_roles: [system]` suppresses the system instruction just as it suppresses the top-level `system` field — and, for the same reason, the Cohere `preamble`, which is that provider's spelling of the system prompt.

Three more shapes carry prompt text that no top-level field reaches. Cohere v1 `/chat` keeps the prior turns in `chat_history[].message`; each turn's `role` is filtered by `exclude_roles` like any message role, matched **case-insensitively** because Cohere spells roles `USER` / `CHATBOT` / `SYSTEM` / `TOOL` while `exclude_roles` is configured in the lower-case OpenAI spelling. Google Vertex legacy `predict` keeps its prompt in `instances[].prompt`; only that field is scanned, since the surrounding instance fields are prediction inputs and identifiers rather than model-visible prose.

The third is the top-level Cohere v1 `documents[]` RAG array, read **member-wise**: a document is an arbitrary string-to-string map and the provider serializes its eligible members into the prompt the model reads, so `{"title": …, "snippet": …, "url": …}` is scanned and redacted member by member rather than through a recognized `text` member alone — which would leave every other member unscanned, and contribute nothing at all for a document whose members are all operator-chosen keys. Two members are skipped because Cohere itself keeps them out of the model-visible rendering: `id` (the citation identifier) and `_excludes` (the control list, plus every member it names, which stay available for citation retrieval only; both the array and the single-string spelling of the control are honoured). Member *names* are never scanned or rewritten — they are structure, not prose, and rewriting a key would change the document the provider receives. An entry that carries a `type` discriminator is a content *part*, not a document map, so it keeps the ordinary text-part gate and non-text multimodal parts stay out. Each retained member value is read through the same bounded one-level traversal a tool-result payload gets. Note that `documents` is an ordinary word in unrelated JSON: on a shared proxy, the string members of a `documents` array are in scope for Content mode.

A content part is scanned when it declares a text `type` (`text`, `input_text`, `output_text`) **or** declares no `type` at all but carries a string `text`. The type-less form is what Amazon Bedrock Converse (`messages[].content[]`) and Gemini (`parts[]`) send; requiring a discriminator those providers never emit would leave their prompts unscanned. Blocks that declare a non-text `type` (`image_url`, `tool_use`, `reasoning`, …) contribute no `text`, and parts whose `text` is not a string are still ignored; tool-call blocks are read only for their arguments, as described below. Extraction is bounded to one level per part: a part contributes only its own `text` and is never recursed into.

A block that is not itself a text part may still carry model-visible text one level down, and four such shapes are scanned: Bedrock Converse `messages[].content[].toolResult.content[]` (each element's own string or `text`), the Anthropic spelling `messages[].content[]` with `type: "tool_result"` and a string or array `content`, Bedrock Converse `messages[].content[].guardContent` under both the nested `{"text": {"text": "…"}}` and flat `{"text": "…"}` spellings (either reaches the model, so reading only one leaves the other uninspected), and Bedrock Converse `messages[].content[].toolUse.input` — the untyped union spelling of a tool call, whose arguments are replayed to the model on the next turn. Tool-result text is content the model reads verbatim from a third party, which is exactly where a smuggled payload hides. Each block inherits its enclosing message's `role`, so `exclude_roles` filters it exactly like that message's own text, and the traversal stays bounded to one level below the block — a chained tool result never recurses.

`toolUse` is the one shape read deeper than one level, because a tool-arguments object follows the tool's own JSON Schema and has no fixed member: every string leaf of `input` is scanned and redacted, down to a fixed depth of 8, and a value nested past that ceiling is neither scanned nor rewritten. Only `input` is read — the sibling `toolUseId` and `name` fields are call plumbing, not model-visible prose, and rewriting either would corrupt the call the provider receives. Member *names* inside `input` are never rewritten for the same reason.

**Tool-call arguments.** A client replays the assistant's earlier tool calls in its request history, so their arguments reach the model on the next turn. Content mode reads them through the same bounded argument walk (a string is scanned as opaque text; an object's string leaves down to depth 8), for every provider spelling: OpenAI Chat Completions `messages[].tool_calls[].function.arguments` and the legacy `messages[].function_call.arguments`, OpenAI Responses `input[]` items of `type: "function_call"` (`arguments`), Anthropic `messages[].content[]` blocks of `type` `tool_use` / `server_tool_use` / `mcp_tool_use` (`input`), Bedrock Converse `toolUse.input` (above), and Gemini `contents[].parts[].functionCall.args` (and the proto `function_call` spelling). Function names, call ids, and other plumbing are not read. Message-level arguments follow their message's `role` for `exclude_roles`; the Responses item carries no role and is never suppressed. Redaction rewrites exactly the same values.

The OpenAI Responses API supplies a tool's result as a top-level `input` item of type `function_call_output`, whose model-visible text lives under `output` rather than `content`. That member is scanned and redacted through the same bounded one-level traversal, accepting both the documented string spelling and the structured array of content items; any other `output` shape carries no text and is left untouched by detection and redaction alike. The item declares no `role`, so `exclude_roles` does not suppress it — there is no operator-authored role to exempt, and third-party tool output is exactly the text a smuggled value hides in.

Consecutive text parts in one logical message — including consecutive Gemini `parts[]` of one turn, which the provider concatenates into a single prompt — are additionally scanned as a boundary-aware concatenation, so splitting a sensitive value between adjacent parts does not evade policy; different messages and text runs separated by a non-text part are never joined. **This pass runs in both scan modes.** All-mode's decoded-token pass visits each part as a separate token and its raw-body pass carries JSON punctuation between them, so neither sees a value the provider will concatenate; the boundary pass is what closes that, and because all-mode scans every value regardless of role it runs there with no role exclusions applied. Reject and warn report a cross-part match normally. Redact fails the request closed when the match cannot be mapped safely to independent JSON strings.
