## WebSocket Plugins

WebSocket plugins share the bidirectional H1 Upgrade, H2 Extended CONNECT, and
H3 Extended CONNECT relay. Ordinary `on_ws_frame` hooks receive complete
WebSocket messages (with continuation frames already reassembled), in both
directions. Parser-level policies such as `ws_message_size_limiting` run before
that hook so they can enforce actual wire-frame boundaries safely. Within the
post-reassembly chain, the first terminal Close from a priority-ordered
admission/mutating hook is preserved: later mutating plugins are skipped for
that frame, while observational hooks still see the final Close.

**Physical fragments.** Because `on_ws_frame` sees only reassembled messages, a
peer could otherwise spend unbounded wire frames — including zero-length
continuation frames, which accumulate no bytes and therefore never trip any size
ceiling — while paying for a single logical message. The relay therefore meters those
frames inside the codec and charges them through `on_ws_reassembly_frames`
before admitting the completing message, in both directions and on all three
frontends (and for an interleaved Ping/Pong; a peer Close stays exempt, as it
already bypasses mutating admission). Each wire frame is charged exactly once: the fragments through the
reassembly hook, the completing frame through the ordinary message hook.
Observational plugins are skipped for fragment batches, and only a returned
`Message::Close` is honored (there is no message to mutate).

Metering cannot bound a message that never completes, so the parser also applies
two independent ceilings — `FERRUM_WEBSOCKET_MAX_INCOMPLETE_MESSAGE_FRAMES`
(physical frame count) and `FERRUM_WEBSOCKET_MAX_INCOMPLETE_MESSAGE_SECONDS`
(wall clock since the first fragment) — and closes the connection with RFC 6455
code **1008** and a fixed, non-secret reason while the message is still
incomplete. Both reset at every message boundary, so legitimately fragmented
traffic on a long-lived connection is unaffected. These are separate from
`ws_message_size_limiting`, which bounds bytes and closes with **1009**.

### `ws_message_size_limiting`

**Priority:** 2810 · **Phases:** parser-level frame/message limits · **Protocols:** WebSocket · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Enforces an actual WebSocket frame-payload ceiling before payload reservation
for Text, Binary, continuation, Ping, and Pong frames, plus an independent bound
on the complete reassembled Text/Binary message. Valid Close frames bypass the
application ceiling so teardown remains protocol-correct; every control frame
still receives the independent RFC 6455 125-byte pre-allocation bound. A
fragmented message may exceed `max_frame_bytes` cumulatively as long as each
individual frame is within that limit and the message remains within
`max_message_bytes`. Fragmented Text keeps incremental UTF-8
validation, and interleaved Ping/Pong frames do not reset message state.

**Ping/Pong count against `max_frame_bytes`.** Only Close bypasses the
configured frame ceiling. Ping and Pong payloads are checked against it like
data frames, so a `max_frame_bytes` (or a direction's override) below 125 — the
RFC 6455 control-frame maximum — closes the connection with 1009 on an
ordinary heartbeat whose payload is larger than the configured value. Keep the
frame ceiling at 125 or more unless every peer's keepalive payload is known to
fit.

On either violation the gateway publishes cancellation before attempting
bounded polite-close writes and sends close code **1009 (Message Too Big)**
with the configured reason to both client and backend when their sinks remain
writable. The same behavior applies in both relay directions and on H1, H2,
and H3 WebSocket frontends. Under `websocket_permessage_deflate: terminate`
the inflate adapter enforces the same ceilings on the compressed wire frame
and on the inflated frame and message; when the violated ceiling is this
plugin's, the Close carries the configured reason too. A fault at an
independent ceiling (the global `FERRUM_MAX_WEBSOCKET_FRAME_SIZE_BYTES` frame
limit or a stricter `FERRUM_WEBSOCKET_PERMESSAGE_DEFLATE_MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES`)
keeps the adapter's fixed reason (`compressed frame too large`,
`decompressed frame too large`, `decompressed message too large`).

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max_frame_bytes` | u64 | *(required)* | Maximum allowed frame payload in bytes, the default for both directions. Must be greater than 0 — configs with `max_frame_bytes` of 0 (or missing) are rejected at config load time. Applies to Text, Binary, continuation, Ping, and Pong frames (Close bypasses it), so values below 125 close the connection on heartbeat Ping/Pong traffic larger than the value. |
| `max_message_bytes` | u64 | `4 × max_frame_bytes` | Maximum reassembled Text/Binary message payload, the default for both directions. Must be greater than or equal to `max_frame_bytes`. This separately bounds continuation accumulation without treating the whole message as one frame. |
| `close_reason` | String | `"Message too large"` | Close-frame reason text, the default for both directions (truncated to 123 UTF-8 bytes — the RFC 6455 §5.5 control-frame payload limit) |
| `client_to_backend` | object | *(none)* | Optional override for frames the **client** sends (the client-side parser). Accepts `max_frame_bytes`, `max_message_bytes`, and `close_reason` with the same rules as the top-level fields. |
| `backend_to_client` | object | *(none)* | Optional override for frames the **backend** sends (the backend-side parser). Accepts the same three fields. |

**Directional overrides.** The top-level fields are the default for both
directions; `client_to_backend` / `backend_to_client` replace any of them for
one direction, so a tight bound on untrusted client input can coexist with
larger backend snapshots or pushes. A field an override omits is inherited from
the top level, except that when `max_message_bytes` is set at neither level the
direction defaults it to four times its own effective `max_frame_bytes`. Each
direction's resolved values must satisfy `max_message_bytes >= max_frame_bytes`;
an inherited explicit top-level `max_message_bytes` below an override's raised
`max_frame_bytes` is rejected with a diagnostic that names the direction, so
set `max_message_bytes` in the override too. Both directions are resolved once
at construction; the relay reads the precomputed values once per session.

Configuration must be a top-level object. The only accepted keys are `max_frame_bytes`, `max_message_bytes`, `close_reason`, `client_to_backend`, and `backend_to_client`; an override object accepts only `max_frame_bytes`, `max_message_bytes`, and `close_reason`. Unknown keys are rejected with path-qualified diagnostics and spelling suggestions (for example `config.backend_to_client.max_frame_bytez`), so a typo cannot silently leave frames unbounded. Registration is `FailClosed`.

```yaml
plugin_name: ws_message_size_limiting
config:
  max_frame_bytes: 65536
  max_message_bytes: 262144
```

Asymmetric limits — 4 KiB client frames and 16 KiB client messages, with
64 KiB backend frames:

```yaml
plugin_name: ws_message_size_limiting
config:
  max_frame_bytes: 4096
  max_message_bytes: 16384
  close_reason: "client payload limit"
  backend_to_client:
    max_frame_bytes: 65536
    max_message_bytes: 262144
    close_reason: "backend payload limit"
```

With multiple applicable limiter instances, the relay uses the smallest frame
ceiling and the smallest message ceiling independently, per direction; ties
retain configured plugin order, including the corresponding close reason. The
plugin opts the connection out of `FERRUM_WEBSOCKET_TUNNEL_MODE` raw-copy mode,
so both peer parsers receive the effective limits before their first frame
read.

**Metrics:** Every session this plugin closes with 1009 increments
`ferrum_ws_message_size_limit_rejected_total{direction}` once, where
`direction` is `client_to_backend` (the client sent the oversized input) or
`backend_to_client`. That includes terminated `permessage-deflate` faults at
this plugin's ceiling. A rejection at the global
`FERRUM_MAX_WEBSOCKET_FRAME_SIZE_BYTES` ceiling (empty 1009 reason) is not this
plugin's decision and is not counted. The counter is process-wide and always
exported, so alerting does not require `ws_frame_logging` or sampled logs.

### `ws_rate_limiting`

**Priority:** 2910 · **Phases:** `on_ws_frame`, `on_ws_reassembly_frames`, `on_ws_disconnect` · **Protocols:** WebSocket · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Rate limits WebSocket frames using a token bucket algorithm — per connection by default, or as an aggregate budget shared by every session of one consumer, client IP, or proxy (`limit_by`). Closes the connection with close code **1008 (Policy Violation)** per RFC 6455 §7.4 when the configured frame rate is exceeded. Both client-to-backend and backend-to-client frames count against the same bucket. Budget is charged per **physical** frame, not per logical message: a message reassembled from N wire frames costs N tokens (the N−1 fragments are charged as one batched admission when the read that surfaced them returns, then the completing message costs one more). A message built from more wire frames than `burst_size` therefore can never be admitted, which is the intended fail-closed answer to a fragmentation flood. An inbound `Message::Close` already synthesized by an earlier admission/mutating frame plugin is ignored: the limiter neither charges local/Redis budget nor replaces that Close. The shared H1/H2/H3 relay also skips later mutating plugins once a terminal Close is selected. Unknown top-level keys are rejected at admission and reload.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `frames_per_second` | u64 | `100` | Sustained frames per second per budget (per connection unless `limit_by` selects an aggregate). Range 1–1000000. Must be greater than zero — `frames_per_second: 0` is rejected at config load time. |
| `burst_size` | u64 | (= `frames_per_second`) | Token bucket capacity (burst allowance). Range 1–1000000. A local-only policy accepts any capacity/refill pair, including a burst smaller than the sustained rate. With `sync_mode: "redis"` it must also be greater than or equal to `frames_per_second`, an integer multiple of `frames_per_second`, and yield a refill window (`burst_size / frames_per_second`) of at most 3600 seconds so local token-bucket and Redis two-window enforcement share the same sustained rate. |
| `close_reason` | String | `"Frame rate exceeded"` | Close-frame reason text (truncated to 123 UTF-8 bytes — the RFC 6455 §5.5 control-frame payload limit) |
| `limit_by` | String | `connection` | Budget dimension, one of `connection`, `consumer`, `ip`, `service` (exact lowercase). `connection` gives every session its own bucket. `consumer` shares one bucket across every session of the authenticated identity (mapped Consumer username, else the external authenticated identity); anonymous sessions share their client IP's bucket. `ip` shares one bucket per resolved client IP (IPv6 clients are keyed per full address). `service` shares one bucket per proxy. The identity is resolved once at upgrade admission, so per-frame admission stays allocation-free. |
| `sync_mode` | String | `local` | `local` (in-memory per instance) or `redis`. In the default `limit_by: connection` mode Redis holds externalized per-connection counters, namespaced per plugin/gateway instance and not portable across reconnects/rebuilds; aggregate `limit_by` counters are keyed by their identity and shared by every replica of the policy. Parsed case-insensitively (`LOCAL`, `Redis`); `redis` requires `redis_url`. |
| `redis_url`, `redis_tls`, `redis_pool_size`, `redis_connect_timeout_seconds`, `redis_health_check_interval_seconds`, `redis_username`, `redis_password` | — | — | Shared [Redis connection options](#redis-connection-options); `redis_url` database selector `0`–`2147483647`. |
| `redis_key_prefix` | String | `{FERRUM_NAMESPACE}:ws_rate_limiting:{plugin-config-id}` | Redis key namespace prefix. Defaults to the gateway namespace, the plugin name, and this plugin config's stable resource id (for example `ferrum:ws_rate_limiting:rl-public-api`), so two independent policies of this type in one namespace never share the surrounding key namespace. Must be non-empty when set. In the default `limit_by: connection` mode this plugin still prepends a per-instance UUID to every logical connection key, so an explicit shared prefix does not opt two plugin or gateway instances into a shared per-connection frame budget. Aggregate `limit_by` keys carry no instance UUID. |
| `redis_failure_policy` | String | `fail_closed` | Behavior when the centralized store cannot be consulted (outage, egress/DNS screen failure, or an endpoint rejected as Redis Cluster). `fail_closed` closes the WebSocket with a policy Close frame; `local_fallback` explicitly opts into per-process budgets for availability. Only meaningful when `sync_mode: "redis"`, but validated in either mode |

> **Note:** When `redis_tls` is enabled, CA certificate verification and skip-verify behavior are controlled by the gateway-level `FERRUM_TLS_CA_BUNDLE_PATH` and `FERRUM_TLS_NO_VERIFY` environment variables, not per-plugin settings. A `redis_url` fragment (`#insecure` or any other) is rejected at plugin construction; it is not a per-URL skip-verify switch. A configured CA bundle is exclusive: if the path is set and verification is on, a load failure refuses plugin construction instead of falling back to system/public roots. `FERRUM_TLS_NO_VERIFY=true` remains the sanctioned skip-verify path and does not treat an unloadable CA as a construction error.

**Redis mode** (`sync_mode: "redis"`): Frame counters are stored in Redis instead of in-memory state. Because WebSocket `connection_id` values are process-local, the plugin prepends a per-instance UUID to every Redis logical rate key (encoded on wire as `{escaped-prefix:escaped-instance-scope}:{window_index}`, where the braces are a Redis Cluster hash tag) so two gateways sharing the same Redis deployment never collide. This mode externalizes the counter backend but does not make per-connection limits portable across reconnects to a different gateway instance. Aggregate `limit_by` budgets (`consumer`, `ip`, `service`) are different: their logical key is the identity itself (`consumer:<identity>`, `ip:<address>`, `service:<proxy id>`) with no instance UUID, so every replica of one policy (same default prefix) charges one shared Redis budget. Admission is charge-then-compensate: the batch is charged before the decision so racing sessions and replicas cannot all admit against one stale read, and a refused batch is handed back (`INCRBY -n` + `EXPIRE`) from a detached task, so a refusal never stays on the shared counter and repeated refused reconnects cannot keep a shared budget exhausted. A batch larger than the whole window budget is refused without touching Redis. Between a refused charge and its hand-back the transient charge is visible to concurrent sessions (a conservative early refusal, never an over-admit); a process exit in between leaves it until the window's TTL. Aggregate keys are indexed by each gateway's own clock, so replicas sharing one budget assume host clocks agree to well within the refill window. Redis approximates the local token bucket as `burst_size` admissions over a window of `burst_size / frames_per_second` seconds, counted with the **two-window weighted approximation** (`previous * (1 - elapsed_fraction) + current`) rather than the sub-bucketed trailing window `rate_limiting` uses — a frame budget charges whole batches with `INCRBY` against a single window index, so it shares the token-accounting shape, and the same residual applies: frames clustered at the end of a window are discounted as the next one runs. With Redis sync, construction rejects a burst below the sustained rate, non-integral ratios, and refill windows longer than 3600 seconds so Redis cannot over-admit (or unexpectedly under-admit) relative to the local sustained rate, including across Redis failure/recovery. A `sync_mode: local` policy has no second enforcement arm to keep in parity, so it accepts any pair within the 1–1000000 bounds. Those arithmetic burst/refill constraints are constructor-only: JSON Schema cannot express them. Uses Redis-native counters (no Lua). If Redis becomes unreachable, `redis_failure_policy` decides: the default `fail_closed` closes the connection with a policy Close frame (a frame stream has no other refusal channel), and `local_fallback` is the explicit opt-in to per-process token-bucket limiting. A background health check pings Redis every `redis_health_check_interval_seconds` to switch back automatically. Compatible with any RESP-protocol server running in single-endpoint topology: Redis, Valkey, DragonflyDB, KeyDB, or Garnet. Database-backed frame counters are intentionally unsupported.

**Memory protection:** Local (and Redis-fallback) state is capped at 50,000 keys. In the default connection mode a session's key is released when the session ends (`on_ws_disconnect`): connection ids are process-unique and never charged again, so connection churn cannot fill the map with finished sessions. Aggregate budgets outlive any one session and are reclaimed by idle sweeps instead. Sampled periodic sweeps (every 100,000 frame hooks, cooldown-gated to at most once per second) prune idle keys below the cap, and once the map reaches the cap every frame runs the same cooldown-gated idle sweep before admission, so idle keys never keep refusing new sessions. Hard cardinality is enforced by atomic reservation on admission: existing keys continue at capacity, and previously unseen local/fallback keys are denied fail-closed (policy close) without deleting active budgets.

**Metrics:** A budget-exceeded close and a capacity refusal count in `ferrum_rate_limit_exceeded_total` (shared by every rate-limit plugin). A fail-closed close while centralized enforcement is unavailable (`redis_failure_policy: fail_closed`) counts in `ferrum_rate_limit_enforcement_unavailable_total` instead, so a Redis outage that closes sessions is visible without log scraping.

```yaml
plugin_name: ws_rate_limiting
config:
  frames_per_second: 50
  burst_size: 100
  close_reason: "Rate limit exceeded"
  sync_mode: redis
  redis_url: "redis://redis-host:6379/2"
```

### `ws_frame_logging`

**Priority:** 9050 · **Phases:** `on_ws_policy_close`, `prepare_ws_frame_delivery`, `emit_ws_frame_delivery`, `on_ws_disconnect` · **Protocols:** WebSocket · **Failure policy:** `OptionalFailOpen`

Logs metadata for every complete WebSocket message the shared H1/H2/H3 relay **successfully delivers** (post-plugin, post-control-frame guard), plus every gateway-published policy Close decision. Provides message-level observability without requiring packet captures. This plugin never transforms or drops frames — it is purely observational (`observes_ws_frame_decisions()`): the relay reports each final policy Close to it once through `on_ws_policy_close` (`outcome=policy_close`), after the full decision is known, so the record does not depend on this plugin's priority (an accepted `priority_override` that orders it before the rejecting plugin still records the rejection). Ordinary Text/Binary/Ping/Pong and peer Close frames are recorded only after the destination sink accepts the write (`outcome=delivered`), on the same success boundary as the per-direction `frames_*` / `bytes_*` counters. Cancelled or failed sends produce no frame event.

**Granularity: one record per message, not per wire frame.** Tungstenite reassembles a fragmented Text/Binary message (the initial non-final frame plus its continuation frames) before the relay or any `on_ws_frame` plugin sees it, so a message sent as 1024 fragments produces **one** `delivered` record whose `size_bytes` is the reassembled payload length, and the disconnect record's `frames_c2b` / `frames_b2c` count delivered messages. Control frames (Ping/Pong/Close) cannot be fragmented and map one-to-one. Under `websocket_permessage_deflate: terminate`, sizes are inflated (plaintext) lengths. Physical frame-count and per-frame size enforcement belong to `ws_message_size_limiting` (parser `max_frame_bytes`), `ws_rate_limiting` (charged per physical frame), and the `FERRUM_WEBSOCKET_MAX_INCOMPLETE_MESSAGE_*` parser bounds; their rejections appear here as `policy_close` records.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `log_level` | String | `"info"` | Log level for frame entries: `trace`, `debug`, `info`, or `warn` (case-sensitive — unknown values and explicit `null` are rejected). Healthy frame traffic remains informational; when the active filter suppresses the configured level but still admits `warn`, construction emits an actionable warning |
| `include_payload_preview` | bool | `false` | Emit a keyed, non-reversible payload fingerprint (`hmac-sha256:<prefix> len=<n>`) in the `preview` field. Raw frame bytes are never logged. Explicit `null` is rejected |
| `payload_preview_bytes` | u64 | `128` | Maximum leading payload bytes folded into the fingerprint digest (hard maximum 65536 — values above that are rejected, not clamped; must be greater than zero when previews are enabled; zero is accepted when previews are disabled; explicit `null` is rejected) |
| `log_ping_pong` | bool | `false` | Log Ping and Pong control frames. Explicit `null` is rejected |
| `sample_rate` | number | `1` | Fraction (0–1) of connections whose `delivered` records are emitted. Deterministic per connection — a session is either fully recorded or not — and unsampled sessions skip fingerprinting. `0` keeps only `policy_close` and disconnect records. Values outside 0–1, non-numbers, and explicit `null` are rejected |
| `direction` | String | `"both"` | Relay direction whose `delivered` records are emitted: `both`, `client_to_backend`, or `backend_to_client` (case-sensitive). Does not filter `policy_close` or disconnect records. Explicit `null` is rejected |
| `max_records_per_connection` | u64 | `0` | Maximum `delivered` records per connection, shared by both directions; `0` is unlimited. On reaching the cap the plugin emits one `event=record_cap_reached` record (with `max_records_per_connection`) and suppresses further `delivered` records for that connection. `policy_close` and disconnect records are not capped. Explicit `null` is rejected |

Only the keys above are accepted. Unknown keys (for example a typo like `log_levle`) are rejected with a field-specific error.

```yaml
plugin_name: ws_frame_logging
config:
  log_level: info
  include_payload_preview: true
  payload_preview_bytes: 256
  log_ping_pong: false
  sample_rate: 0.1
  direction: both
  max_records_per_connection: 1000
```

**Volume controls.** `sample_rate`, `direction`, and `max_records_per_connection` bound how many `delivered` records a busy proxy produces (each one costs an observation, an optional HMAC fingerprint, and a formatted record on the relay task, and a saturated non-blocking log sink drops records silently). They are applied before any per-message work. `policy_close` decisions (at most one per relay half) and the per-session disconnect record are always emitted at the configured level, so a sampled-out or capped session is never invisible.

Frame log entries are emitted to the `ws_frame_log` tracing target with structured fields: `plugin_id`, `proxy_id`, `connection_id`, `direction` (`client->backend` or `backend->client`), `frame_type` (`text`, `binary`, `ping`, `pong`, `close`), `size_bytes`, `outcome` (`delivered` for successful forwards, `policy_close` for gateway-published policy Close decisions), and (when `include_payload_preview` is true) `preview`. `plugin_id` is the plugin-config resource id (`-` when the instance was built without one), so two effective `ws_frame_logging` instances on one proxy — for example a routine `info` instance and a `debug` instance with previews — produce distinguishable records; each instance also uses its own fingerprint key. For Close frames, `close_code` and `close_reason_len` are included when a status code is present; the raw Close reason string is never logged (application reasons may contain secrets). `size_bytes` for a Close with a code is `2 + reason.len()` (status-code bytes plus UTF-8 reason length); Close without a code is `0`.

Peer-originated Close frames are forwarded without entering mutating `on_ws_frame` admission hooks (so a later plugin cannot replace the peer's code/reason) and are logged once on the delivery path after a successful forward. Policy Closes are logged once as `outcome=policy_close` (never also as `delivered`) with the direction of the rejected input, whatever produced them: a terminal Close from any `on_ws_frame` plugin (`ws_rate_limiting`, `waf`, a custom plugin — regardless of priority order), a fragment-budget Close from `on_ws_reassembly_frames`, and the relay's parser rejections of an inbound message (`ws_message_size_limiting` or the global `FERRUM_MAX_WEBSOCKET_FRAME_SIZE_BYTES` ceilings with 1009, the incomplete-message bounds with 1008, and terminated `permessage-deflate` faults). The record is a decision record emitted before the bounded Close write. Session-level stops (idle timeout, drain, maximum lifetime, credential expiry, client-trust withdrawal) and relay transport faults are not policy Closes; they are reported by the disconnect record's `termination_reason` and failure fields.

Disconnect events on the same `ws_frame_log` target include `plugin_id`, the same `connection_id` that every frame event for that session carried, plus identity/endpoint fields (`namespace`, `proxy_id`, `proxy_name`, `client_ip`, `backend_target`, `listen_port`), `duration_ms`, success-only `frames_c2b` / `frames_b2c` (delivered **messages**) / `bytes_c2b` / `bytes_b2c`, `direction`, `io_side` (`read`, `write`, or `none`), `error_class`, `termination_reason` (the relay's bounded session-end classification: `normal_peer_close`, `relay_error`, `idle_timeout`, `drain`, `max_lifetime`, `credential_expired`, or `trust_withdrawn`; `-` if absent), `consumer`, `auth_method`, and `correlation_id`. Message and byte totals increment only after the destination sink accepts a forward (including successfully forwarded peer Close frames); cancelled or failed writes are omitted. On HTTP/3 the relay's client transport is an in-process bridge to the QUIC stream, so the relay settles the bridge's send pump before emitting this record: a QUIC DATA or FIN failure toward the client after the relay already accepted the final Close (for example a client `STOP_SENDING`) is attributed as `direction=backend_to_client`, `io_side=write` with the transport class (or `read_write_timeout` when the bounded pump drain expires), instead of reading as a clean close. `io_side` disambiguates read-from-source versus write-to-destination failures within a relay direction (for example `BackendToClient` + `write` means the client sink failed while delivering backend traffic). The ID is allocated once at WebSocket upgrade admission and preserved through H1/H2/H3 relay teardown, peer close/error, plugin cancellation, idle/drain timeout, and H1/H2 upgrade-handoff failure — plugins receive it on `WsDisconnectContext` without a per-frame lookup map. The value is **process-local** (monotonic per gateway process), not globally unique across instances; when aggregating logs from multiple gateways, join on `(gateway_instance_id, proxy_id, connection_id)` (or an equivalent host/process identity + `proxy_id` + `connection_id` tuple). A live session keeps the accepting plugin snapshot and this admission `connection_id` across config reload.

Privacy / retention: disconnect records carry endpoint identity and success-only traffic totals suitable for incident response; they do not include application payloads. Retain them under the same policy as other `ws_frame_log` traffic.

**Default filter compatibility.** The plugin defaults healthy per-frame and disconnect records to `log_level: info`; it does not turn routine traffic into warnings. Under the gateway default `FERRUM_LOG_LEVEL=warn`, constructing the plugin with `config: {}` emits an actionable construction-time warning naming the filtered `info` level, while frame records remain suppressed. Validation and cache publication can construct an enabled instance separately, so the diagnostic can repeat. A filter stricter than `warn` (or a directive such as `ws_frame_log=off`) also suppresses the diagnostic; operators using such a filter must ensure it deliberately admits the configured `ws_frame_log` level. Raise `FERRUM_LOG_LEVEL` (or use an equivalent EnvFilter directive) to `info` or more verbose to admit the default records. Explicit `trace` / `debug` similarly require a sufficiently verbose filter; `warn` is available only when an operator deliberately chooses warning-level frame output.

**What filtering does and does not skip.** When the configured tracing level is filtered out, fingerprint computation and tracing event construction are skipped. Frame parsing, plugin selection (`requires_ws_frame_hooks()` is always true while this plugin is attached), `on_ws_frame` / `on_ws_policy_close` dispatch, delivery prepare/emit hooks, and disconnect-hook dispatch still occur. Consequently, attaching this plugin keeps the connection on the parsed WebSocket relay path and prevents the H1 raw-copy tunnel fast path even if every record is filtered.

**Admission / failure policy.** `ws_frame_logging` is registered `OptionalFailOpen` (see [Config admission and failure policy](#config-admission-and-failure-policy)): the Admin API returns HTTP 400 for an invalid enabled config, and serving loads omit the instance. Invalid configs include unknown keys, out-of-range `payload_preview_bytes`, invalid `log_level`, wrong types, and explicit `null` fields.

**Raw frame contents are never logged.** WebSocket payloads routinely carry credentials — bearer tokens, session cookies, API keys (for example a GraphQL-over-WS `connection_init` payload or a custom auth handshake). To honor the project's never-log-secrets invariant, `preview` contains only a keyed, non-reversible fingerprint of the form `hmac-sha256:<12 hex chars> len=<bytes>` (with a trailing `+` after the digest when only the first `payload_preview_bytes` of the payload were hashed). The key is generated per plugin instance and is not exposed in logs, so log access alone cannot confirm guessed payloads offline. The digest lets operators correlate identical payloads observed by that plugin instance without disclosing plaintext; the payload byte length is also always available as `size_bytes`. Close reasons are treated as application payload: only `close_code` and `close_reason_len` are logged.

---

## UDP Plugins

UDP plugins operate at the datagram level via the `on_udp_datagram` lifecycle hook. They fire on every **application** datagram of a UDP or DTLS stream proxy in both directions (client-to-backend and backend-to-client): raw datagrams on plain UDP, every wire record on DTLS passthrough, and decrypted application datagrams on a DTLS-terminating frontend. On **DTLS passthrough** the gateway runs no DTLS stack, so the hook sees and counts every datagram on the wire — the opening ClientHello, the rest of the handshake, retransmits, and alerts as well as application records — and a passthrough budget must be sized for that traffic. On a **DTLS-terminating** frontend, handshake, retransmit, and alert records are consumed by the gateway's DTLS stack before the application relay and never reach the hook (pre-handshake work there is bounded by the per-source DTLS handshake admission, a concurrency cap rather than a rate). HTTP/3 CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298) tunnels and HBONE UDP relays carry datagrams inside HTTP-family or mesh streams and do not invoke `on_udp_datagram`. Use `UdpDatagramContext.direction` to distinguish directions and `UdpDatagramContext.client_ip_addr` for the typed canonical client address (computed once per session).

### `udp_rate_limiting`

**Priority:** 2915 · **Phases:** `on_udp_datagram` · **Protocols:** UDP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Rate limits UDP datagrams per resolved client IP using a fixed-window algorithm with atomic counters. Excess datagrams are silently dropped (standard UDP flood mitigation — there is no equivalent of an HTTP 429 response in plain UDP). By default (`direction: both`) client-to-backend and backend-to-client datagrams count toward the same per-client window.

Applies to UDP and DTLS stream proxies only. A proxy- or proxy-group-scoped attachment whose effective targets include a TCP/TCP+TLS or HTTP-family proxy is refused during configuration admission and plugin-cache validation, the mirror of `tcp_connection_throttle`'s rule, instead of loading as protection that never runs. A global policy keeps per-protocol filtering, so in a mixed deployment it applies to the UDP/DTLS listeners only.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `datagrams_per_second` | u64 (optional) | — | Sustained datagram rate per second per client IP. The effective per-window cap is `datagrams_per_second × window_seconds`. With the default `direction: both`, client-to-backend and backend-to-client datagrams count against the same cap. |
| `bytes_per_second` | u64 (optional) | — | Sustained payload-byte rate per second per client IP (sum of datagram payload sizes). The effective per-window cap is `bytes_per_second × window_seconds`. With the default `direction: both`, both directions count against the same cap. |
| `window_seconds` | u64 | `1` | Window length in seconds. Range 1–2678400 (31 days). The effective per-window cap is `datagrams_per_second × window_seconds` (and similarly for bytes). |
| `ipv6_prefix` | u64 | `64` | IPv6 prefix length (1–128) that groups client addresses into one budget, the same contract as `rate_limiting`'s `ipv6_prefix`. Widen it (for example `56` or `48`) so a client rotating source addresses across a delegated prefix cannot multiply its budget or fill the state map. IPv4 and IPv4-mapped IPv6 clients stay host-specific. Part of the effective semantics: changing it starts fresh state. |
| `direction` | String | `both` | Which datagrams are counted and limited: `both` (one combined budget for requests and responses), `client_to_backend`, or `backend_to_client`. A one-direction policy neither counts nor drops datagrams travelling the other way. Part of the effective semantics: changing it starts fresh state. |
| `sync_mode` | String | `local` | `local` (in-memory per instance) or `redis` (centralized). Parsed case-insensitively (`LOCAL`, `Redis`); `redis` requires `redis_url`. |
| `redis_url`, `redis_tls`, `redis_pool_size`, `redis_connect_timeout_seconds`, `redis_health_check_interval_seconds`, `redis_username`, `redis_password` | — | — | Shared [Redis connection options](#redis-connection-options); `redis_url` database selector `0`–`2147483647`. |
| `redis_key_prefix` | String | `{FERRUM_NAMESPACE}:udp_rate_limiting:{plugin-config-id}` | Redis key namespace prefix. Defaults to the gateway namespace, the plugin name, and this plugin config's stable resource id (for example `ferrum:udp_rate_limiting:rl-public-api`), so two independent policies of this type in one namespace never share counters. Must be non-empty when set; setting it explicitly is the documented opt-in for a deliberately shared budget. |
| `redis_failure_policy` | String | `fail_closed` | Behavior when the centralized store cannot be consulted (outage, egress/DNS screen failure, or an endpoint rejected as Redis Cluster). `fail_closed` drops the datagram; `local_fallback` explicitly opts into per-process budgets for availability. Only meaningful when `sync_mode: "redis"`, but validated in either mode |

> **Note:** When `redis_tls` is enabled, CA certificate verification and skip-verify behavior are controlled by the gateway-level `FERRUM_TLS_CA_BUNDLE_PATH` and `FERRUM_TLS_NO_VERIFY` environment variables, not per-plugin settings. A configured CA bundle is exclusive: if the path is set and verification is on, a load failure refuses plugin construction instead of falling back to system/public roots. `FERRUM_TLS_NO_VERIFY=true` remains the sanctioned skip-verify path and does not treat an unloadable CA as a construction error.

At least one of `datagrams_per_second` or `bytes_per_second` must be set; if both are configured each is enforced independently and the first to trip drops the datagram. Unknown top-level keys are rejected. A configured rate times `window_seconds` that overflows an unsigned 64-bit integer is refused at construction (a residual the OpenAPI schema cannot express).
IP-based keys group IPv6 addresses by `ipv6_prefix` (default `/64`); IPv4 and
IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses share one per-address budget. The key is the masked
client address itself, derived from the typed address the session computed once
at admission, so no datagram parses, formats, or allocates a key on the local
path (the `ip:<address>` text form is built only when Redis is consulted).

**Counter storage** (`sync_mode`): UDP rate-limit counters support `local` and `redis` only. Database-backed counters are intentionally unsupported. Redis mode centralizes datagram and byte counters across data planes; it uses the same `redis_failure_policy` and Cluster screening as `rate_limiting`. Counting is a **plain fixed window** (`{prefix:key}:datagrams|bytes:{window_index}`, one counter per configured window with no previous-window term at all) — neither the sub-bucketed trailing window nor the weighted approximation — so a datagram flood may straddle a window boundary and spend two consecutive windows' budgets back to back. While the centralized store is unavailable the default `fail_closed` policy drops the datagram (a datagram has no error channel, so failing closed *is* the drop) and counts each such drop in `ferrum_rate_limit_enforcement_unavailable_total` — not in `ferrum_rate_limit_exceeded_total`, so an outage is never silent traffic loss and never mistaken for clients over their limit. `local_fallback` is the explicit opt-in to per-process counters. The datagram and byte keys of one client share a hash tag so their transaction is slot-stable.

> **Redis sizing and eviction policy.** In Redis mode every distinct client key (after `ipv6_prefix` grouping) creates its own counter keys, and UDP sources are unauthenticated and spoofable, so the *centralized* key population is driven by the traffic — the 100,000-entry cap below bounds only the local/fallback map. Every counter key is written with its TTL (`window_seconds + 1`) in the same `MULTI`/`EXEC` that increments it, so stale keys always expire, but a long window keeps keys for that long. Run these counters on a Redis whose `maxmemory-policy` is `noeviction` (ideally a dedicated database or instance, sized for the expected distinct-source count × windows in flight). Under an evicting policy (`allkeys-*` or `volatile-*`; every counter has a TTL, so `volatile-*` applies) memory pressure can evict a live counter mid-window and restart that client's budget — a silent fail-open. Under `noeviction` the same pressure surfaces as write errors, which the configured `redis_failure_policy` handles visibly. Ferrum does not probe the server's eviction policy for rate-limit clients; this is an operator requirement.

> **Redis-mode throughput.** Each counted datagram awaits one Redis transaction (`INCR`/`INCRBY` + `EXPIRE`) before it is forwarded. Established plain-UDP sessions run client-to-backend hooks on one FIFO worker per session, and backend-to-client hooks on that session's reply task, so a single session is bounded near **one datagram per Redis round trip per direction** (for example about 1,000–2,000 datagrams per second at a 0.5–1 ms RTT) regardless of the configured rate, and every datagram gains that latency. Bursts beyond it fill the bounded per-session hook queue (256 datagrams / 256 KiB) and are dropped fail-closed as `hook_ingress_drops`, not as rate-limit drops. `redis_pool_size` parallelizes across sessions, not within one. Prefer `sync_mode: local` (per-gateway budgets) for high-rate single flows; use Redis mode where a shared cross-gateway budget matters more than per-flow throughput.

```yaml
plugin_name: udp_rate_limiting
config:
  datagrams_per_second: 1000
  bytes_per_second: 1048576
  window_seconds: 4
```

With `window_seconds: 4` this admits 4000 datagrams and 4194304 payload bytes per window, not 1000 datagrams / 1048576 bytes per window — the configured values are per-second rates.

**Memory protection:** The plugin tracks per-client state in a `DashMap` capped at 100,000 entries. Resident entry count is maintained by an `AtomicUsize` coordinated with insert and remove (expiry prune), so steady per-datagram capacity checks never call `DashMap::len()` or take every state-shard read lock — including Redis mode, which still observes only the atomic local/fallback count. Hard cardinality is enforced by atomic reservation on admission: existing client IPs continue at capacity, and previously unseen local/fallback IPs are dropped fail-closed without inserting state. Cleanup never force-evicts still-active budgets (that would reset consumed windows). Stale entries (idle for `window_seconds × 2`, minimum 10 seconds) are pruned by a sampled periodic sweep (every 100,000 datagram hooks) even while the map is below the hard cap. Once the map is **full** (at the cap — atomic admission never lets it grow past it), every datagram hook observes capacity pressure and reclaims idle keys at most once per second, before that datagram's own admission, so a map filled by clients that have since gone idle reopens to new clients within a second instead of waiting for the next sampled sweep. Both sweep paths share an atomic `compare_exchange` gate so concurrent scans cannot pile up under load, and Redis-fallback local maps use the same below-cap prune / atomic admission rules.

**Direction handling:** With the default `direction: both`, both directions update the same per-client window, capping total UDP traffic per client IP (which also bounds reflected responses). For request-response protocols this means the effective request rate is roughly half the configured datagram rate, and response bytes consume the byte budget. Set `direction: client_to_backend` to budget only inbound traffic (or `backend_to_client` for responses only); the other direction is then neither counted nor dropped. To limit each direction separately, attach two instances with different `direction` values.

**Established sessions and reloads:** A UDP/DTLS session binds its datagram-hook list once, at first-datagram admission. Before each later datagram's side effects (and again after its hooks await), the session compares the published configuration generation with the one it last verified (two atomic loads while nothing changed). When the generation moves, it compares a **policy digest** of the proxy's datagram-hook plugins — each plugin config's namespace, id, kind, scope and target, priority override, trigger, and config document, in chain order, computed once when the plugin cache builds the proxy's entry — with the digest it was admitted under. When a reload changes that policy — adding, removing, reordering, or reconfiguring `udp_rate_limiting` or any other datagram plugin — the session is **ended** and the datagram is dropped; the client's next datagram is admitted as a new session under the current policy (stream-connect chain, trigger decisions, and hook list), so a tightened limit applies to existing flows within one datagram. A plain-UDP client sees a new backend source port; a DTLS-terminating client must handshake again. Compatible reloads keep local counters (see **Local counters survive a compatible reload**), so a re-admitted client keeps its consumed budget. Reloads that leave the proxy's datagram-hook configs unchanged do not end sessions — including full reloads that reconstruct every plugin instance (file-mode `SIGHUP`, a data plane's full control-plane snapshot, a database-mode full reload). Changes to non-datagram plugins (for example stream-connect auth) are not re-applied to established sessions. A global `udp_rate_limiting` whose effective targets include no UDP/DTLS proxy logs a warning that it is inert.

**Rejection diagnostics:** Count- and byte-limit drops still increment the existing per-rejection metrics/counters, but tracing warnings are bounded per plugin instance and process-wide. Each rejection first increments lock-free pending aggregates at both scopes. A warning is emitted only after both the instance and global monotonic one-second gates admit it, so each instance emits at most one summary per second and all configured instances together emit at most one. If the global gate denies an instance, neither pending aggregate is cleared; the counts carry into a later summary. Concurrent events may fall into the current or next summary depending on the counter-swap boundary, but they are not discarded, and counters saturate at `u64::MAX` rather than wrapping. Warnings identify only the configured `proxy_id` and a static `limit_kind` (`datagram_count` or `byte_count`) — never client addresses, payloads, or usage snapshots.

---

## Mesh and Alert Plugins

These plugins are registered built-ins even when they are most often generated or auto-injected by mesh mode.

### `mesh_authz`

**Priority:** 2075 · **Phases:** `authorize`, `before_proxy`, `after_proxy`, `apply_websocket_handshake_response_headers`, `on_stream_connect` · **Protocols:** HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, TCP, UDP · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Applies Istio-style mesh authorization (`MeshPolicy` ALLOW / DENY / AUDIT / CUSTOM) to the SPIFFE identity established by the `spiffe_identity` plugin or carried in the HBONE baggage of an ambient mTLS stream. It runs in the `authorize` phase at priority **2075** (after authentication, after `access_control`, before `opa`) and in `on_stream_connect` for Layer-4 sessions, so it covers every protocol family in the matrix: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, gRPC, WebSocket, raw TCP/TLS, and UDP/DTLS. Its failure policy is `FailClosed`.

Mesh mode auto-injects it as the reserved global `__mesh_authz` on every applicable topology, carrying a `mesh_slice`. Operators can also configure it directly on a non-mesh gateway with a flat `mesh_policies` list; that is the form documented here. An operator-managed global `mesh_authz` suppresses ordinary injection of `__mesh_authz`. Transparent inbound capture is the exception: because it admits unauthenticated direct plaintext, capture keeps the operator instance (enabled or disabled) and additionally force-injects the slice-fed `__mesh_authz`, so both run. Native/xDS MeshSlice feeds do not currently carry operator plugin configs, so this override applies only where plugin configs reach mesh preparation directly; configuring a plugin with the reserved `__mesh_authz` id yourself is not a supported override, because mesh preparation replaces that row with the mesh-managed instance.

**Evaluation order.** DENY rules are evaluated first and the first match wins. `CUSTOM` delegations run before the DENY/ALLOW tiers. If any ALLOW rule is loaded and none matches, the request is denied by the implicit-deny floor (`mesh_authz.deny_policy=implicit-deny`). A configuration with no policies at all evaluates nothing and allows every request — an empty `mesh_policies: []` is a valid scaffold, not a lockdown.

**Configuration.** Unknown top-level keys are rejected at construction, and a non-object, non-null `config` (a string, number, or array) is rejected too — a misspelled `mesh_policies` or a malformed root would otherwise build a policy-free instance whose implicit-deny floor never engages, allowing every request. The eleven accepted keys:

| Key | Type | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mesh_policies` | Array of `MeshPolicy` | `[]` | Operator-facing policy list, used when no slice is available. See [MeshPolicy](mesh.md#meshpolicy) for the document shape and [Rule Matching](mesh.md#rule-matching) for the matcher semantics. A `CUSTOM` rule here always denies: a flat list carries no `extensionProviders` source. |
| `namespace` | String | `""` | This proxy workload's namespace, used by the construction-time `PolicyScope` filter. Overrides any namespace embedded in `mesh_slice`. Must be a string. |
| `labels` | Object of string → string | `{}` | This proxy workload's labels, used by the scope filter for `WorkloadSelector`-scoped policies. Overrides any labels embedded in `mesh_slice`, and clears the slice's shared-SPIFFE ambiguity marker — supplying it asserts these are the workload's authoritative labels. |
| `trust_domain_aliases` | Array of trust-domain strings, or `null` | `[]` | Additional SPIFFE trust domains accepted as equivalent to the peer certificate's own when authorizing HBONE baggage `source.principal`. Empty (the default) means strict same-trust-domain match. Each entry must be a valid trust domain; `null` is treated as absent. |
| `trusted_hbone_assertors` | Array of strings or objects, or `null` | `["ztunnel", "waypoint"]` | Identity-asserting infrastructure whose HBONE baggage may rewrite the authz principal. Absent or `null` restores the built-in defaults; an explicit `[]` disables baggage rewriting entirely. Matching a peer is necessary but **not** sufficient — see [Trusted HBONE Assertors](mesh.md#trusted-hbone-assertors) for the per-entry grant contract. |
| `per_pod_policy_scoping` | Boolean | `false` | Skips the construction-time scope filter and resolves policy scope per connection from the pod-scoped cache instead. Auto-set by mesh injection on `NodeWaypoint` topology, where one listener serves many pods. Must be a real boolean; a string or number is rejected rather than read as `false`. |
| `mesh_slice` | Object | — | **Injection-only.** The embedded mesh slice: the filtered policy set plus the workload identity, ext-authz providers, and destination inventory. Operator-managed instances pass `mesh_policies` instead. |
| `ambient_udp_source_scoping` | Boolean | `false` | **Injection-only.** Enables node-waypoint ambient UDP source-policy scoping. Same strict boolean admission as `per_pod_policy_scoping`. |
| `cluster_domain` | String | `cluster.local` | **Injection-only.** Primary Kubernetes cluster domain, used for node-waypoint service-host matching. |
| `cluster_domains` | Array of strings | `[]` | **Injection-only.** Deduplicated cluster-domain aliases for the same host matching. |
| `node_waypoint_route_upstreams` | Array of objects | `[]` | **Injection-only.** Mesh-generated route upstream metadata used to precompute destination policy scopes for node-waypoint dispatch. |

The five injection-only keys are populated by mesh mode and are documented here only so an operator reading a live `/plugins` response can identify them; do not hand-author them.

**Direct policy example.** A namespace-scoped policy that denies `/admin` and every path under `/admin/` outright and otherwise allows only one service account. Both patterns are needed: `/admin/*` is a prefix match on `/admin/`, so it does not match the bare `/admin` path.

```yaml
plugin_name: mesh_authz
config:
  namespace: "default"
  labels:
    app: "payments"
  mesh_policies:
    - name: "deny-admin"
      namespace: "default"
      scope:
        kind: namespace
        namespace: "default"
      rules:
        - action: deny
          to:
            - paths: ["/admin", "/admin/*"]
    - name: "allow-checkout"
      namespace: "default"
      scope:
        kind: namespace
        namespace: "default"
      rules:
        - action: allow
          from:
            - spiffe_id_pattern: "spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/checkout"
```

**Strict configuration admission.** The policy grammar is closed at every level — the policy, its `scope` (each `kind` admits only its own members, including `kind: mesh_wide`), each target-ref attachment, each rule, its workload selector, each `from` / `to` / `when` / `source_negation` matcher, and the `custom` action object reject unknown members — and `action` is **required** on every rule. The injection-only objects are closed too: the `mesh_slice` root, its `ext_authz_providers` entries (with their `include_additional_headers_in_check` and `include_request_body_in_check` objects), its `peer_authentications` and `request_authentications` entries (with their JWT rules), its `telemetry_resources` entries, its `multi_cluster` object (with its remote-cluster and east-west-gateway entries), and each `node_waypoint_route_upstreams` entry and target. Misspellings remove a restriction rather than adding one: `not_paths` typed `not_path` would deserialize as an unconstrained rule, and `action` typed `actoin` would fall back to the `Allow` default and turn a DENY into a grant. Both fail admission with a field-specific diagnostic.

**Never-match matchers are refused.** Construction also runs the same per-policy matcher validation a mesh document gets from `MeshConfig::validate`, on both the flat `mesh_policies` form and an embedded `mesh_slice`: a `to.headers` pseudo-header (`:path`, `:method`, `:authority`, `:scheme` — use `to.paths` / `to.methods` / `to.hosts`, or `when: request.headers[:path]`), an invalid `hosts` / `not_hosts` pattern, an inadmissible `port_patterns` / `not_port_patterns` entry (for example `70000*` or `8*0`), an empty `from: [{}]` or `to: [{}]` entry, and an empty policy `name` / `namespace` are rejected with a field-specific diagnostic. Each would otherwise be accepted and never match — fail-open for a DENY.

**Repeated headers.** A header the client sends as several field lines is judged as ONE value — every line joined with `, ` (`; ` for `cookie`) — by `to.headers`, `when: request.headers[...]`, and the headers forwarded to a `CUSTOM` provider alike, independent of whether anything materialized the headers first. See [Rule Matching](mesh.md#rule-matching).

Plugin-written case variants use the shared [request-map folding rule](#plugin-written-request-header-names), so those authorization surfaces and backend egress select the same value.

**Trusted identity is required for identity-constrained rules.** `mesh_authz` authorizes the identity another plugin established; it does not authenticate. Without the `spiffe_identity` plugin (or an authenticated HBONE peer), `source_principal` is absent, so every rule carrying a nonempty positive `from` source-principal constraint misses, and a policy set whose ALLOW rules all carry such constraints denies everything. An ALLOW rule with no source-principal (or request-principal / source-negation) constraint is unconstrained and still matches an anonymous request — intentional Istio-style semantics — unless an independent DENY or CUSTOM refusal applies. Deploy it behind mesh mTLS, not on a plaintext listener.

**Layer-4 sessions.** A raw TCP/TLS/UDP/DTLS session carries no HTTP request, so HTTP-only fields (`to.operation` methods/paths/hosts/headers, `request_principals`, `when: request.*`) are unsourceable there. Following Istio, a `DENY` or `CUSTOM` rule ignores an unsourceable field and still matches on its remaining constraints, while an `ALLOW` or `AUDIT` rule can never match on it. Scope such rules with `to.ports` when the workload also serves non-HTTP ports. On an HTTP-family request a header the client simply did not send is **absent**, not unsourceable, and fails a positive `to.headers` predicate for every action — see [Rule Matching](mesh.md#rule-matching).

**CUSTOM delegation.** `action: {custom: {provider: <name>}}` delegates the decision to a `meshConfig.extensionProviders` entry carried on the mesh slice. Each check carries the gateway-asserted caller identity (`x-ferrum-source-principal`, `x-ferrum-source-namespace`, `x-ferrum-source-service-account`, `x-ferrum-request-principal`), which a client cannot forge. On an allowed check, `headersToUpstreamOnAllow` is applied to the backend request in this plugin's `before_proxy` hook (the listed names are provider-owned: client copies are always removed) and `headersToDownstreamOnAllow` to the backend response in its `after_proxy` hook (`Set-Cookie` appended); repeated provider response headers (two `Set-Cookie` lines on a denial) are all preserved. A direct flat `mesh_policies` configuration carries no provider source, so its CUSTOM rules have no bound provider and always refuse with a fixed `403` — whether an (empty-provider) executor exists depends on the construction path: the normal plugin factory builds one, which denies the unbound provider as `provider_unbound`, while the no-HTTP-client seam has no executor and takes the other fixed-403 branch. A provider that does not bind likewise refuses with a fixed `403` that no provider's `failOpen` can admit. See [AuthorizationPolicy `action: CUSTOM`](mesh.md#authorizationpolicy-action-custom-issue-3235) in the mesh guide for the outcome vocabulary, the failure table, and the process-wide in-flight budget.

See [Authorization](mesh.md#authorization), [MeshPolicy](mesh.md#meshpolicy), [Trusted HBONE Assertors](mesh.md#trusted-hbone-assertors), and [plugin execution order](plugin_execution_order.md#why-this-order-matters).

### `mesh_route_dispatch`

**Priority:** 2995 · **Phases:** `before_proxy` · **Protocols:** HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket · **Failure policy:** `FailClosed`

Applies per-request route overrides generated from mesh/Istio routing resources. It runs in `before_proxy` after authentication and admission plugins, so policy evaluates the original public proxy identity before the backend override is applied. For WebSockets, the override selects the upgrade backend only; individual frames are not re-routed.

```yaml
plugin_name: mesh_route_dispatch
scope: proxy
proxy_id: reviews
config:
  rules:
    - match:
        uri:
          prefix: /reviews/legacy
      redirect:
        uri: /reviews/v2
        match_prefix: /reviews/legacy
        redirect_code: 301
```

Full configuration reference, behavior, and examples: [plugins/mesh_route_dispatch.md](plugins/mesh_route_dispatch.md).

#### Route request deadline

Moved to [plugins/mesh_route_dispatch.md — Route request deadline](plugins/mesh_route_dispatch.md#route-request-deadline).

### `proxy_alerts`

**Priority:** 9250 · **Phases:** `log`, `on_stream_disconnect`, `on_ws_disconnect` · **Protocols:** HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, TCP, UDP · **Failure policy:** `OptionalFailOpen`

Evaluates in-gateway anomaly rules over completed HTTP/gRPC, stream, and WebSocket transactions, then sends notifications through configured channels. It is a normal operator-configurable plugin. HTTP status rules stay independent of terminal gRPC application status; use `grpc_status_count` / `grpc_status_rate` for RPC outcome alerts.

Incident lifecycle (Trigger → Active → Recovering → Resolve) is tracked per `(rule, proxy, channel)`, so a channel that missed an event retries it independently of its siblings; an in-flight reminder holds recovery until it settles; and a 5-second background re-evaluation resolves incidents on proxies that stopped receiving traffic. Webhook/email templates get a stable `${incident_key}`, scoped to the plugin-config id, for receiver-side Trigger/Resolve correlation (PagerDuty `dedup_key`). State is per gateway node — count thresholds see only one replica's traffic.

**Admission / failure policy.** `proxy_alerts` is registered `OptionalFailOpen` (see [Config admission and failure policy](#config-admission-and-failure-policy)). `ferrum-edge validate` can therefore exit 0 with optional-plugin warnings; operators must inspect those warnings to verify the alert instance is active.

See [Proxy Alerts](proxy_alerts.md) for rule types, channel configuration, templates, tuning guidance, and the constructor-versus-OpenAPI admission notes.

### `workload_metrics`

**Priority:** 9360 · **Phases:** `on_request_received`, `before_proxy`, `after_proxy`, `log`, `on_stream_connect`, `on_stream_disconnect` · **Protocols:** HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, TCP, UDP · **Failure policy:** `OptionalFailOpen`

Adds Istio/GAMMA workload identity labels to request, stream, and log metadata, and can emit mesh telemetry spans when mesh Telemetry providers are configured. Mesh mode auto-injects this plugin when workload metrics are needed, but standalone use is supported for non-mesh gateway deployments that want the same identity labels.

HBONE `source.principal` attribution uses the same trusted-assertor relation as `mesh_authz`. Direct / user-created instances honor that relation from this plugin's own `trusted_hbone_assertors` / `trust_domain_aliases` config. Mesh injection additionally stamps an internal `_effective_mesh_authz_baggage_gates` list that is an exact, fail-closed conjunction of every enabled global `mesh_authz` baggage gate PluginCache will execute (including a force-injected reserved `__mesh_authz` under transparent inbound capture), plus every enabled proxy- or proxy-group-scoped `mesh_authz` gate (a scoped instance replaces the global one on its routes, and this global instance cannot vary per proxy); a deduplicated set above 16 gates becomes a single `trusted_hbone_assertors: []` lockdown gate. Disabled operator rows are omitted; each gate keeps its own absent/null/default, explicit `[]`, and alias contract; a sibling cannot silently widen another gate. Malformed or over-bound internal lists fail construction. The baggage itself is read exactly as `mesh_authz` reads it — every pristine wire field-line plus the folded request map — and at `before_proxy` only the wire field-lines count while they are held, so a `baggage` header added by a request transform after authorization is never honored. See [Trusted HBONE Assertors](mesh.md#trusted-hbone-assertors).

Configuration must be an object. Unknown top-level keys and wrong types for recognized fields are rejected at construction, including non-string map values and string-valued disable flags. Every disable alias must be boolean even when a higher-precedence alias is present. `workload_metrics` uses OptionalFailOpen: file/runtime validation warns and omits an invalid optional instance; direct admin admission rejects it. Omit fields for defaults; null is supported only where explicitly listed below.

#### Standalone configuration

This complete file-mode example labels requests and exports sampled spans to an OTLP/HTTP collector. Point the backend and collector URLs at your services; the collector must accept OTLP JSON at `/v1/traces`.

```yaml
version: "1"
proxies:
  - id: reviews
    name: reviews
    listen_path: /reviews
    backend_scheme: http
    backend_host: 127.0.0.1
    backend_port: 8081
plugin_configs:
  - id: reviews-telemetry
    plugin_name: workload_metrics
    scope: global
    enabled: true
    config:
      namespace: default
      workload_spiffe_id: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/gateway
      labels:
        app: gateway
      sampling_percentage: 100
      custom_tags:
        deployment_region: local
      tracing_provider:
        kind: opentelemetry
        config:
          endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/traces
      batch_size: 50
      flush_interval_ms: 5000
      metrics:
        tag_overrides:
          - metric: REQUEST_COUNT
            name: destination_service
            operation:
              type: set
              value: reviews
          - metric: REQUEST_DURATION
            name: response_code
            operation:
              type: set_expr
              cel: string(response.code)
```

The plugin stamps metric plans; configure `prometheus_metrics` to export those metric families. Standalone workload labels are hints and do not authenticate a remote peer. With no listener direction, source labels describe the configured local workload and destination labels describe the routed proxy.

| Field | Type / default | Admission and behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `node_id`, `topology` | String; omitted | Optional `mesh.node_id` / `mesh.topology` hints. Blank strings are treated as absent. |
| `namespace` | String; omitted | Local workload namespace and fallback span service-name suffix. Blank means absent. |
| `workload_spiffe_id` | String; omitted | Valid SPIFFE ID, or blank for no identity hint. |
| `labels` | String map; `{}` | Workload label hints. Workload chooses the first nonblank `service.istio.io/canonical-name`, `app.kubernetes.io/name`, `app`, `k8s-app`, or `workload`, then SPIFFE service account, then `unknown`. App chooses `app.kubernetes.io/name`, `app`, or `k8s-app`; service chooses `service.istio.io/canonical-name`, `service`, or `app`; both fall back to workload. Other keys are accepted but unused. |
| `trusted_hbone_assertors` | Array or null; `[ztunnel, waypoint]` | Strings name service accounts or exact SPIFFE IDs; objects specify `assertor` with optional `asserts` or `scope`. Omitted/null uses defaults; `[]` trusts no baggage assertors. See [trusted assertor rules](mesh.md#trusted-hbone-assertors). |
| `trust_domain_aliases` | String array or null; `[]` | Valid SPIFFE trust domains treated as equivalent for baggage attribution. Null means empty. |
| `sampling_percentage` | Number; omitted | Inclusive 0–100. Omission leaves new roots unsampled. Valid upstream W3C/B3 sampling decisions take precedence; metric/graph recording is independent of sampling. |
| `custom_tags` | String map; `{}` | Literal transaction and span tags; values at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes. |
| `custom_header_tags` | String map; `{}` | Tag name → valid HTTP header name. Source names are normalized; sensitive headers are rejected, including credential-class names such as `x-session-id` and `x-csrf`, a `pat` (personal access token) segment such as `x-pat`, and a terminal `auth` segment such as `x-basic-auth`. A present value of at most 1024 bytes overrides the literal/environment fallback; absent or oversized headers leave the fallback. A header not declared in `safe_tag_sources` is copied as `[REDACTED]`. Streams have no request headers. |
| `custom_env_tags` | String map; `{}` | Tag name → portable environment name (`[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`, at most 256 bytes). Resolved in the data-plane process at construction/reload. Present values, including empty strings, override literals; missing variables retain literals or omit the tag. Non-UTF-8 or oversized values reject construction. Sensitive variable names are rejected, including every credential class the metadata redactor recognizes (`GPG_PASSPHRASE`, `HSM_PIN`, `USER_SESSION_ID`, …), a `PAT` segment (`GITHUB_PAT`), and a terminal `AUTH` segment (`BASIC_AUTH`; a non-terminal `AUTH_TYPE` stays allowed). A variable not declared in `safe_tag_sources` is emitted as `[REDACTED]`. |
| `safe_tag_sources` | String[]; `[]` | Header names (case-insensitive) and environment variable names (case-sensitive) whose values `custom_header_tags` / `custom_env_tags` may copy verbatim (at most 64 entries of at most 256 bytes). Every undeclared source is copied as `[REDACTED]` (fail closed). Credential-shaped entries are rejected; diagnostics name only the entry index. Tag values in transaction logs additionally need the tag name in `FERRUM_LOG_SAFE_METADATA_KEYS`. |
| `metrics` | Object; `{}` | Optional `disabled_metrics` array and `tag_overrides` array. The object, each `tag_overrides` entry, and each `operation` are closed: unknown keys, and keys another operation `type` reads, are rejected. See operations below. |
| `tracing_provider` | Provider object or null; omitted | Singular fallback; ignored whenever `tracing_providers` is present. Null means no provider. |
| `tracing_providers` | Provider array or null; omitted | Fan-out to each configured exporter. Present null or `[]` selects no exporters, including when the singular field is set. A `zipkin` provider also turns on B3 propagation: the active span is injected as `x-b3-*` headers beside W3C `traceparent` (B3 is always refreshed from the active span when the backend request still carries B3). Spans refused at enqueue or discarded at delivery (`reason="export_failed"`) are counted on `ferrum_mesh_tracing_spans_dropped_total{provider,reason}`. |
| `allow_plaintext` | Boolean; omitted | Admit a cleartext `http://` provider URL whose host is not a loopback IP literal (`127.d.d.d` or `[::1]`). Without it, such a provider fails construction. Mesh injection writes `true` whenever a translated Telemetry/MeshConfig provider uses `http://`, so in-cluster collectors keep working and the cleartext posture stays visible in the injected config. |
| `direction_emit` | Object or null; `{server: true, client: false}` | Boolean `server` and `client` members select inbound SERVER and outbound CLIENT spans; omitted members use those defaults. Unstamped direction uses `server`. Null selects defaults; unknown members are rejected. |
| `span_reporting_disabled` | Boolean; `false` | Suppresses span export while preserving configuration and trace-context propagation (W3C, and B3 under a Zipkin provider). No span is built while export is inactive. |
| `disable_span_reporting`, `disableSpanReporting` | Boolean; omitted | Aliases, in decreasing precedence after `span_reporting_disabled`. First present spelling wins, including explicit false. |
| `service_name` | String; derived | Defaults to `ferrum-edge-mesh-<namespace>` for a nonblank namespace, otherwise `ferrum-edge-mesh`. Active exporters require a nonblank explicit value and trim it. |
| `deployment_environment` | String; omitted | Exported `deployment.environment` resource attribute. Active exporters require a nonblank value and trim it. |
| `batch_size` | Unsigned integer; `50` | Active exporter range: 1–10000 spans per batch. |
| `flush_interval_ms` | Unsigned integer; `5000` | Active exporter range: 100–600000 milliseconds. |
| `buffer_capacity` | Unsigned integer; `10000` | Active exporter range: 1–100000 queued spans. |
| `buffer_max_bytes` | Unsigned integer; `16777216` | Active exporter range: 65536–268435456 retained queue bytes; also subject to the process-wide observability byte ceiling. |
| `max_retries` | Unsigned integer; `2` | Active exporter range: 0–10 retries. |
| `retry_delay_ms` | Unsigned integer; `1000` | Active exporter range: 0–60000 milliseconds; retry backoff follows the shared exporter policy. |
| `_effective_mesh_authz_baggage_gates` | Internal object array; omitted | Mesh injection only: 1–16 objects, each containing only `trusted_hbone_assertors` and/or `trust_domain_aliases`, with the same null/default contracts as above. Direct instances normally omit this field. |

Exporter-specific ranges, nonblank resource names, endpoint validation, and Lightstep credential lookup apply when at least one provider is selected and span reporting is enabled. Numeric options always require unsigned 64-bit integer values. Sampling at zero does not disable exporter admission.

Custom names contain 1–128 ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `_`, or `-`; reserved telemetry names and sensitive names are rejected. The union across the three tag maps and all effective instances on a proxy is limited to 32 distinct names, including potentially triggered instances. Exceeding the effective-chain bound rejects publication. Executed instances compose their allowed names for every exporter; later values win for names they stamp. Empty or skipped instances do not remove earlier names. Within an instance, precedence is present valid header > resolved environment > literal fallback. A header-backed tag clears its previous value when restamped, so without its own fallback an absent header does not retain a stale earlier value.

Direct providers use these envelopes (they are different from Istio's name-only provider references):

| `kind` | Required `config` fields | Optional fields / behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `opentelemetry` | `endpoint` string | OTLP/HTTP JSON; supply the complete `/v1/traces` URL. |
| `zipkin` | `url` string | Zipkin v2 JSON; supply the complete `/api/v2/spans` URL. |
| `datadog` | `agent_url` string | Optional `service` string or null overrides the span service name; the exporter appends `/v0.3/traces` if needed. |
| `lightstep` | `collector_url`, `access_token_env` strings | OTLP with a local environment bearer token; `access_token_env` must name a `FERRUM_PLUGIN_SECRET_<NAME>` variable (any other variable is refused at admission, even while span reporting is disabled). `accessTokenEnv` is an accepted alias, but supplying both spellings is an error. |

Provider objects require `kind` and `config`; unknown keys in the envelope or in `config` are rejected. Active endpoint URLs must be absolute HTTP(S), have a host, and contain no embedded credentials. Lightstep's variable must be readable and its value valid for the bearer header.

`metrics.disabled_metrics` accepts `ALL_METRICS`, `REQUEST_COUNT`, `REQUEST_DURATION`, `REQUEST_SIZE`, `RESPONSE_SIZE`, `TCP_OPENED_CONNECTIONS`, `TCP_CLOSED_CONNECTIONS`, `TCP_SENT_BYTES`, `TCP_RECEIVED_BYTES`, `GRPC_REQUEST_MESSAGES`, `GRPC_RESPONSE_MESSAGES`, or the corresponding `ferrum_mesh_*` names. Selectors are trimmed and case-insensitive. Unknown names fail direct construction; Istio translation separately warns and omits recognized families Ferrum does not emit.

Each `metrics.tag_overrides` entry requires `name` and `operation`; optional `metric` uses the same selectors, with omitted/null meaning all metrics. Names and rename targets must belong to the fixed mesh label vocabulary (Istio underscore or Ferrum `mesh.*` spelling), which includes `grpc_response_status` for the HTTP/gRPC families. Operations are `remove`, `rename` with string `new_name`, `set` with string `value` (at most 256 UTF-8 bytes), or `set_expr` with exactly one of string `cel` or compiled `expression` (supplying both is rejected). CEL uses the [bounded mesh attribute language](mesh.md#telemetry-api): at most 512 source bytes, 32 tokens, depth 8, and 24 AST nodes. Compiled ASTs require the operation-specific fields shown in OpenAPI and reject unknown fields. HTTP-only attributes cannot target TCP or all metrics. At most 128 entries and 16384 encoded plan bytes are admitted per instance and across the surviving effective family plans. Later instances replace only the families they configure.

The HTTP-family service graph records each terminal client transaction once across effective instances, using final metadata and the memoized execution triggers. HTTP errors, transport/body failures, and nonzero finalized gRPC status contribute to error totals; mirror attempts are excluded. Each configured tracing exporter remains independent.

See [Mesh Observability](mesh.md#observability) for metric names, service graph aggregation, and tracing behavior.

### `__mesh_bpf_metrics`

**Priority:** 9365 · **Phases:** (no lifecycle hooks; passive Prometheus surface populated by the BPF SOCK_OPS event consumer) · **Protocols:** HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, TCP, UDP · **Failure policy:** `OptionalFailOpen`

Reserved internal plugin auto-injected only for mesh `NodeWaypoint` topology as a **global** instance. It exposes TCP-layer BPF SOCK_OPS counters and fixed-bucket SRTT, SYN-to-ACK, and captured accept-to-first-application-byte latency histograms on the Prometheus scrape surface. Operator-managed plugin configs should not create names prefixed with `__`. Mesh injection still uses this constructor: documenting the contract does not recommend creating the plugin by hand.

Enabled instances must use `scope: global`. Composition admits at most one enabled instance per process so authenticated `GET /metrics` never double-emits the surface. Disabled rows are not constructed and are ignored by that ownership check.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefix` | String | `ferrum_mesh_bpf` | Prometheus metric-name prefix applied to every emitted family (`{prefix}_tcp_events_total`, `{prefix}_drops_total`, `{prefix}_srtt_microseconds`, `{prefix}_syn_to_ack_microseconds`, `{prefix}_accept_to_first_byte_microseconds`, and the ringbuf families). Surrounding Unicode `White_Space` characters are trimmed before validation. After trimming the value must be a nonempty ASCII identifier matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`. There is no declared length limit beyond that grammar. Omit the key, or supply a non-object config, to keep the default. |

The config object is closed: unknown top-level keys are rejected at construction (for example a misspelled `prefx` cannot silently publish the default metric namespace). Non-object configs (`null`, string, array, number, boolean) keep the default prefix. Wrong-typed, empty, blank, or non-identifier `prefix` values fail construction.

An invalid enabled config is handled per [`OptionalFailOpen`](#config-admission-and-failure-policy); an omitted instance means the scrape surface is absent.

```yaml
plugin_name: __mesh_bpf_metrics
scope: global
enabled: true
config:
  prefix: tenantA_bpf
```

See [BPF SOCK_OPS observability](mesh.md#bpf-sock_ops-observability-gap-sc3) for emitted counters, histogram bucket bounds, pin retry behavior, and the node-agent/process split.

---

## Custom Plugins

Ferrum supports drop-in custom plugins. Create a `.rs` file in the `custom_plugins/` directory, export both the required `create_plugin()` factory function and the required `failure_policy()` metadata function, and rebuild — the build script auto-discovers and registers it. The generated registry calls every selected module's `failure_policy()`, so omitting it fails the build; see [CUSTOM_PLUGINS.md](../CUSTOM_PLUGINS.md) for the complete required-export recipe.

Optionally set `FERRUM_CUSTOM_PLUGINS=plugin_a,plugin_b` at **build time** to include only specific custom plugins. Pedagogical examples under `custom_plugins/examples/` are opt-in only (list them in `FERRUM_CUSTOM_PLUGINS`); default and Docker builds leave them out of the registry and migration collector.

Custom plugins can also declare database migrations via `plugin_migrations()` for creating private tables; see [migrations.md](migrations.md#custom-plugin-migrations).

See [CUSTOM_PLUGINS.md](../CUSTOM_PLUGINS.md) for the full developer guide, trait reference, and working examples.
